# Key Highlights: Strategies to achieve a carbon neutral society: a review

**Authors:** Lin Chen, Goodluck Msigwa, Mingyu Yang, Ahmed I. Osman, Samer Fawzy, David W. Rooney, Pow-Seng Yap
**Journal / Year:** Environmental Chemistry Letters, vol. 20, pp. 2277–2310 (2022) (2022)
**Official DOI:** [https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01435-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01435-8)

## Core Statistics & Results

| Metric | Finding / Significance |
| --- | --- |
| **4.5%** | of 198 countries have already reached carbon neutrality |
| **124** | countries declared net-zero aims for 2050 or 2060 (Feb 2021) |
| **8.24 PgC** | sink from low-carbon farming in South America, 2016–2050 |
| **1.09 °C** | warming, 1850–2022 (range 0.97–1.21 °C) |

## Important Findings & Key Takeaways

### 01. CO₂ is far above pre-industrial levels
Atmospheric CO₂ rose from about 285 ppm (around 1850) to about 419 ppm (2022).

*(Reference: p. 2278)*

### 02. Warming is already above 1 °C
The UK Met Office estimates 1.09 °C of warming over 1850–2022 (range 0.97–1.21 °C).

*(Reference: p. 2278)*

### 03. Few countries have reached neutrality
Only 4.5% of 198 countries have reached carbon neutrality; 60.6% (120 countries) aim for 2050–2070, and most target dates fall after 2050. India's target is 2070.

*(Reference: pp. 2281–2290, Table 1)*

### 04. COP26: coal, cars, cash and trees
Phase out coal, move to electric transport, deliver the US$100 billion a year pledged to developing countries, and protect forests.

*(Reference: pp. 2279–2280)*

### 05. Mapping tools
Input–output models, gridded spatial systems, GIS maps, LiDAR and LMDI-I map direct and indirect emissions.

*(Reference: pp. 2292–2296, Table 2)*

### 06. Three sectors, nearly 80% of CO₂
In a Chinese input–output study, power and heat supply, petroleum processing and coking, and metal mining caused nearly 80% of CO₂ emissions.

*(Reference: p. 2293 (Bai et al. 2018))*

### 07. Two routes to net zero
Cut emissions (policy plus sector technologies) and remove CO₂ (negative emission technologies and nature-based solutions).

*(Reference: p. 2296)*

### 08. Carbon pricing works
China's carbon trading (2008–2018 study) cut emissions sharply in several provinces; carbon-tax incentives can raise airline fuel efficiency.

*(Reference: p. 2297)*

### 09. Biogas to biomethane
Biomethane use in EU CNG and LNG vehicles is expected to reach 30 billion m³/yr by 2030.

*(Reference: p. 2300 (Prussi et al. 2019))*

### 10. Low-carbon farming is a large sink
In South America it could store 8.24 PgC (2016–2050) and add 17.6 Mt/yr of food and 1.6 Mt/yr of meat.

*(Reference: p. 2300 (Sa et al. 2017))*

### 11. Which practices matter most
Pasture restoration 31%, crop-livestock-forestry integration 25.6%, no-till 24.3%, forestation 12.8%, biological N fixation 4.2%, industrial organic waste recycling 2%.

*(Reference: p. 2300)*

### 12. Diet and food waste
An EU study found that a more vegetarian diet, less meat and less food waste mitigate climate change.

*(Reference: p. 2300 (Strapasson et al. 2020))*

### 13. Cheap and costly removal options
In Scotland, enhanced weathering cost the most (US$25–1600 per t CO₂); BECCS and forestation cost less; biochar and soil carbon sequestration could be cost-effective.

*(Reference: p. 2301 (Alcalde et al. 2018))*

### 14. Combine removal methods
A BECCS + soil carbon + enhanced weathering mix could cut 8.3–36.8 Mt CO₂, up to 89.8% of Scotland's annual emissions.

*(Reference: p. 2301)*

### 15. Start with energy
The first step is to shift from fossil fuels to renewables and low-carbon technologies, then electrify energy services and raise efficiency.

*(Reference: pp. 2305–2306)*

# Strategies to achieve a carbon neutral society: a review


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Strategies to achieve a carbon neutral society: a review Lin Chen, Goodluck Msigwa, Mingyu Yang, Ahmed I. Osman, Samer Fawzy, David W. Rooney, Pow- Seng Yap

**Authors:**
Lin Chen, Goodluck Msigwa, Mingyu Yang, Ahmed I. Osman, Samer Fawzy, David W. Rooney, Pow-Seng Yap

**Journal:**
Environmental Chemistry Letters, vol. 20, pp. 2277–2310 (2022)

**Dates:**
Received 2 March 2022 · Accepted 9 March 2022 · Published online 8 April 2022

**Paper type:**
Review article (open access, CC BY 4.0)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01435-8

**Cite as:**
Chen, L., Msigwa, G., Yang, M., Osman, A. I., Fawzy, S., Rooney, D. W., & Yap, P.-S. (2022). Strategies to achieve a carbon neutral society: a review. Environmental Chemistry Letters, 20, 2277–2310. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01435-8 Open access article under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0). Figures in this summary are quoted from the review; most come from the studies it cites.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Only 4.5% of 198 countries have reached carbon neutrality, and most others aim for dates after 2050. The review sets out how to get there: cut emissions with policy and sector technologies, remove CO₂ with negative emission technologies and nature-based solutions, map emissions to target effort, and check every option with life cycle analysis.


## 1. Background

Industrial growth and heavy use of fossil fuels have released large amounts of greenhouse gases. The paper reports that atmospheric CO₂ rose from about 285 ppm around 1850 to about 419 ppm in 2022. Over 1850–2022 the UK Met Office estimates a rise in global average surface temperature of 0.97 to 1.21 °C, with a central estimate of 1.09 °C. Global GHG emissions are expected to rise by 50% by 2050, mainly from CO₂ from non-renewable energy. Under the Paris Agreement, adopted on 12 December 2015 by 197 parties, countries agreed to keep warming below 2 °C and to work to limit it to 1.5 °C. By February 2021, 124 countries had declared that they intend to become carbon neutral by 2050 or 2060.


> **DEFINITION:**

Carbon neutrality (net-zero carbon emissions) is reached when the CO₂ or greenhouse gases that a country, company, product, activity or person emits, directly or indirectly, over a period are balanced by carbon offsets or removals. The authors stress that emission cuts alone are not enough; CO₂ must also be removed from the atmosphere, for example by sequestration in land and ocean ecosystems.


## 2. Aim of the study

The review presents a strategy to reach a carbon neutral society. It:

- examines the outcomes of COP26 (Glasgow, 31 October–12 November 2021);
- compiles carbon neutrality initiatives and target years for 198 countries;
- reviews the links and synergies between adaptation and mitigation strategies;
- reviews methods for mapping direct and indirect carbon emissions;
- summarises policies and technologies that cut emissions and that remove CO₂;
- reviews life cycle analysis (LCA) of carbon neutral systems and the environmental, social and economic impacts of carbon neutrality.

## 3. What the authors did

This is a literature review, not a field or laboratory study. The authors collected published studies, policy documents and national pledges. They compiled three tables: national carbon neutrality initiatives (Table 1), methods used to map direct and indirect emissions (Table 2), and LCA studies of carbon neutral systems (Table 3). They group solutions into two routes: (1) reducing emissions through policy (carbon trading, carbon tax) and sector technologies in energy, industry, buildings and cities, transport, and agriculture, food and waste; and (2)  removing CO₂ from the atmosphere with negative emission technologies (NETs) and nature-based solutions.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Status of national targets

Table A. Carbon neutrality status of 198 countries (as of February 2022; from the review's Table 1 and text) Status Countries Share Achieved (self-declared) 9 4.5% Declared or pledged 21 10.6% Legislated 17 8.6% Mentioned in policy documents 58 29.3% Proposed or in discussion 93 47% In all, 120 of 198 countries (60.6%) aim for carbon neutrality in 2050–2070, and most target dates fall after 2050. India's 2070 net-zero target, announced at COP26, is listed as a declaration or pledge.


### 4.2 COP26

COP26 made progress in four areas, summed up as coal, cars, cash and trees: phasing out coal, moving to electric transport, delivering the US$100 billion a year that developed countries pledged in 2010 to developing countries, and protecting forests and habitats. Before the summit, enhanced 2030 targets had been submitted only by countries responsible for 55% of global GHG emissions, and long-term strategies by countries responsible for 32%.


### 4.3 Adaptation and mitigation

Some measures help both mitigation and adaptation, such as distributed solar power, afforestation, agroforestry and green roofs. Others involve trade-offs: hydropower cuts emissions but competes for

local  water.  Synergies  remain  weak  in  practice:  of  885 European  climate  action  plans,  only  147 considered both mitigation and adaptation, and only about a quarter analysed their synergies in depth. Cameroon's policies focused on mitigation only.


### 4.4 Mapping emissions

Methods for mapping direct and indirect emissions include input–output models, spatial (gridded) systems, GIS maps, LiDAR and the logarithmic mean Divisia index (LMDI-I). Example results: Table B. Selected mapping studies cited in the review (Table 2 and text) Method Study and place Result Input–output Bai et al. 2018, industry, China Power and heat supply, petroleum processing and coking, and metal mining accounted for nearly 80% of CO₂ emissions 1 km gridded map Cai et al. 2018, Beijing–Tianjin– Hebei Per-capita CO₂ in Beijing and Tianjin metro areas was below provincial averages Landsat time series Skole et al. 2021, Malawi Deforestation: 22,410 ha/yr (2000–2009) and 38,937 ha/yr (2009–2015) GIS and LiDAR Mihut et al. 2019, Romania 27,800 m³ of green biomass and 13,066 t of carbon in the forest studied City input–output Wiedmann et al. 2016, Melbourne 25.1 t CO₂-eq per capita; households 64%, businesses 21%, government 15%


### 4.5 Reducing emissions

- Policy: a study of China's carbon trading (2008–2018) found that emissions fell sharply in several provinces after trading began. A carbon-tax incentive study for aviation found that, under the right conditions, incentives could push airlines to raise fuel efficiency.
- Energy: moving from fossil fuels to renewable energy is described as the most important approach in the energy sector. European models show carbon neutrality by mid-century is technically feasible.
- Industry: in UK iron and steel, heat recovery and similar technologies could cut energy use by 18% and GHG emissions by 12%.
- Buildings and cities: resilient design, decentralised energy, better building envelopes and timber construction (1 m³ of wood stores about half a tonne of carbon).
- Transport: electrification was found to be the best way to cut transport emissions; electricity could supply 72.3% of EU transport energy with existing technology. Biogas upgraded to biomethane could reach 30 billion m³/yr in EU CNG and LNG vehicles by 2030.
- Households: a typical European household emits 6.93 t CO₂-eq/yr, equal to the annual uptake of 0.51 ha of forest. 4.6 Agriculture, food and waste An EU land-use study (Strapasson et al. 2020) found that a more vegetarian diet, less meat and less food waste would mitigate climate change, as would higher livestock yields and more soil carbon in pastures. In South America, low-carbon agriculture could provide a carbon sink of 8.24 PgC between 2016 and 2050 (Sa et al. 2017) and raise food output by 17.6 Mt/yr and meat output by 1.6 Mt/yr.
Table C. Contribution of each practice to mitigation from low-carbon agriculture, South America Practice Share of mitigation Pasture restoration 31% Crop-livestock-forestry integration 25.6% No-till farming 24.3% Forestation 12.8% Biological nitrogen fixation 4.2% Industrial organic waste recycling 2%


### 4.7 Removing CO₂

The NETs reviewed include bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), direct air capture, biochar,  soil  carbon  sequestration,  afforestation  and  reforestation,  enhanced  weathering,  wetland construction and restoration, ocean alkalinity enhancement and ocean fertilisation. In a Scottish study (Alcalde et al. 2018), enhanced weathering had the highest costs (US$25–1600 per t CO₂), BECCS and forestation were less expensive, and biochar and soil carbon sequestration could be cost-effective. A mix of BECCS, soil carbon sequestration and enhanced weathering could reduce emissions by 8.3–36.8 Mt CO₂; at maximum capacity, the mix could remove up to 89.8% of Scotland's annual emissions. Direct air capture could deliver 3 Gt CO₂/yr of negative emissions by 2035.


### 4.8 Life cycle analysis and impacts

Every decarbonisation technique and carbon removal project should pass a life cycle assessment to avoid greenwashing; the authors call for cradle-to-grave analysis of whole systems. Carbon neutrality is expected to improve air quality and restore ecosystems, create jobs in clean energy, and cost jobs in coal and related sectors.


## 5. Conclusions

1. The first step is to shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy and to develop low-carbon technologies. The energy transition should electrify energy services, raise energy efficiency and promote renewables. 2. Low-carbon agriculture, changes in diet (more vegetarian food, less meat, less food waste) and adding value to food and farm waste are essential steps toward net zero. 3. Buildings should be resilient to natural hazards; cities need decentralised energy systems and technologies such as electric vehicles, the Internet of things and big data. 4. Emission mapping tools help decision-makers target the places and sectors that matter most. 5. Negative emission technologies are needed alongside emission cuts, and every option should be checked by life cycle analysis.


## 6. Limitations

- It is a broad global review. Most case studies come from China and Europe; it gives no village-level or Indian emission factors (India appears only as a 2070 target in Table 1 and in a cross-country study).
- Nearly all numbers are quoted from other studies, not newly measured. Check the original source before citing a value.
- Our assessment: agriculture gets a short section compared with energy, industry and transport.

**Cite as:**

H., Bastviken, D., Beerling, D. J., Belikov, D. A., Blake, D. R., Castaldi, S., … Zhuang, Q. (2025). Global Methane Budget 2000–2020. Earth System Science Data, 17, 1873–1958. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-17-1873-2025 Open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License (CC BY 4.0). All values in this summary are taken from the paper; Tg CH₄/yr = teragrams (million tonnes) of methane per year.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Over 2010–2019 the world emitted about 575 Tg CH₄ per year (atmospheric inversions), 65% of it directly from human activity. Bottom-up estimates are higher (669 Tg), but for the first time the two ranges overlap. Agriculture and waste is the largest human source group, livestock the largest single source, the tropics give 64% of emissions, and South Asia is the third-largest region. Emissions reached 608 Tg in 2020 and have tracked no-policy scenarios since 2012.


## 1. Background

Methane (CH₄) is the second most important greenhouse gas influenced by humans, after CO₂. Its mean atmospheric concentration reached 1912 ppb in 2022, 2.6 times the estimated pre-industrial value of 1750, and both emissions and concentrations have risen again since 2007 after a temporary pause (pp. 1875–1876).

Methane stays in the air for a shorter time than CO₂ but has a stronger radiative effect. The paper gives its 100-year global warming potential (GWP-100) as 27 for methane from microbial sources and 29.8 for fossil methane; over 20 years the values are 79.7 and 82.5 (p. 1876, from Forster et al. 2021).


> **WHY THE BUDGET IS HARD:**

Sources such as wetlands, lakes and rivers, livestock, rice paddies, landfills, fossil fuels and fires overlap in space, and the main sink, destruction by short-lived hydroxyl (OH) radicals, is uncertain and variable. The Global Carbon Project therefore brings scientists together to update the budget regularly (p. 1875).


## 2. Aim of the study

This is the third edition of the living review on the global methane budget (after Saunois et al. 2016, 2020). It aims to:

- estimate all CH₄ sources and sinks for 2010–2019, 2000–2009 and the year 2020;
- compare top-down (atmospheric) and bottom-up (source-by-source) estimates and explain their differences;
- give budgets by latitude band, by 18 regions and by source sector;
- improve inland freshwater estimates and, for the first time, estimate double counting with wetlands and the human-caused part of these natural fluxes.

## 3. What the authors did

Top-down: an ensemble of  24 inversion runs works backwards from methane measured at surface stations and by the GOSAT satellite to the emissions needed to explain it.  Bottom-up: emissions are added up source by source from anthropogenic inventories (EDGAR, CEDS, GAINS, USEPA, FAO-CH₄), 16 process-based wetland models, fire products, and data-driven estimates for lakes, ponds, reservoirs, rivers and geological seeps. Sinks come from chemistry–climate models and soil-uptake estimates (pp. 1875–1876, Sects. 2–4). Fluxes are reported in Tg CH₄ per year (1 Tg = 1 million tonnes). Uncertainty is the minimum–maximum range across the studies used, after removing outliers (Table 3 caption, p. 1885).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 The global budget

Table A. Global methane budget for 2010–2019 (Tg CH₄/yr, mean [min–max]; from Table 3 of the paper) Category Top-down Bottom-up Wetlands + inland freshwaters 165 [145–214] 248 [159–369] Other natural sources 43 [40–46] 63 [24–93] Agriculture and waste 228 [213–242] 211 [195–231] of which livestock and manure – 112 [107–118] of which rice cultivation – 32 [25–37] of which landfills and waste – 69 [56–80] Fossil fuels 115 [100–124] 120 [117–125] Biomass and biofuel burning 27 [26–27] 28 [21–39] Total direct anthropogenic 369 [350–391] 358 [329–387] Total sources 575 [553–586] 669 [512–849] Total sinks 554 [550–567] 633 [507–796] Top-down, 575 Tg CH₄/yr were emitted over 2010–2019, of which 369 Tg (about 65%) came directly from fossil fuels, agriculture and waste, and anthropogenic biomass burning. Bottom-up methods give 669 Tg/yr, 16% (94 Tg) more. The gap was 167 and 156 Tg in the two earlier budgets; for the first time the two uncertainty ranges overlap (pp. 1875–1876). Agriculture and waste is the largest human source group. Within it, enteric fermentation and manure management give 112 Tg/yr, about one third of global anthropogenic emissions (p. 1889). For rice, water management, especially periodic drainage and aeration, is described as one of the most promising mitigation approaches (p. 1889).


### 4.2 Trend and the year 2020

Emissions in 2000–2009 were 32 Tg/yr lower (range 9–40) than in 2010–2019. The year 2020 had the highest emissions of the period, 608 Tg CH₄/yr (581–627), 12% above the 2000s average. Since 2012, direct anthropogenic emissions have followed the IPCC scenarios that assume no or minimal climate policy (SSP5 and SSP3) (p. 1875). Atmospheric growth was 15.2 ppb/yr in 2020, 17.8 in 2021 and 14 in 2022 (pp. 1925–1926).


### 4.3 Where methane comes from

Top-down, the tropics (90° S–30° N) give 64% of emissions (364 Tg/yr), the mid-latitudes 32% (187 Tg/yr) and the high northern latitudes above 60° N about 4% (p. 1916). Southeast Asia (63 Tg/yr), China (57) and South Asia (52 [43–60]) are the top three regions and together emit 30% of the global total (p. 1917).

Table B. South Asia in the regional budget, 2010–2019 (Tg CH₄/yr; Table 7 and Sect. 5.3) Quantity Value Budget Total emissions 52 [43–60] Top-down Total emissions 58 [49–72] Bottom-up Direct anthropogenic emissions 45 [44–47] Bottom-up Agriculture and waste 39 [33–43] Top-down Livestock (highest of all regions) 20 [18–22] Bottom-up Rice methane comes mostly from Southeast Asia, China and South Asia (p. 1919).


### 4.4 Natural sources and sinks

Combined wetland and inland freshwater emissions average  248 Tg/yr [159–369] bottom-up, with possible double counting of about 23 Tg/yr. Natural emissions, especially from wetlands and inland freshwaters, remain the largest source of uncertainty. Tropospheric chemical loss, the main sink, is 563 Tg/yr, with about 25% uncertainty; most inversions use the same OH field, so their sink ranges are likely too narrow (p. 1876).


## 5. Conclusions

1. For 2010–2019, global CH₄ emissions are 575 Tg/yr top-down; about 65% are anthropogenic (range 63–68%). 2. Bottom-up totals are larger, mostly because of larger and more uncertain natural emissions and likely double counting, but for the first time the two budgets agree within their uncertainty ranges. 3. Tropical emissions dominate (~64%), compared with mid-latitudes (~32%) and high northern latitudes (~4%). 4. The authors list five priorities: a high-resolution map of CH₄-emitting wet areas, process models for inland waters, more observations from local to global scales, better transport and sink representation in inversions, and inclusion of satellite-detected super-emitters in inventories. 5. The budget will be updated as a living review about every 3–4 years (p. 1925).


## 6. Limitations

- Results are global, by latitude and by 18 large regions; there are no district or village values, and South Asia is treated as one region.
- Uncertainty ranges are wide, especially for natural sources; regional uncertainty can reach 40–60% (e.g. India) (p. 1877).
- Gridded anthropogenic inventories are updated only every 3 to 5 years, so recent years rely on extrapolation (p. 1879).
- Our assessment: the paper gives no breakdown by animal type, breed or feed, which village livestock calculations need.

#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

**Authors:**

Schmidt, Markus Reichstein, Nuno Carvalhais, Philippe Ciais, Lifen Jiang, Johannes Lehmann, Ying-Ping Wang, Benjamin Z. Houlton, Bernhard Ahrens, Umakant Mishra, Gustaf Hugelius, Toby D. Hocking, Xingjie Lu, Zheng Shi, Kostiantyn Viatkin, Ronald Vargas, Yusuf Yigini, Christian Omuto, Ashish A. Malik, Guillermo Peralta, Rosa Cuevas- Corona, Luciano E. Di Paolo, Isabel Luotto, Cuijuan Liao, Yi-Shuang Liang, Vinisa S. Saynes, Xiaomeng Huang, Yiqi Luo

**Journal:**
Nature, vol. 618, pp. 981–985 (29 June 2023)

**Dates:**
Received 16 August 2021 · Accepted 3 April 2023 · Published online 24 May 2023

**Paper type:**
Research article: meta-analysis, global data assimilation and deep learning (open access, CC BY 4.0)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06042-3

**Cite as:**
Tao, F., Huang, Y., Hungate, B. A., Manzoni, S., Frey, S. D., Schmidt, M. W. I., Reichstein, M., Carvalhais, N., Ciais, P., Jiang, L., Lehmann, J., Wang, Y.-P., Houlton, B. Z., Ahrens, B., Mishra, U., Hugelius, G., Hocking, T. D., Lu, X., Shi, Z., … Luo, Y. (2023). Microbial carbon use efficiency promotes global soil carbon storage. Nature, 618, 981–985. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06042-3 Open access article under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0). All values in this summary are taken from the paper (main text pp. 981–985 and Methods).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using 132 field CUE–SOC pairs and 57,267 soil profiles fed into a microbial model with data assimilation and deep learning, the authors show that microbial carbon use efficiency (CUE) is positively linked to soil organic carbon and is at least four times as important as plant inputs, decomposition or vertical transport in setting global SOC storage. A 2% rise in CUE would raise global SOC by 10% (136 PgC).


## 1. Background

Soils store more carbon than other terrestrial ecosystems. Losses of soil organic carbon (SOC) could accelerate warming, whereas storing CO₂ in soils can help mitigate it. The classical view holds that SOC storage depends mainly on how much plant carbon enters the soil and how fast it decomposes, yet studies of these controls have not explained SOC storage well (p. 981). KEY TERM Microbial carbon use efficiency (CUE) is the ratio of microbial growth to carbon uptake: the share of carbon used in metabolism that goes to growth rather than respiration. It is an integrative measure of whether microbes build or lose soil carbon (pp. 981–982).

Whether CUE is positively or negatively linked to SOC was debated. High CUE could build SOC through microbial by-products and necromass, or it could speed SOC loss by raising enzyme production and priming (Fig. 1, p. 982).


## 2. Aim of the study

To test how CUE relates to SOC storage across the globe, to rank it against six other controls (plant carbon inputs, input allocation, non-microbial carbon transfer, substrate decomposability, environmental modifiers and vertical transport), and to find which environmental variables shape CUE (pp. 981–984).


## 3. What the authors did

- Meta-analysis: 132 pairs of measured CUE and SOC at 46 locations from 16 isotope-labelling studies, analysed with linear mixed-effects models (p. 982; Methods).
- PRODA: a microbial-explicit soil carbon model was fitted to each of 57,267 vertical SOC profiles by data assimilation, assuming steady state, and a deep-learning neural network then generalised the parameters to the globe (p. 982).
- Sensitivity analyses: (1) removing the spatial variation of one component at a time; (2) finding the change in each component needed to raise global SOC by 10% (p. 984).
- Permutation analysis of environmental variables to explain spatial CUE patterns (p. 984; Methods).

## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 CUE and SOC are positively linked

In the meta-analysis, CUE was positively correlated with SOC after accounting for method differences: log₁₀(SOC) = 1.16 + 0.76 × CUE, explaining 54.7% of the variation (Fig. 2a). High CUE went with both more microbial and more non-microbial carbon. Measured CUE averaged 0.33 with both carbon and oxygen isotope methods (Methods). The CUE retrieved from the 57,267 global profiles also correlated positively with SOC, although the link weakens with depth (pp. 982–983).


### 4.2 CUE is the strongest control

Table A. Change needed in each component to raise global SOC storage by 10% (136 PgC) (p. 984, Fig. 4b) Component Change needed Equivalent Microbial CUE +2.0% Global median CUE 0.28 → 0.29 Baseline decomposition rate –8.4% 0.066 → 0.060 per year Environmental modifiers +11% Median temperature 10.3 → 12.2 °C, or precipitation 503 → 611 mm Non-microbial carbon transfer +11% Fraction 0.35 → 0.39 Carbon inputs, allocation, vertical transport – Only marginal influence on global SOC In the first sensitivity analysis, using one global CUE value caused a total absolute deviation of 812 PgC from the model's global estimate of 1,358 PgC in the top metre, and cut the explained spatial variation in SOC from 53% to 15%. Making other components uniform caused smaller errors. Overall, CUE was at least four times as important as any of the other six components (p. 984).


### 4.3 Global patterns and what controls CUE

CUE and SOC share similar patterns, with lower values in tropical than in boreal regions. Tropical plants supply much more carbon, but low CUE and high decomposition prevent high SOC stocks. In boreal regions decomposition rates are high, but cold, permafrost and waterlogging restrict loss; vertical transport is strongest in permafrost regions (pp. 983–984).  Soil structural properties (such as bulk density, texture and porosity) explained more of the spatial variation in CUE than geographic, climatic, soil chemical or vegetation variables (p. 984).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Microbial CUE plays a pivotal role in determining SOC storage at the global scale. 2. A high CUE promotes SOC storage more than loss: more carbon goes to biomass and by-products, whereas low CUE sends more carbon to respiration. 3. Future research should prioritise microbial processes, alongside decomposition and carbon inputs, to predict SOC feedbacks to climate and to enhance SOC sequestration (pp. 984–985).


## 6. Limitations

- The meta-analysis lacks data from tropical and arid regions and from clay soils (Methods).
- A steady-state soil carbon cycle is assumed at each profile; projecting future change needs time- varying parameters and microbial acclimation and adaptation (pp. 982, 984).
- How sensitive the ranking of CUE is to different model structures still needs testing (p. 984).
- Our assessment: CUE requires isotope incubations, so a village study can use it as a concept and measure soil structure and SOC instead; the paper does not test farm management practices.

# Key Highlights: Global stocks and capacity of mineral-associated soil organic carbon

**Authors:** Katerina Georgiou, Robert B. Jackson, Olga Vindušková, Rose Z. Abramoff, Anders Ahlström, Wenting Feng, Jennifer W. Harden, Adam F. A. Pellegrini, H. Wayne Polley, Jennifer L. Soong, William J. Riley, Margaret S. Torn
**Journal / Year:** Nature Communications, vol. 13, article 3797 (2022), 13 pages (2022)
**Official DOI:** [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31540-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31540-9)

## Core Statistics & Results

| Metric | Finding / Significance |
| --- | --- |
| **899 Pg C** | MOC to 1 m in mineral soils |
| **42% / 21%** | of capacity filled, topsoil / subsoil |
| **104 Pg C** | cropland gain at natural saturation |
| **3×** | faster accrual at <10% vs 50% saturation |

## Important Findings & Key Takeaways

### 01. Global MOC stock
899 Pg C to 1 m (448 topsoil, 451 subsoil), 66% and 70% of soil carbon in surface and deeper layers.

*(Reference: pp. 1, 4)*

### 02. Capacity
Mineralogical capacity 4596 Pg C to 1 m; soils are only 42% (topsoil) and 21% (subsoil) saturated.

*(Reference: p. 5)*

### 03. Mineral type matters
MOCmax 86 ± 9 (high-activity) vs 48 ± 6 mg C/g (low-activity) clay + silt.

*(Reference: pp. 2–3, Fig. 1)*

### 04. Farm soils are emptier
Agricultural soils 31% saturated vs 46% in natural ecosystems; deep soils 19% vs surface 43%.

*(Reference: p. 3, Fig. 2)*

### 05. Cropland deficit
184 Pg C (topsoil) and 509 Pg C (subsoil).

*(Reference: p. 5)*

### 06. Realistic gain
Croplands at natural saturation would gain about 104 Pg C (62 topsoil + 42 subsoil).

*(Reference: p. 5)*

### 07. Emptiest soils gain fastest
Across 103 accrual measurements, rates were 3× higher at <10% than at 50% saturation.

*(Reference: p. 6, Fig. 4d)*

### 08. India is a hotspot
Extensive cropping regions such as the Midwestern US and India are sequestration hotspots.

*(Reference: p. 6)*

### 09. Rates slow down
Accrual falls as soils fill; >1 Pg C/yr over all croplands is possible only for a time.

*(Reference: p. 6)*

### 10. Warming risk
MOC declines with temperature; unsaturated soils are more temperature-sensitive.

*(Reference: p. 4, Fig. 3)*

# Global stocks and capacity of mineral-associated soil organic carbon


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Global stocks and capacity of mineral-associated soil organic carbon Katerina Georgiou, Robert B. Jackson, Olga Vindušková … Margaret S. Torn (12 authors)

**Authors:**
Katerina Georgiou, Robert B. Jackson, Olga Vindušková, Rose Z. Abramoff, Anders Ahlström, Wenting Feng, Jennifer W. Harden, Adam F. A. Pellegrini, H. Wayne Polley, Jennifer L. Soong, William J. Riley, Margaret S. Torn

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 13, article 3797 (2022), 13 pages

**Dates:**
Received 20 January 2022 · Accepted 9 June 2022

**Paper type:**
Research article: global observational synthesis and machine learning (open access, CC BY 4.0)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31540-9

**Cite as:**
Georgiou, K., Jackson, R. B., Vindušková, O., Abramoff, R. Z., Ahlström, A., Feng, W., Harden, J. W., Pellegrini, A. F. A., Polley, H. W., Soong, J. L., Riley, W. J., & Torn, M. S. (2022). Global stocks and capacity of mineral-associated soil organic carbon. Nature Communications, 13, Article 3797. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31540-9 Open access article under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0). Page numbers refer to the 13-page article PDF. Pg C = petagrams (billion tonnes) of carbon.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

From 1144 soil profiles, the authors estimate that mineral-associated organic carbon (MOC) totals 899 Pg C to 1 m, 66–70% of soil carbon, but only 42% (topsoil) and 21% (subsoil) of what soil minerals could hold. Croplands and subsoils are the most undersaturated. If croplands reached natural-land saturation they could gain about 104 Pg C, and the least saturated soils accrue carbon about three times faster.


## 1. Background

Soil holds more carbon than the atmosphere and vegetation combined, and human land use has caused a large net loss of soil carbon over two centuries (p. 2). More than half of soil organic carbon is bound chemically or physically to minerals. This mineral-associated organic carbon (MOC) is hard for microbes to reach, so it can persist up to 1000 times longer (100–10,000 years) than particulate organic carbon (POC), the loosely held plant debris (p. 2). KEY TERMS MOCmax is the maximum MOC a soil's minerals can hold, set by the amount and type of clay and silt. %C saturation = MOC ÷ MOCmax. The carbon deficit = MOCmax – MOC (pp. 2–5).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate global MOC stocks and the mineralogical capacity to store MOC, map undersaturation by land use and depth, and test whether soils further from capacity gain carbon faster after management changes (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

- Synthesised MOC (by size and density fractionation), POC and SOC from 1144 soil profiles spanning clay + silt of 1.5–100%, mean annual temperature of −2.9 to 29 °C and rainfall of 79–3806 mm/yr (p. 2).
- Classified soils as high-activity (illite, smectite, vermiculite, chlorite) or low-activity (kaolinite, gibbsite) minerals and fitted MOCmax as the 95th quantile of MOC against clay + silt (pp. 2–3).
- Used random forest models to study climate and input effects (R² = 0.60) and to map current MOC globally at 0.5° (R² = 0.79), excluding tundra, peatlands and deserts (pp. 3–4).
- Synthesised 103 carbon-accrual measurements following management interventions lasting 2–65 years (p. 6).

## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Mineral capacity

MOCmax was 86 ± 9 mg C per g mineral for high-activity and 48 ± 6 for low-activity mineral soils. There is no universal linear MOC–clay relationship; mineral type must be considered, and studies that ignored it gave much lower capacities (pp. 2–3).


### 4.2 Saturation by land use and depth

Soils averaged 40% saturation. Natural ecosystems (forest, grassland) averaged 46%, agricultural systems only 31%; surface soils were 43% and deeper soils 19% saturated. Grasslands were closer to saturation than forests at depth, showing the role of roots (pp. 3–4).


### 4.3 Global stocks, capacity and deficit

Table A. Global estimates to 1 m, excluding tundra, peatlands and deserts (pp. 4–5; Supplementary Tables 1–2) Quantity Topsoil (0–30 cm) Subsoil (30–100 cm) Total to 1 m MOC stock (Pg C) 448 (296–536) 451 (372–538) 899 (668–1074) MOC as share of SOC 0.66 ± 0.13 0.70 ± 0.17 0.69 ± 0.15 Capacity MOCmax (Pg C) 1443 ± 141 3153 ± 312 4596 ± 453 Average %C saturation 42% (24–61%) 21% (14–30%) – Cropland deficit (Pg C) 184 (148–225) 509 (439–569) – Cropland gain at natural saturation (Pg C) 62 42 ~104 The greatest deficits are in temperate and subequatorial zones, partly because of the prevalence of agricultural soils. Reaching MOCmax is difficult and strongly limited by climate; the realistic aim is to restore managed soils to natural saturation levels. Grazing lands in arid and semi-arid regions need tailored strategies (p. 5).


### 4.4 Climate effects

MOC declined with mean annual temperature, suggesting a global vulnerability of MOC to warming; soils far from saturation were more temperature-sensitive than near-saturated soils, so restoring degraded soils may also make them more resilient to warming (p. 4). Aboveground litter was a weak predictor of MOC (p. 3).


### 4.5 Sequestration efficiency

Across 103 accrual measurements, soils furthest from capacity accrued carbon fastest: rates averaged three times higher at sites with <10% saturation than at 50% saturation. Hotspots lie in extensive cropping regions such as the Midwestern United States and India. Average accrual over all croplands could store over 1 Pg C per year for a time, but rates fall as soils fill up (p. 6).


## 5. Conclusions

1. MOC makes up most (69%) of soil carbon in the top metre of non-permafrost mineral soils but less than half of the mineralogical capacity. 2. The degree of undersaturation indicates sequestration efficiency over years to decades and can guide where soil carbon management works best. 3. Long-cropped, grazed, abandoned and degraded lands are priority areas; practices that store carbon deeper (e.g. deep-rooted vegetation) are promising. 4. Incentives and valuation of soil carbon are needed to scale action across more than 500 million farms (p. 6).


## 6. Limitations

- MOCmax is a theoretical ceiling; climate often prevents soils from reaching it, and it is not a recommended target (p. 5).
- Global maps are at 0.5° resolution and exclude tundra, peatlands, deserts and organic soils (Histosols) (pp. 4, 7).
- Low-activity mineral soils are represented by far fewer measurements (93) than high-activity soils (1303) (Fig. 1).
- High accrual rates decline as soils approach saturation, so gains are time-limited (p. 6).
- Our assessment: the maps are not calibrated for Indo-Gangetic alluvial soils, and MOC fractionation data are not part of routine Indian soil testing.

# Diversifying crop rotation increases food production, reduces net greenhouse gas emissions and improves soil health


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Diversifying crop rotation increases food production, reduces net greenhouse gas emissions and improves soil health Xiaolin Yang, Jinran Xiong, Taisheng Du … Klaus Butterbach-Bahl (13 authors)

**Authors:**
Xiaolin Yang, Jinran Xiong, Taisheng Du, Xiaotang Ju, Yantai Gan, Sien Li, Longlong Xia, Yanjun Shen, Steven Pacenka, Tammo S. Steenhuis, Kadambot H. M. Siddique, Shaozhong Kang, Klaus Butterbach-Bahl

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 15, article 198 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 4 September 2023 · Accepted 14 December 2023

**Paper type:**
Research article: six-year field experiment (open access, CC BY 4.0)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-44464-9

**Cite as:**
Yang, X., Xiong, J., Du, T., Ju, X., Gan, Y., Li, S., Xia, L., Shen, Y., Pacenka, S., Steenhuis, T. S., Siddique, K. H. M., Kang, S., & Butterbach-Bahl, K. (2024). Diversifying crop rotation increases food production, reduces net greenhouse gas emissions and improves soil health. Nature Communications, 15, Article 198. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023- 44464-9 Open access article under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0). Page numbers refer to the article PDF. Results come from one six-year field experiment in the North China Plain.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

In a six-year field trial in the North China Plain, adding sweet potato, peanut or soybean to the wheat– maize double crop raised equivalent yield by up to 38%, cut field N₂O by 30–49%, stored 1.4–2.0 t C/ha/yr in soil to 90 cm and lowered net GHG emissions by 83–92%, while soil health scores rose 41– 59%. Scaled up, the authors estimate 107 Mt CO₂-eq/yr less and 20% more farmer income.


## 1. Background

Since the Green Revolution, intensive cereal farming has relied on synthetic fertilisers and pesticides that emit large amounts of greenhouse gases and degrade soils. China's crop production rose 74% in 1986– 2016 while synthetic fertiliser use rose by more than 300%; in 2019 China's food-related GHG emissions reached 2.4 Gt CO₂-eq, about half from crop production (p. 1). The North China Plain, which supplies about 23% of China's cereal food, is dominated by winter wheat– summer maize double cropping on 70% of its arable land (p. 2). Diversified rotations with legumes could partly replace synthetic N through biological N fixation (Fig. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To assess whether rotations diversified with cash crops, legumes, other cereals or forage can increase food production and farmer income, reduce GHG emissions and improve soil health compared with wheat–maize (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

A field experiment ran from October 2016 to October 2022 at the Luancheng Agro-Ecosystem Station, Hebei Province (37°50  N, 114°40  E), with a semi-humid monsoon climate (mean 14.7 °C; 472 mm rain ′ ′

per year). The loam soil started with pH 7.6, bulk density 1.49 g/cm³ and SOC 11.5 g/kg (pp. 8–9).

- Six rotations: wheat–maize (control, WM) and sweet potato (SpWM), peanut (PWM), soybean (SWM), spring maize (SmWM) or ryegrass–sweet sorghum (RSWM) followed by wheat–maize.
- N₂O and CH₄ measured weekly; indirect emissions from fertiliser, pesticide, diesel, electricity for irrigation, seed and labour.
- SOC stocks to 90 cm in 2016 and 2022; net GHG = indirect + direct (N₂O + CH₄) – ΔSOC × 44/12 (p. 10).
- Soil health scored with the Cornell Soil Health Assessment from ten soil properties; microbial diversity by DNA sequencing.

## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Yield and income

The sweet potato rotation increased annual equivalent yield by 38% over wheat–maize (13,185 kg/ha/yr) and net income by 60%; peanut and soybean rotations raised income by 13–22%. Wheat–maize grown after non-cereal crops had 26–32% more grain. The all-cereal spring maize rotation lowered equivalent yield by 16% and protein yield by 23% (pp. 2–3).


### 4.2 Greenhouse gases and soil carbon

Table A. Emissions and soil carbon by rotation (pp. 3–4, Fig. 3) Rotation N₂O vs WM GWP (N₂O + CH₄) vs WM SOC gain 0–90 cm (t C/ha/yr) Net GHG vs WM Wheat–maize (control) 8.9 kg N/ha/yr 3764 kg CO₂-eq/ha/yr 0.21–0.69 (range of 3 rotations) 10,025 kg CO₂-eq/ha/yr Peanut → WM –30% –32% 2.03 –92% Soybean → WM –42% –43% 1.91 –90% Sweet potato → WM –49% –51% 1.44 –83% Spring maize → WM – –19% 0.21–0.69 – Ryegrass–sorghum → WM – –22% 0.21–0.69 – All soils were net CH₄ sinks, and the diversified rotations increased the sink by 33–76%. Indirect emissions from agrochemicals and irrigation were highest for wheat–maize (8802 kg CO₂-eq/ha/yr) and 34–41% lower for four diversified rotations. The legume rotations needed 37% less fertiliser (p. 8). The abstract summarises the results as a 39% cut in N₂O and an 88% improvement in the GHG balance.


### 4.3 Soil health and microbes

After six years the soil health score was highest for peanut (59.5), soybean (56.8) and sweet potato (52.9) rotations, 41–59% above wheat–maize (33.2). Peanut soils had 6.5% more SOC and 29.7% more DOC. Microbial Shannon diversity rose 7–10% in these three rotations but not in the cereal systems; legumes stimulated soil microbial activity and raised SOC stocks by about 8% (pp. 1, 4–5).


### 4.4 Scaling up (authors' estimates)

Across the North China Plain, diversified systems could cut net emissions by 106.8 ± 31.7 Mt CO₂-eq per year (5.6% of China's food-system GHG), mainly by using 3.6 Mt less synthetic N; raise farmer income by 20% (84 billion yuan); raise wheat and maize yields by 32% (73.5 Mt/yr) when grown after alternative crops; and raise soil health scores by 45% (p. 5).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Diversifying wheat–maize with legumes (peanut, soybean) and cash crops (sweet potato) can increase food production, reduce net GHG emissions and improve soil health together. 2. Reduced synthetic N and higher soil carbon sequestration drive the GHG benefit. 3. The authors recommend diversified cropping as a key consideration in agricultural policy and a priority for on-farm decisions, designed for local conditions (p. 8).


## 6. Limitations

- Results come mainly from one representative research station; multi-location experiments are needed (p. 11).
- Inter-annual weather is highly variable, so the authors call multiyear sustainability assessments tentative (p. 8).
- Regional benefits are upscaled estimates, not measurements (p. 5).
- Our assessment: rice was not tested, so paddy CH₄ is outside the results; six years of SOC data may overstate long-term rates; research-station management may exceed what farmers achieve.

# River ecosystem metabolism and carbon biogeochemistry in a changing world


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

River ecosystem metabolism and carbon biogeochemistry in a changing world Tom J. Battin, Ronny Lauerwald, Emily S. Bernhardt … Pierre Regnier (13 authors)

**Authors:**
Tom J. Battin, Ronny Lauerwald, Emily S. Bernhardt, Enrico Bertuzzo, Lluís Gómez Gener, Robert O. Hall, Jr., Erin R. Hotchkiss, Taylor Maavara, Tamlin M. Pavelsky, Lishan Ran, Peter Raymond, Judith A. Rosentreter, Pierre Regnier

**Journal:**
Nature, vol. 613, no. 7944, pp. 449–459 (2023) Version used Authors' accepted manuscript (White Rose Research Online, eprint 195538)

**Paper type:**
Review with a global carbon mass-balance synthesis

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05500-8

**Cite as:**
Battin, T. J., Lauerwald, R., Bernhardt, E. S., Bertuzzo, E., Gómez Gener, L., Hall, R. O., Jr., Hotchkiss, E. R., Maavara, T., Pavelsky, T. M., Ran, L., Raymond, P., Rosentreter, J. A., & Regnier, P. (2023). River ecosystem metabolism and carbon biogeochemistry in a changing world. Nature, 613, 449–459. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05500-8 Summary based on the authors' accepted manuscript (White Rose Research Online). Page numbers (AM p.) refer to that manuscript, not the printed Nature pages 449–459. Pg C = billion tonnes of carbon.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Rivers are active biogeochemical reactors. Land delivers about 3.2 Pg C/yr to rivers (0.72 organic, 2.44 inorganic), roughly a quarter of terrestrial NEP. Rivers are strongly heterotrophic: they respire about 37% of the incoming organic carbon and emit 1.9–2.3 Pg C/yr of CO₂, over 70% from the tropics, and only about a quarter of the land carbon reaches the coast. Land use, dams and climate change are altering these fluxes, so the authors call for a global River Observing System.


## 1. Background

Rivers were long considered pipes that move carbon from land to the ocean. Today they are understood as biogeochemical reactors that metabolise organic carbon, emit CO₂ and CH₄ and bury carbon in sediments, floodplains and deltas. The IPCC and the Global Carbon Project include rivers in their budgets, but usually as a black box, which prevents prediction of how global change will alter river carbon fluxes (AM pp. 2–3). KEY TERMS GPP (gross primary production) is carbon fixed in the river; ER (ecosystem respiration) is carbon respired by all organisms; NEP = GPP – ER. Negative NEP means the river is heterotrophic and is subsidised by carbon from land (AM pp. 4–5).


## 2. Aim of the study

To  review  river  ecosystem  metabolism  research,  synthesise  best  estimates  of  river  metabolism worldwide, quantify organic and inorganic carbon flows from land through rivers to the coast, discuss

global-change impacts, and set research priorities, including a global River Observing System (AM pp. 2, 4).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors summarised published metabolism budgets for tropical, temperate and high-latitude rivers and built a global mass balance of river carbon fluxes, including CH₄ and reservoir emissions and burial. Uncertainty follows IPCC guidelines, with lower and upper bounds from sensitivity analyses (AM pp. 6–8).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Rivers are strongly heterotrophic

Table A. Mean areal metabolism by latitude (g C/m²/yr; AM p. 7, Table SI 1) Zone GPP ER NEP Tropical 153 –760 –606 Temperate 331 –591 –260 High-latitude 279 –827 –438 The  mean  global  river  NEP  (about  –426  g  C/m²/yr)  places  rivers  among  the  most  heterotrophic ecosystems on Earth, compared with a terrestrial average NEP of +74 and estuaries at –189 g C/m²/yr. Tropical and high-latitude records are few and skewed toward small rivers (AM p. 7).


### 4.2 Global river carbon budget

Table B. Global fluxes from the mass balance (Pg C/yr; AM pp. 9–12, Fig. 2) Flux Best estimate Bounds Organic carbon from land to rivers 0.72 0.58–1.23 Inorganic carbon from land to rivers 2.44 2.37–3.17 Total land-to-river transfer 3.2 UB 4.2 River NEP –0.27 –0.13 to –0.33 River CO₂ emissions 1.9–2.3 two upscaling studies River CH₄ emissions ~0.005 (mean) 0.008 (median) Reservoir emissions / burial 0.037 / 0.027 UB 0.3 / 0.18 River OC export to coast 0.38 UB 0.7 The 3.2 Pg C/yr transfer is about a quarter of global terrestrial NEP (11 Pg C/yr). The low organic to inorganic ratio (0.3) shows that CO₂ from soils and roots is a dominant input. Rivers transform about 37% (12–42%) of incoming organic carbon to CO₂; river NEP supplies only about 12% of river emissions. The ratio rises to 1.1 at the coast, and only about 26% of land carbon delivered to rivers reaches the ocean, excluding weathering-derived bicarbonate (AM pp. 10–12). Over  70% of  river  CO₂  is  emitted  in  the  tropics,  and  low-order,  high-slope  streams  contribute disproportionately (AM p. 9).


### 4.3 Global change

- Terrestrial subsidies: higher NPP and wetter climates deliver more carbon to rivers, mostly recycled to CO₂; Earth system models predict accelerating delivery this century (AM pp. 14–15).
- Land use: deforestation and peatland conversion mobilise old carbon; agricultural soils are a major source of OC and nutrients and alter river GPP and ER (AM pp. 15–16).
- Flow regimes: drying makes non-perennial rivers more heterotrophic and can promote CH₄; flashier flows reduce GPP and ER (AM pp. 16–17).
- Dams: reservoirs can emit large amounts of CO₂ and CH₄, with methane produced in deep anoxic water; CO₂ evasion from Chinese rivers fell 32% over three decades, partly attributed to damming (AM pp. 17–18).
- Deoxygenation: eutrophication can switch rivers to denitrification and methanogenesis, producing N₂O and CH₄ (AM p. 18).

## 5. Conclusions

1. River networks are proficient at retaining, metabolising and emitting terrestrial carbon and matter for continental carbon budgets. 2. Global change will alter the timing and location of river carbon storage and emissions in complex ways. 3. A global River Observing System (RIOS), combining sensor networks, field surveys, satellites, scaling laws and models, is needed, with more multi-year time series from the tropics, high latitudes and mountains and funding that includes the Global South (AM pp. 18–20).


## 6. Limitations

- Many fluxes are poorly constrained; reservoir fluxes could be up to an order of magnitude larger, and high-flow exports are undersampled (AM pp. 10–12).
- Sensor records are biased toward temperate rivers; tropical data are scarce (AM p. 19).
- This summary uses the accepted manuscript; page numbers differ from the printed Nature article.
- Our assessment: the review is global and gives no Indian or basin-specific values, so it is context rather than an emission factor source.

# Greenhouse gas emissions and mitigation in rice agriculture


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Greenhouse gas emissions and mitigation in rice agriculture Haoyu Qian, Xiangchen Zhu, Shan Huang … Yu Jiang (21 authors)

**Authors:**
Haoyu Qian, Xiangchen Zhu, Shan Huang, Bruce Linquist, Yakov Kuzyakov, Reiner Wassmann, Kazunori Minamikawa, Maite Martinez-Eixarch, Xiaoyuan Yan, Feng Zhou, Bjoern Ole Sander, Weijian Zhang, Ziyin Shang, Jianwen Zou, Xunhua Zheng, Ganghua Li, Zhenhui Liu, Songhan Wang, Yanfeng Ding, Kees Jan van Groenigen, Yu Jiang

**Journal:**
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, vol. 4, no. 10, pp. 716–732 (2023) Version used Authors' accepted manuscript

**Paper type:**
Review with synthesis of in-situ field measurements

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00482-1

**Cite as:**
Qian, H., Zhu, X., Huang, S., Linquist, B., Kuzyakov, Y., Wassmann, R., Minamikawa, K., Martinez-Eixarch, M., Yan, X., Zhou, F., Sander, B. O., Zhang, W., Shang, Z., Zou, J., Zheng, X., Li, G., Liu, Z., Wang, S., Ding, Y., … Jiang, Y. (2023). Greenhouse gas emissions and mitigation in rice agriculture. Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, 4(10), 716– 732. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00482-1 Summary based on the authors' accepted manuscript. Page numbers (AM p.) refer to that manuscript, not the printed pages 716–732. CO₂e uses 100-year GWP.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Rice paddies give about 48% of cropland GHG emissions. Field data average 283 kg CH₄ and 1.7 kg N₂O per ha per year, or 7,870 kg CO₂e/ha/yr (94% from CH₄) and 0.9 kg CO₂e per kg grain. Organic matter and continuous flooding drive CH₄; the N rate drives N₂O. Warming may raise CH₄ by 15–23%. New varieties, non-continuous flooding and straw removal cut GHG by 24%, 44% and 46% on average, but the best mix depends on the local seasonal CH₄ pattern (AM pp. 2–3, 15).


## 1. Background

Rice is the staple for more than half of the world's people and provides 20% of dietary energy. Paddies cover about 1.7 million km², and production was about 757 million tonnes in 2020, led by China, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia and Vietnam. Global consumption rose from 157 million tonnes in 1960 to 520 million tonnes in 2022 (AM p. 2). Rice gives about 48% of cropland GHG emissions, 22% of agricultural CH₄ and about 11% of agricultural N₂O. Current paddy emissions are estimated at 24–31 Tg CH₄/yr and 130 Gg N₂O/yr (AM p. 2). HOW PADDIES EMIT In flooded, oxygen-free soil, methanogens produce CH₄ from organic matter; up to 90% of it escapes through the rice plant. N₂O forms during nitrification and denitrification and peaks when soils are alternately wet and dry (Box 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To review how much CH₄ and N₂O rice paddies emit, what drives the emissions, how elevated CO₂ and warming will change them, and which practices cut emissions while keeping yields (AM p. 3).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors compiled in-situ field measurements worldwide (Supplementary Data) to estimate mean emissions per hectare and per kg of grain, grouped seasonal CH₄ patterns at several hundred sites, and reviewed experiments and meta-analyses on elevated CO₂, warming and management: cultivar, water, organic matter, mineral N, tillage and crop establishment, liming and new techniques. Gases were combined with 100-year GWP (AM pp. 3–4).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Emission levels

Table A. Mean paddy emissions from field data (AM p. 3) Measure Value CH₄ 283 kg/ha/yr N₂O 1.7 kg/ha/yr Area-scaled GHG 7,870 kg CO₂e/ha/yr (~94% CH₄) Yield-scaled GHG 0.9 kg CO₂e/kg grain CH₄ at 10°S–10°N 614 kg/ha/yr CH₄ above 40°N 272 kg/ha/yr Emissions vary up to two orders of magnitude, even within a country. China, India and Indonesia emit 22–38%, 11–19% and 7–9% of global rice CH₄, and 27%, 17% and 15% of rice N₂O (AM p. 3).


### 4.2 Drivers

- Organic matter: straw raises CH₄ by 92% and manure by 60%; organic additions raise area-scaled GHG by 66–85% (AM p. 4).
- Water: non-continuous flooding (NCF: mid-season drainage, intermittent irrigation, AWD) cuts CH₄ by 53% in the rice season; multiple drainages could cut 4.1 Tg CH₄/yr globally (AM p. 4).
- Nitrogen: N fertiliser raises N₂O by 182%; the direct N₂O-N emission factor is 0.52% (0.15–1.3%), close to IPCC's 0.3% (flooded) and 0.5% (NCF) (AM p. 4).
- Seasonal patterns: early peak (~40% of sites), two peaks (~27%), late peak (~24%; 43% of Indian sites) and bell-shaped (~8%) (AM pp. 4–5). 4.3 Trends and climate change Yield-scaled CH₄ fell 38–55% from the 1980s to the 2010s, mainly through higher yields and more drainage (AM pp. 6, 15). Elevated CO₂ raises CH₄ by 4–40% (the global effect may be only 3.7% given straw use) and N₂O by 27%; warming raises CH₄ by 15–23% and N₂O by 26%; together they raised CH₄ by 71% and N₂O by 36% (AM pp. 2, 6–8).

### 4.4 Mitigation

Table B. Average reductions reported (AM pp. 2, 4, 9–14) Practice Effect New rice varieties –24% GHG Non-continuous flooding –44% GHG; –53% CH₄ in rice season Straw removal –46% GHG Optimised N rate ~–43% N₂O (estimate) Enhanced-efficiency N fertilisers –20 to –60% N₂O No-till –23% CH₄ Direct seeding –40 to –60% CH₄ Biochar –13% CH₄; –22% N₂O (≥2 yr) Liming acid paddies ~–20% CH₄

- Drainage raises N₂O by 105% on average but usually not enough to cancel the CH₄ gain; 33 kg N₂O/ha/season occurred when fields dried at high soil N (AM pp. 9–10).
- NCF could suit 76% of rice area without yield loss, but uptake is low in parts of South and Southeast Asia where monsoon rain makes drainage hard (AM p. 10).
- Straw addition raised CH₄ with a GWP 3.2–3.9 times its SOC gain, so organic additions generally give no net climate benefit (AM p. 10).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Optimising organic matter, water and nitrogen management is the most promising way to cut paddy GHG while keeping yields. 2. The best mix depends on the local seasonal CH₄ pattern. 3. More field data are needed in low latitudes such as the Philippines, Indonesia and southern India, and models such as DNDC need more processes (AM pp. 15–16).


## 6. Limitations

- Global means hide up-to-100-fold local variation; low-latitude values rest on few observations (AM p. 3).
- Most climate-change experiments are short (under 5 years) (AM p. 16).
- Fallow-season emissions and nursery emissions are poorly measured (AM pp. 5, 13).
- This summary uses the accepted manuscript; check details against the published version.

Mo, L., Zohner, C. M., Reich, P. B., Liang, J., de Miguel, S., Nabuurs, G.-J., Renner, S. S., van den Hoogen, J., Araza, A., Herold, M., Mirzagholi, L., Ma, H., Averill, C., Phillips, O. L., Gamarra, J. G. P., Hordijk, I., Routh, D., Abegg, M., Adou Yao, Y. C., … Crowther, T. W. (2023). Integrated global assessment of the natural forest carbon potential. Nature, 624(7990), 92–101. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06723-z Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers are the printed Nature pages 92–101; Methods are cited as Methods. Gt C = billion tonnes of carbon.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Combining 1.19 million forest inventory plots with three satellite biomass maps, the authors estimate that forests hold 328 Gt C (221–472) less carbon than they would naturally. Ground and satellite results differ by only 12% globally. Outside urban and agricultural land the potential is 226 Gt C (151–363): 61% (139 Gt C) in existing degraded forests that can recover if protected, and 39% (87 Gt C) where forests were removed or fragmented. Forests cannot replace emission cuts, but conserving and restoring diverse forests, led by local communities, can help (pp. 92, 96–98).


## 1. Background

Forests hold 80–90% of global plant biomass and much of land biodiversity. Humans have removed almost half of Earth's natural forests, and deforestation still releases 0.9–2.3 Gt C per year, about 15% of annual human carbon emissions (p. 92). Earlier satellite-based estimates of extra forest carbon potential ranged from 200 to 300 Gt C, and critics suggested  they  could  be  4–5  times  too  high.  No  independent  ground-based  estimate  existed  to benchmark them (p. 92).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate the natural forest carbon potential, the carbon forests could hold without extensive human degradation under current climate, by combining ground-sourced and satellite-derived approaches, and to split the gap between existing forests and deforested land (pp. 92–93).


## 3. What the authors did

- Ground-sourced (GS): the GFBI database of 1,188,771 plots (1,089,026 kept after quality control, about 25.8 million trees) with DBH for each tree, converted to biomass with allometric equations and mapped with random-forest models (p. 93; Methods).
- Satellite-derived (SD): three biomass maps (ESA-CCI, Walker et al. and a harmonised product) (p. 93).
- Natural state: type 1 models set human-disturbance variables to zero; type 2 models learn only from undisturbed areas, giving 4 GS and 6 SD models (p. 93).
- Total carbon: tree carbon scaled up with root fractions, soil carbon (0–2 m), dead wood and litter, and compared with a meta-analysis of earlier estimates (pp. 93, 95–96).

## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Agreement between methods

GS and SD estimates of potential differed by only 12% globally. Existing live tree carbon was 367 Gt C (GS) and 394 Gt C (SD), under 7% apart; average R² between the two was 0.72. SD models predicted higher potential in 82% of pixels, especially in South American tropics (pp. 92, 94–95).


### 4.2 Living tree carbon

Potential living tree carbon is about 600 Gt C (487–712) in a natural canopy area of 4.4 billion ha; the gap to current stocks is 217 Gt C (153–267): tropical 123, temperate 55, dryland 25 and boreal 14 Gt C. This lies at the lower end of earlier estimates (150–446 Gt C) and is probably conservative (pp. 95–97).


### 4.3 Total ecosystem carbon by land use

Table A. Gap between current and natural carbon stocks (Gt C, all pools; Table 1 and Fig. 5, pp. 97–98) Land Gt C Notes Existing forests 138.9 Conservation potential; 11 Gt in plantations Low-human-pressure land 53.3 Restoration potential Rangeland 33.7 Restoration potential Cropland 56.8 Restoration highly unlikely Pasture 43.3 Restoration highly unlikely Urban 1.7 Restoration highly unlikely Total 328 Range 221–472 Excluding urban, cropland and pasture (102 Gt C), the potential is 226 Gt C (151–363): 61% (139 Gt C) in existing forests and 39% (87 Gt C) where forests were removed or fragmented. About 41% of the gap outside forests is on grazing land, and 36% of crop yields feed animals (pp. 96–98). CARBON POOLS Of the 328 Gt C gap, aboveground biomass is 52.1%, dead wood and litter 18.9%, soil 15.0% and roots 14.0% (Fig. 5d, p. 97). India is one of nine countries that together hold more than half of the gap (Fig. 5e).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Forests cannot substitute for emission reductions, but conserving, restoring and sustainably managing diverse forests can help meet climate and biodiversity targets (p. 92). 2. Most of the realistic gain (61%) comes from letting existing degraded forests recover, with few land conflicts (pp. 96–98). 3. Restoration must be socially responsible and led by local and indigenous communities; agroforestry and similar approaches can provide livelihoods (pp. 97, 99).


## 6. Limitations

- Detailed local land use is not resolved, so social and economic limits may reduce the real potential (p. 98).
- The estimate is biophysical, based on 1979–2013 climate, and ignores future human pressure, warming, drought, fire and CO₂ fertilisation (pp. 98–99).
- Reduced surface albedo from forests warms high latitudes (p. 97).
- Tropical ground data are sparse; soil carbon dominates uncertainty at high latitudes (pp. 95–96, 98).
- Cropland and urban land, most of the Varuna basin, are outside the 226 Gt C estimate.

# Greenhouse gas emissions from global production and use of nitrogen synthetic fertilisers in agriculture


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Greenhouse gas emissions from global production and use of nitrogen synthetic fertilisers in agriculture Stefano Menegat, Alicia Ledo, Reyes Tirado

**Authors:**
Stefano Menegat, Alicia Ledo, Reyes Tirado

**Journal:**
Scientific Reports, vol. 12, article 14490 (2022)

**Paper type:**
Research article: global supply-chain emissions analysis

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18773-w

**Cite as:**
Menegat, S., Ledo, A., & Tirado, R. (2022). Greenhouse gas emissions from global production and use of nitrogen synthetic fertilisers in agriculture. Scientific Reports, 12, Article 14490. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18773-w Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF (pp. 1–13). Reference year 2018; N₂O GWP = 265.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The synthetic N fertiliser supply chain emitted about 1.13 Gt CO₂e in 2018 (1,129 ± 171 Mt), 10.6% of agricultural and 2.1% of global GHG emissions. Field use gave 58.6%, manufacture 38.8% and transport 2.6%. China, India, the USA and the EU28 gave 62%; India emitted 165.5 Mt CO₂e (14.7%) from 17.6 Mt N. Field N₂O estimates change by about 2× with the emission factor used. Cutting excess synthetic N use offers large, realistic mitigation (pp. 1–5, 7).


## 1. Background

Food systems cause about one-third of human GHG emissions, roughly 16.5 of 54 Gt CO₂e per year. FAO puts 2019 farm-gate emissions at 7.2 Gt CO₂e, with livestock 51.4% and synthetic N fertiliser 8.3% (p. 1). Synthetic N fertiliser emits at three stages: manufacture (ammonia made from fossil-derived hydrogen, releasing CO₂ and CH₄), transport, and field use, where soil microbes turn part of the N into N₂O, a gas with 265 times the warming effect of CO₂ over 100 years. Inventories place manufacture in the industry sector, so farm studies often miss it (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate GHG emissions from the whole synthetic N fertiliser chain, from manufacture to field, for each country in 2018; to derive better direct N₂O emission factors from a large field dataset; to test how emission-factor choice and uncertainty affect results; and to review trends in N use (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

- Country N use from FAOSTAT (107 Mt N in 2018); 96% (102 Mt) assigned to eight fertiliser product groups (pp. 8–9).
- Manufacture and transport emission factors from the Agri-footprint 6.0 dataset; a cross-check with Brentrup et al. factors gave 492 vs 438.5 Mt CO₂e (pp. 7, 9).
- Direct N₂O from the largest field-level dataset of soil N₂O measurements, giving country, regional and global EFs; indirect N₂O (volatilisation, leaching) and urea CO₂ from IPCC methods (pp. 1, 9–10).
- N₂O-N converted with 44/28 and GWP 265; uncertainty by Monte Carlo simulation (pp. 4, 10).

## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Global emissions

Table A. Global emissions by stage, 2018 (Mt CO₂e; Table 1, p. 3) Stage World India Manufacture 438.5 ± 37.1 52.8 ± 7.9 Transport 29.8 ± 4.0 2.4 ± 0.7 CO₂ from urea 86.0 ± 39.1 23.5 ± 10.7 Direct soil N₂O 379.9 ± 160.5 51.7 ± 53.3 Indirect N₂O, volatilisation 66.3 ± 11.3 11.5 ± 5.6 Indirect N₂O, leaching 130.1 ± 31.4 23.7 ± 15.6 Total 1129.1 ± 171.1 165.5 ± 57.4 The total is 10.6% of agricultural emissions, 2.1% of global GHG emissions and 6.8% of agri-food system emissions. Average carbon intensity is 10.48 t CO₂e per t N; the global per-capita footprint is 148.1 kg CO₂e (pp. 1, 3, 6).


### 4.2 Countries

China (316.1 Mt CO₂e, 28.0%), India (165.5, 14.7%), the USA (115.5, 10.2%) and the EU28 (102.4, 9.1%) together emit 62%. China, India, the USA, the EU28 and Brazil use 68% of synthetic N. India has 13.6% of global direct soil N₂O (p. 3). Dividing India's Table 1 values gives about 9.4 kg CO₂e per kg N (our calculation).


### 4.3 Emission factors and uncertainty

- Global direct soil N₂O ranged from 380 to 666 Mt CO₂e (0.91–1.60 Mt N₂O-N) depending on the EF; IPCC Tier 1 gave 1.07 Mt N₂O-N (p. 3).
- The empirical country EF averaged 0.0085 ± 0.0036 (0.85%), against the IPCC default 0.0100 and the wet-dry disaggregated 0.0148 (p. 5).
- Total uncertainty (CV) was 15.1%; manufacture 8.5%, transport 13.5%, direct N₂O 42.2%, urea CO₂ 45.5%. Direct N₂O drives the overall uncertainty because it is both large and uncertain (pp. 4–5). 4.4 Trends and scenarios Per-capita N use rose from about 3 kg (1960) to 15 kg per person (2018). FAO reports a 44% rise in synthetic fertiliser N₂O from 1990 to 2019. N use could reach 260 Mt N/yr by 2050 under an intensive scenario or fall to 85 Mt N/yr with higher NUE; only the latter stays within the planetary boundary for N (pp. 5–6).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Reducing production and use of synthetic N fertiliser offers large and often realistic mitigation; manufacture is a major and overlooked share (pp. 1, 7).

2. Over-application is common; a 48% cut in cereal fertiliser use could keep yields, and better N management helps smallholders (p. 7). 3. Recycling manure, green manures and N-fixing crops, and eating less meat and dairy, reduce the need for synthetic N (pp. 7–8). 4. Better empirical EFs are needed, especially for Asia and Africa (p. 8).


## 6. Limitations

- Data refer to 2018 and are national, not spatially explicit (pp. 7–8).
- Field EFs are scarce for most countries and biased to North America and Europe (pp. 1, 7).
- About 4% of N with unknown product type is missing from manufacture and transport, so totals are underestimated (p. 9).
- Activity data have no uncertainty estimates (p. 7).

# Biochar for agronomy, animal farming, anaerobic digestion, composting, water treatment, soil remediation, construction, energy storage, and carbon sequestration: a review


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Biochar for agronomy, animal farming, anaerobic digestion, composting, water treatment, soil remediation, construction, energy storage, and carbon sequestration: a review Ahmed I. Osman, Samer Fawzy, Mohamed Farghali … David W. Rooney (11 authors)

**Authors:**
Ahmed I. Osman, Samer Fawzy, Mohamed Farghali, Marwa El-Azazy, Ahmed M. Elgarahy, Ramy Amer Fahim, M. I. A. Abdel Maksoud, Abbas Abdullah Ajlan, Mahmoud Yousry, Yasmeen Saleem, David W. Rooney

**Journal:**
Environmental Chemistry Letters, vol. 20, no. 4, pp. 2385–2485 (2022)

**Paper type:**
Review article (101 pages)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01424-x

**Cite as:**
Osman, A. I., Fawzy, S., Farghali, M., El-Azazy, M., Elgarahy, A. M., Fahim, R. A., Maksoud, M. I. A. A., Ajlan, A. A., Yousry, M., Saleem, Y., & Rooney, D. W. (2022). Biochar for agronomy, animal farming, anaerobic digestion, composting, water treatment, soil remediation, construction, energy storage, and carbon sequestration: a review. Environmental Chemistry Letters, 20(4), 2385–2485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01424-x Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers are the journal pages 2385–2485.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Biochar, biomass heated with little oxygen, stores carbon for centuries if it is not burned or oxidised later; its final stores are soils, infrastructure and landfills. The review covers its uses across sectors. On farms, biochar-based fertilisers can raise nutrient use, 1% biochar in cattle diets cut enteric methane by 11–13% in vivo, biochar stabilises biogas digesters, and in compost it cuts methane and N₂O. Most evidence comes from single studies. Barriers are cost, poor kilns, weak policy and awareness; EBC and IBI standards exist (pp. 2385–2386, 2402–2403, 2461–2462).


## 1. Background

Carbon sequestration captures atmospheric carbon and stores it in a stable form. Biochar is a charcoal- like material made by pyrolysis of crop residues, wood or manure. It turns quickly decaying plant carbon into a stable form; a cited meta-analysis found a stable pool (97% of the carbon) with a mean residence time of about 556 years and a labile pool (3%) of 108 days (pp. 2385–2386). THE SINK RULE Biochar counts as a carbon sink only if it is not used for energy and is not thermally degraded or oxidised during or after use. Its final reservoirs are soils, civil infrastructure and landfills (p. 2386).


## 2. Aim of the study

To review  biochar  applications that  act  as carbon  sinks, in  agronomy, animal  farming, anaerobic digestion, composting, environmental remediation, construction and energy storage, and to discuss barriers to large-scale use (p. 2386).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors reviewed a large body of literature and summarised it in 21 tables covering standards, biochar-based fertilisers, feed trials, digestion experiments, composting, pollutant removal, cement and asphalt, and battery electrodes. This summary focuses on soil, animals, biogas and compost, which matter most for the thesis.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Agronomy

Biochar contains few nutrients, so using it as a fertiliser alone needs 10–50 t/ha, which is costly; rates above 50 t/ha harm soil microbes and germination. It is mainly used as an amendment, or at about 1 t/ha as a nutrient carrier. In one tropical study, biochar-based N fertilisers raised corn yield by about 26% over urea alone. Reported effects on soil GHG emissions are inconsistent (pp. 2387, 2395).


### 4.2 Animal farming

Table A. Enteric methane results cited in the review (pp. 2402–2403) Study design Methane change Biochar incubated with rumen fluid –15% 9% biochar –11 to –17% 1% biochar in cattle diets, in vivo –11 to –13% Biochar; biochar + nitrate (one study) –22%; –41% 3.8% biochar in cattle –12.6 L per animal per day 0.8% biochar, growing; finishing cattle –9.5%; –18.4% 0.5% biochar, in vitro –25% Feed biochar also improved growth and feed conversion in goats, pigs and poultry, reduced gut pathogens, and cut ammonia emissions by 17% in broiler chickens. Biochar-amended poultry bedding lowered composting GHG to 63 and 50 kg CO₂e/t, against 183 for the control (pp. 2401–2403).


### 4.3 Anaerobic digestion and composting

- In digesters, biochar buffers volatile fatty acids, reduces ammonia inhibition, supports microbial biofilms and electron transfer, and can raise methane yield and upgrade biogas by adsorbing CO₂ (pp. 2404–2409).
- In compost, biochar cut methane by up to 80% (wheat straw and sewage sludge, 12% biochar) and up to 32% (chicken manure), and reduced N₂O; effects on CO₂ were conflicting (–26.1% to +53.2%) (pp. 2419–2420).

### 4.4 Other uses

Biochar can remove pollutants from water and soil, improve cement, asphalt and building composites, and serve as a precursor for battery and supercapacitor electrodes, though these often need 700 °C or more and chemical activation (pp. 2385, 2460–2461).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Biochar-based carbon removal adds value in many sectors beyond the carbon it stores, if the final use keeps the carbon intact and follows standards (p. 2461). 2. Poorly built stoves and drum kilns in developing countries can raise GHG and toxic emissions; feedstock drying adds cost (p. 2461). 3. Wider use needs awareness among the public and governments, supporting policy, and universal standards beyond EBC and IBI (pp. 2461–2462).


## 6. Limitations

- The review is very broad and summarises other studies, often lab-scale or short-term; many numbers come from a single study.
- Soil GHG effects are reported as inconsistent (p. 2387).
- There are few Indian field examples, and smallholder costs are not worked out (thesis author's assessment).

B., Bange, H. W., Berthet, S., Bian, Z., Bianchi, D., … Zhu, Q. (2024). Global nitrous oxide budget (1980–2020). Earth System Science Data, 16(6), 2543– 2604. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-2543-2024 Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers are the journal pages 2543–2604. Tg N = million tonnes of nitrogen; multiply by 44/28 for N₂O.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Atmospheric N₂O rose from 270 ppb (1750) to 336 ppb (2022), higher than at any time in 800,000 years. Human N₂O emissions rose 40% from 1980 to 2020 (4.8 to 6.7 Tg N/yr). In 2020, direct agriculture gave


### 3.9 Tg N/yr, other direct sources 2.1 and indirect sources 1.3. Total emissions were 18.5 (BU) and 17.0

(TD) Tg N/yr. Europe cut emissions by 31%; China (+82%) and South Asia (+92%) grew most, driven by agricultural N. Concentrations now exceed all CMIP6 scenarios (pp. 2544–2546).


## 1. Background

N₂O is a long-lived greenhouse gas and ozone-depleting substance. It rose by nearly 25%, from 270 ppb in 1750 to 336 ppb in 2022, higher than at any time in the last 800,000 years. Growth exceeded 1.3 ppb/yr in 2020 and 2021, the fastest since 1980. IPCC AR6 attributes 6.4% of enhanced GHG radiative forcing over 1750–2022 to N₂O (pp. 2544–2545).


## 2. Aim of the study

To quantify global N₂O sources and sinks for 1980–2020 in 21 natural and human categories and 18 regions, using bottom-up and top-down methods, and to identify trends and uncertainties (p. 2545).


## 3. What the authors did

Bottom-up (BU) estimates combined inventories (EDGAR v7.0, FAOSTAT), statistical extrapolation of flux measurements and process-based land and ocean models. Top-down (TD) estimates used atmospheric measurements in inverse models. Human sources were split into direct agricultural (fertiliser and manure applied to soils, manure left on pasture, manure management, aquaculture), other direct (fossil fuel and industry, waste and wastewater, biomass burning) and indirect emissions from nitrogen deposited or leached (pp. 2545, 2564). UNITS Results are in Tg N per year (million tonnes of N in N₂O). Multiply by 44/28 to get N₂O mass, then by its GWP for CO₂e.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Global totals

Table A. Human N₂O sources (Tg N/yr; Table 3, p. 2564) Source 1980s 2010s 2020 Direct agricultural (subtotal) 2.4 3.6 3.9 of which direct soil emissions 1.2 2.0 2.1 manure left on pasture 0.9 1.3 1.4 manure management 0.2 0.3 0.3 Other direct (fossil, waste, burning) 2.0 2.1 2.1 Indirect (N deposition, inland waters) 0.9 1.2 1.3 Climate, CO₂, land-cover effects –0.4 –0.6 –0.6 Total human 5.0 6.5 6.7 Total 2020 emissions were 18.5 Tg N/yr (BU; 10.6–27.0) and 17.0 Tg N/yr (TD; 16.6–17.4). In 2010–2019, natural sources gave 65% and human sources 35% of BU emissions; direct agriculture was 56% of human emissions (pp. 2545–2546).


### 4.2 Regions

- Europe, the top emitter in the 1980s (23.6% of human N₂O), cut emissions by 31%, mostly from fossil fuel and industry (pp. 2546, 2574).
- China (+82%) and South Asia (+92%) grew most; in the 2010s they gave 17.8% and 13.2% of human N₂O and 40% and 30% of the global increase (p. 2574).
- In South Asia, direct agricultural N₂O rose from 0.19 to 0.55 Tg N/yr (1980–2020) because of more N fertiliser (p. 2572). 4.3 Atmosphere and uncertainty The atmospheric burden rose from 1527 Tg N (2000s) to 1606 Tg N (2020). Satellite data suggest the lifetime fell from 119 to 117 years. Inversions are least certain over South America, Africa and central and southern Asia; soil N₂O is least certain in tropical forests and in high-fertiliser regions including northern India, eastern China and the US Corn Belt (pp. 2546, 2563).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Human N₂O emissions, driven mainly by agriculture, keep rising and concentrations exceed all CMIP6 scenarios (p. 2545). 2. Tier 2/3 national methods are needed where nitrogen surplus is high, such as eastern China, India and the USA (p. 2576). 3. The authors propose a global N₂O monitoring and modelling network, from surface to stratosphere, to support the UNFCCC Global Stocktake (pp. 2545–2546).


## 6. Limitations

- BU ranges are wide (2020: 10.6–27.0 Tg N/yr) (p. 2545).
- Inversions are poorly constrained in southern Asia because stations are few (p. 2546).
- Results are regional, not district or field level.
- Effects of rising CO₂, forest conversion and biomass burning are poorly quantified (p. 2546).
