# Soil moisture controls over carbon sequestration and greenhouse gas emissions: a review


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Soil moisture controls over carbon sequestration and greenhouse gas emissions: a review Yuefeng Hao, Jiafu Mao, Charles M. Bachmann … Yongjiu Dai (22 authors)

**Authors:**
Yuefeng Hao, Jiafu Mao, Charles M. Bachmann, Forrest M. Hoffman, Gerbrand Koren, Haishan Chen, Hanqin Tian, Jiangong Liu, Jing Tao, Jinyun Tang, Lingcheng Li, Laibao Liu, Martha Apple, Mingjie Shi, Mingzhou Jin, Qing Zhu, Steve Kannenberg, Xiaoying Shi, Xi Zhang, Yaoping Wang, Yilin Fang, Yongjiu Dai

**Journal:**
npj Climate and Atmospheric Science, vol. 8, article 16 (2025)

**Paper type:**
Review article

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-024-00888-8

**Cite as:**
Hao, Y., Mao, J., Bachmann, C. M., Hoffman, F. M., Koren, G., Chen, H., Tian, H., Liu, J., Tao, J., Tang, J., Li, L., Liu, L., Apple, M., Shi, M., Jin, M., Zhu, Q., Kannenberg, S., Shi, X., Zhang, X., … Dai, Y. (2025). Soil moisture controls over carbon sequestration and greenhouse gas emissions: a review. npj Climate and Atmospheric Science, 8, Article 16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-024-00888-8 Open access article under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF. WFPS = water-filled pore space.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Soil moisture controls photosynthesis, respiration, microbial activity and organic matter dynamics, so it governs carbon sequestration and GHG emissions. In the compiled studies, CO₂ shows a 'Peak and Decline' pattern at about 40% WFPS, while CH₄ peaks at 60–80% and N₂O near 80% WFPS, with wide site variation. Drought cuts uptake; floods favour methane. Conservation agriculture, agroforestry and optimised water management (AWD can cut paddy CH₄ by up to 50%) help. Better sensing, hybrid models and long-term policy incentives are needed (pp. 1, 4–9).


## 1. Background

Soil moisture affects plant photosynthesis and respiration, soil microbes, and the breakdown and stabilisation of soil organic matter. Variability in soil moisture accounts for about 90% of interannual variability in global land carbon uptake, and soil moisture limits cut annual photosynthesis by about 15% globally. Drying trends may reduce the land sink by 2–3 Gt C per year (pp. 2–4). Moderate moisture favours storage, but drought and flooding disrupt it. Flooded soils lose oxygen, favouring CH₄ and N₂O; dry soils limit growth and microbial activity (pp. 1, 3).


## 2. Aim of the study

To synthesise how soil moisture regulates carbon sequestration and GHG emissions (CS-GHG) across ecosystems,  identify  moisture  thresholds,  review  how  models  represent  moisture,  and  assess management practices and policies (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors reviewed field and lab studies, compiled the effect of moisture on carbon sequestration by location and land cover (Table 1) and the correlation patterns and peak-emission WFPS thresholds for CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O (Table 2), compared eight ecosystem models (Table 3), and discussed observation methods and policy (pp. 4–8).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Mechanisms

- Root (autotrophic) respiration is more sensitive than microbial respiration: drought cut its share of soil respiration from 33% to 16% in a subtropical forest and from 66% to 35% in dry grasslands (p. 3).
- Aerobic soils mainly emit CO₂; waterlogged soils favour denitrification (N₂O) and methanogenesis (CH₄) (p. 3).
- CO₂ production was 31–40% higher at 65% than at 45% water holding capacity (p. 3). 4.2 Moisture thresholds for emissions Table A. Typical peak-emission WFPS in the compiled studies (pp. 4–5, Table 2) Gas Pattern Typical peak Examples of variation CO₂ Peak and Decline ~40% WFPS Consistent across land covers CH₄ Positive, PD or Trough and Rise 60–80% WFPS 95% European wetlands; 99% Chinese paddies N₂O Positive, PD or Trough and Rise ~80% WFPS 75% UK cropland; 60% Danish forest 4.3 Extremes Drought caused a net biomass carbon loss of 1.2–1.6 Pg in the Amazon and soil carbon losses up to 12.2% in subtropical forests. Drying-rewetting cycles raise CO₂ emissions by 35.7% on average, and freeze-thaw cycles can raise CO₂ up to 1.7 times and N₂O up to 5.8 times. Floods favour CH₄ (pp. 4–5). 4.4 Management and policy
- Conservation agriculture (residue cover, legumes, cover crops, mulching, reduced tillage) keeps moisture and raises soil carbon; practices should be location-specific (pp. 6–7).
- Agroforestry maintains soil moisture and adds carbon inputs (p. 7).
- In rice, AWD can cut CH₄ by up to 50% compared with continuous flooding; irrigation scheduling and drip irrigation avoid waterlogging (p. 7).
- Policy should move from short-term yields to long-term carbon, using subsidies, payments for ecosystem services, carbon credits with robust MRV, and local soil information systems (p. 8).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Soil moisture is pivotal: optimal levels raise sequestration, extremes reduce it (p. 9). 2. Gas-specific thresholds call for targeted moisture management (p. 9). 3. Conservation agriculture, agroforestry and optimised water management are key; predictions need high-resolution sensing, ground networks and hybrid models within a model-experiment (ModEx) loop (pp. 8–9).


## 6. Limitations

- Thresholds are general patterns from varied studies and differ by soil and site (pp. 4–5).
- The AWD figure is an upper value from cited studies, not a mean (p. 7).
- Models still represent moisture effects and human management imperfectly (pp. 6, 8).
- Few Indian or rice-wheat studies are included (thesis author's assessment).

# Biofuel production: exploring renewable energy solutions for a greener future


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Biofuel production: exploring renewable energy solutions for a greener future R. El-Araby Author R. El-Araby

**Journal:**
Biotechnology for Biofuels and Bioproducts, vol. 17, article 129 (2024)

**Paper type:**
Review article (32 pages)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1186/s13068-024-02571-9

**Cite as:**
El-Araby, R. (2024). Biofuel production: exploring renewable energy solutions for a greener future. Biotechnology for Biofuels and Bioproducts, 17, Article 129. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13068-024-02571-9 Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF (32 pages).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This broad review covers biofuels from feedstock to end use. It groups them into four generations (food crops, non-food residues, algae, engineered microbes), describes the main conversion routes including anaerobic digestion to biogas, and weighs benefits (lower GHG, cleaner air, waste use, rural income) against challenges (feedstock supply, land-use change, cost). Most numbers are cited from other studies, such as a GHG cut of up to 90% for cellulosic ethanol.


## 1. Background

Fossil fuels still meet about 80% of energy needs, but reserves are finite and exposed to price shocks and geopolitical tension (pp. 1, 3). Biofuels are fuels made from biomass: plants, algae, agricultural waste, animal waste and food waste. Many can be blended into existing engines and infrastructure (p. 3). IRENA's low-carbon road to 2050 proposes a fivefold rise in biofuel use, from 130 billion litres in 2016 to about 650 billion litres by 2050 (p. 21). Aviation causes 2% of global CO₂ emissions (705 million tonnes), which biojet fuel could help reduce (p. 19).


## 2. Aim of the study

To  review  the  current  state  of  biofuel  production:  feedstock  options,  conversion  technologies, environmental benefits, energy security, economic prospects for farmers and rural areas, and challenges such as land competition and sustainability (p. 1).


## 3. What the author did

The author reviewed published literature across the whole biofuel chain, from feedstock selection to end use. The review compares the generations of biofuels (Table 2, p. 10), describes processes (fermentation, distillation,  transesterification,  anaerobic  digestion  and  thermochemical  routes)  and  discusses sustainability and economic viability. It is a narrative review with no new data or meta-analysis.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Four generations

Table A. Biofuel generations as described in the review (pp. 3, 7–10) Generation Feedstock Strength Weakness First Corn, sugarcane, vegetable oils Mature, economically viable Competes with food; marginal GHG gain Second Crop residues, wood, grasses, municipal waste No food competition; cellulosic ethanol up to 90% GHG cut (cited) Complex, costlier conversion Third Algae Fast growth, non-arable land High start-up and pilot costs Fourth Genetically modified microbes Can turn CO₂ directly into fuel such as ethanol Uncommon, still in development; harvesting costly


### 4.2 Conversion and biogas

- Transesterification of oils to biodiesel runs at about 60 °C for about 90 minutes and gives over 98% of the potential yield (p. 14).
- Anaerobic digestion breaks down organic matter without oxygen to give methane-rich biogas for electricity or fuel. The digestate is used as fertiliser and biosolids condition soil (p. 14).
- Purified biomethane has a methane concentration above 80% (p. 15). 4.3 Use and markets
- The EU standard specifies a 5% bioethanol blend. The USA is the largest ethanol producer (a 10% ethanol, 90% petrol blend), followed by Brazil (27% ethanol) (p. 14).
- India led the Global Biofuel Alliance, agreed on 10 September 2023 (p. 7).
- Solid biomass makes up 85% of global biomass supply; liquid biofuels grew about 2% a year from 2000 to 2018 (p. 12). 4.4 Benefits and challenges
- Benefits: lower GHG emissions, cleaner air (less sulfur dioxide), use of agricultural and food waste, jobs and extra income for farmers (pp. 24–25).
- Challenges: sustainable feedstock supply, land-use change (erosion, nutrient loss, water use, biodiversity loss, GHG from clearing land such as peat) and dependence on fossil fuel prices (pp. 23– 25).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Biofuels can significantly reduce fossil fuel dependence and GHG emissions (p. 28). 2. Cellulosic ethanol from waste biomass and algae fuels are becoming commercially viable (p. 28). 3. Land use and sustainable feedstock supply must remain a priority (p. 28). 4. Supportive policy, R&D to cut costs and integrated biorefineries are needed for a long-term role alongside solar and wind (pp. 28–29).


## 6. Limitations

- Broad narrative review with few quantitative comparisons; most numbers are cited from other studies.
- GHG savings depend on life-cycle assumptions.
- Focus is on liquid transport fuels rather than household biogas.
- No Indian village data or emission factors (thesis author's assessment). NOTE ON THE SOURCE The review places 'dedicated energy crops and algae' in the third generation on p. 3 but treats the third generation as algae on pp. 7–8. This summary follows pp. 7–8.

# Exploring negative emission potential of biochar to achieve carbon neutrality goal in China


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Exploring negative emission potential of biochar to achieve carbon neutrality goal in China Xu Deng, Fei Teng, Minpeng Chen, Zhangliu Du, Bin Wang, Renqiang Li, Pan Wang

**Authors:**
Xu Deng, Fei Teng, Minpeng Chen, Zhangliu Du, Bin Wang, Renqiang Li, Pan Wang

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 15, article 1085 (2024)

**Paper type:**
Research article (national spatial and economic analysis)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45314-y

**Cite as:**
Deng, X., Teng, F., Chen, M., Du, Z., Wang, B., Li, R., & Wang, P. (2024). Exploring negative emission potential of biochar to achieve carbon neutrality goal in China. Nature Communications, 15, Article 1085. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45314-y Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF. NET = negative emission technology.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The authors mapped China's biomass residues on a 0.5° grid and modelled biochar made at 550 °C with syngas co-production. In the sustainable scenario, which keeps residues needed for fodder and ecology, biochar could remove up to 0.92 Gt CO₂ a year at an average net cost of about 90 $/t CO₂. That covers the negative emission demand in most scenarios for China's 2060 neutrality target. Syngas sales cover 32–57% of costs, yield gains only 1–23%. Guangxi, Henan and Shandong are the priority pilot provinces.


## 1. Background

Human activity caused 0.9–1.3 °C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with pre-industrial times. For China to reach carbon neutrality, integrated assessment model scenarios expect negative emission technologies (NETs) to remove 0.01–2.91 Gt CO₂ per year between 2050 and 2060 (p. 1). BECCS can cost more than 100 $ and DACCS more than 200 $ per tonne of CO₂, and both face resource and geological limits; BECCS also competes with crops for land and water. Biochar is an established technology, but its national potential, cost and best locations in China were uncertain (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate, on a map grid, the negative emission potential, economics and priority deployment sites of biochar from several feedstocks in China, and to test whether biochar could meet China's negative emission needs for carbon neutrality by 2060 (pp. 1–2).


## 3. What the authors did

They estimated 16 types of crop residue, 10 types of forestry residue, grass residues and energy crops (such as sweet sorghum and miscanthus) on a 0.5° × 0.5° grid under three scenarios (pp. 2–4, 7–8). Livestock manure was left out (p. 7).

Table A. Feedstock scenarios (pp. 2–4, Table 1) Scenario Collection assumption Biomass available Maximum theoretical 100% of crop and forestry residues


### 2.43 Gt/yr

Sustainable technical 95% crop, 80% forestry; minus feed, rural fuel, raw material and ecological needs


### 1.73 Gt/yr

Current technical 88% crop, 28% forestry; no competition with current uses


### 0.81 Gt/yr

Biochar production was modelled at 550 °C using gasification that co-produces biochar and syngas (p. 8). Costs, syngas income and yield benefits gave net cost curves and maps of priority provinces; a Monte Carlo analysis tested uncertainty (pp. 4, 7).


## 4. Main findings

- Negative emission potential is 1.29 Gt CO₂/yr (maximum theoretical), 0.92 Gt CO₂/yr (sustainable) and 0.43 Gt CO₂/yr (current) (p. 4).
- The median NET demand for China is 1.43 Gt CO₂/yr in 2050 or 2060; with a managed-forest sink of 0.63 Gt CO₂/yr, biochar could meet demand in most scenarios without immature BECCS or DACCS (p. 4).
- Avoided emissions (syngas replacing fossil fuel, lower soil GHG) are about 1.5 times the removal (p. 4).
- The average net cost is about 90 $/t CO₂: 60–96 for agricultural and forestry residues and 101–144 for energy crops and grass residues. BECCS is typically 30–400 and DACCS 30–1000 $/t CO₂ (pp. 4–5).
- Syngas sales offset 32–57% of total costs; yield co-benefits offset only 1–23%. A cited meta-analysis puts biochar's yield gain at about 10% in China against 35% globally (p. 4).
- Agricultural-residue biochar can give a net benefit in some places, driven by yield gains on high-yield cereals in Shandong and Henan and sugarcane in Guangxi; the cost map scale runs down to −52 $/t CO₂ (pp. 5, 7, Fig. 4b).
- Guangxi, Henan and Shandong are priority pilot provinces; pilots could start with agroforestry residues (p. 6).
- Monte Carlo: mean potential 1.07 Gt CO₂/yr (0.68–1.46) and mean cost 92 $/t CO₂ (−13 to 197) (p. 7).

## 5. Conclusions

Biochar is a promising near-term NET for China that should be in the climate mitigation toolbox. Deployment should target regions with high potential and low cost, starting with pilots in Guangxi, Henan and Shandong. Biochar is in the IPCC 2019 Refinement, but local accounting methods are still needed, and the authors call for its inclusion in national emission trading and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (pp. 6–7).


## 6. Limitations

- Not all biomass types are covered; livestock manure was excluded (p. 7).
- The co-production technology does not maximise biochar yield (p. 7).
- Technology learning, economies of scale and changing carbon prices are not modelled (p. 7).
- Land-use change, food competition and biodiversity trade-offs are not fully addressed (p. 7).
- Results use Chinese biomass, soil and price data.
CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The −52 $/t CO₂ figure is the lowest value on the cost map scale for agricultural residues (Fig. 4b), not a reported value for Henan. The paper only says net benefits occur in some places in Shandong, Henan and Guangxi.

# The role of biochar in enhancing soil health & interactions with rhizosphere properties and enzyme activities in organic fertilizer substitution


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

The role of biochar in enhancing soil health & interactions with rhizosphere properties and enzyme activities in organic fertilizer substitution Aamir Ali, Nida Jabeen, Zaid Chachar … Zhenping Yang (10 authors)

**Authors:**
Aamir Ali, Nida Jabeen, Zaid Chachar, Sadaruddin Chachar, Shoaib Ahmed, Nazir Ahmed, Azhar Ali Laghari, Zulfiqar Ali Sahito, Rasulov Farruhbek, Zhenping Yang

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Plant Science, vol. 16, article 1595208 (2025)

**Paper type:**
Review article (qualitative)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1595208

**Cite as:**
Ali, A., Jabeen, N., Chachar, Z., Chachar, S., Ahmed, S., Ahmed, N., Laghari, A. A., Sahito, Z. A., Farruhbek, R., & Yang, Z. (2025). The role of biochar in enhancing soil health & interactions with rhizosphere properties and enzyme activities in organic fertilizer substitution. Frontiers in Plant Science, 16, Article 1595208. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1595208 Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF (23 pages). CEC = cation exchange capacity; SOM = soil organic matter.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This qualitative review explains how biochar, especially combined with compost, manure or bio-organic fertilisers, improves the rhizosphere: better structure, water retention, CEC and pH, more enzyme activity, and less nutrient leaching and runoff. Its stable carbon can last decades to centuries. The review gives no effect sizes, notes that gains are larger in sandy than clay soils, and lists cost, inconsistent quality and logistics as the main barriers.


## 1. Background

Biochar is the carbon-rich product of pyrolysis of crop residues, forestry by-products or municipal waste, typically at 300–700 °C with little oxygen (p. 2). Temperatures above 500 °C give more stable carbon and larger surface area; below 400 °C the biochar keeps more nutrients (p. 8). Heavy use of chemical fertiliser has caused soil degradation, water pollution through runoff, loss of soil biodiversity and GHG emissions from production and transport (p. 2). Organic fertilisers can replace part of it, but how biochar interacts with the rhizosphere (the soil around roots) and soil enzymes in this setting had not been explored enough (p. 3).


## 2. Aim of the study

To compile knowledge on the short- and long-term effects of biochar, especially with organic fertilisers, on rhizosphere properties, soil enzyme activity and nutrient dynamics, and to identify challenges and gaps. The review starts from the hypothesis that combining biochar with organic fertilisers significantly improves rhizosphere properties and enzyme activity (p. 3).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors reviewed published studies on rhizosphere properties, organic fertilisers and their limits, biochar's properties and mechanisms, enzyme activity, short- and long-term effects, environmental implications (GHG, runoff, ISFM) and practical barriers. Two summary tables cover soil properties (Table 1, p. 16) and plant growth (Table 2, p. 19). No new data or meta-analysis was produced.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Soil and rhizosphere

Table A. Effects of biochar on soil properties (p. 16, Table 1) Property Effect Detail Structure Improves aggregation, reduces compaction More porosity and water infiltration Water retention Raises moisture-holding capacity Especially in sandy or arid soils pH Raises pH in acidic soils Acts as a liming agent CEC Improves nutrient retention Better use of N, K and Ca Microbial habitat Space for microbes More microbial biomass and enzyme activity SOM Long-term stabilisation of organic carbon Supports carbon sequestration


### 4.2 Nutrients, enzymes and time

- Organic fertilisers release nutrients slowly and vary in composition, which can delay supply and reduce yield in intensive systems (p. 7).
- With biochar and manure, dehydrogenase, phosphatase and protease activity rise in the short term; N retained in biochar pores supports urease and other N-cycle enzymes (pp. 10, 13).
- Short term: better aeration, water retention and less leaching, particularly in sandy or highly permeable soils (p. 13).
- Long term: stable carbon can remain for decades or centuries; more SOM and stable aggregates reduce erosion (p. 14).
- Biochar holds N, P and K and releases them gradually, reducing leaching and volatilisation and the frequency of fertiliser applications (p. 14). 4.3 Environment and practice
- Biochar adsorbs ammonium, potassium, calcium, nitrate and phosphate, keeping them out of rivers and lakes and reducing eutrophication (p. 17).
- The review states biochar reduces N₂O and CH₄ (pp. 15, 17) but gives no effect sizes and lists GHG effects as needing further investigation (p. 19).
- Biochar is described as a cornerstone of integrated soil fertility management (ISFM) (p. 18).
- Barriers: cost for smallholders, no quality standard, limited production capacity, technical skill needs, possible heavy metals, and pH effects of over-application (p. 18).

## 5. Conclusions

Combining biochar with organic fertilisers can raise productivity, reduce environmental impacts and support climate mitigation. Research should focus on long-term effects across seasons, crop-specific

responses in maize, wheat and rice, site-specific recommendations by soil type, use with synthetic fertilisers, and the best feedstock, pyrolysis temperature and dose (pp. 1, 19–20).


## 6. Limitations

- Qualitative review with no effect sizes for yield, SOC or GHG.
- Benefits depend on soil, feedstock and dose; clay soils may gain less than sandy soils (p. 19).
- Most cited evidence is short-term (p. 19).
- The GWP values quoted (N₂O ~300, CH₄ ~25) are older values; use the GWPs of the IPCC report the thesis follows.

# Carbon for soils, not soils for carbon


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Carbon for soils, not soils for carbon Gabriel Y. K. Moinet, Renske Hijbeek, Detlef P. van Vuuren, Ken E. Giller

**Authors:**
Gabriel Y. K. Moinet, Renske Hijbeek, Detlef P. van Vuuren, Ken E. Giller

**Journal:**
Global Change Biology, vol. 29, issue 9, pp. 2384–2398 (2023)

**Paper type:**
Opinion / critical review

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16570

**Cite as:**
Moinet, G. Y. K., Hijbeek, R., van Vuuren, D. P., & Giller, K. E. (2023). Carbon for soils, not soils for carbon. Global Change Biology, 29(9), 2384–2398. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16570 Open access article under a CC BY licence. Page numbers refer to the early-view PDF (pp. 1–15); the issue version is pp. 2384–2398. SOC = soil organic carbon.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Soil carbon is promoted as a win-win for climate and food. The authors show that almost no global estimates include saturation; adding it cuts the potential contribution by 53–81% to 2100. Gains can also reverse, and across more than 21 meta-analyses the yield effect of more SOC is negative, neutral or positive. They argue against global SOC targets for farm soils and for soil-smart, locally adapted agriculture, with SOC gains treated as a co-benefit.


## 1. Background

Keeping warming below 1.5 °C needs net-zero CO₂ within decades, and nearly all 1.5 °C scenarios rely on CO₂ removal (p. 1). Soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration is promoted by high-level initiatives such as 4p1000 (launched at COP21 in 2015) as a way to help both the climate and food security (p. 2). IPCC WG3 (2022) estimated 1.8–4.1 Gt CO₂ per year for croplands, grasslands, agroforestry and biochar, and ranked SOC sequestration fourth among options in 2030 (pp. 3–4).


## 2. Aim of the study

To critically re-examine whether global SOC sequestration strategies deliver both climate mitigation and food production benefits, by accounting for saturation and reviewing the evidence on SOC and crop yields (p. 1).


## 3. What the authors did

The  authors  reviewed  top-down  (recovering  historical  losses  or  plant  inputs)  and  bottom-up (extrapolating measured rates) estimates of global potential. Starting from Bossio et al.'s 3.3 Gt CO₂/yr, they recalculated cumulative sequestration to 2100 under a constant rate, a slowly decreasing rate and a rapidly decreasing rate (30-year half-life), and compared it with the 1.5 °C budget (pp. 3–5). They reviewed more than 21 meta-analyses on SOC and yield (Table 1, pp. 7–8) and discussed measurement problems (p. 3).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Climate potential

Table A. Effect of saturation on cumulative SOC sequestration to 2100 (pp. 4–5, Fig. 1) Assumption Cumulative 2100 (Gt CO₂) Share of 1.5 °C effort (Lal / Bossio start) Constant rate 257 23.7% / not stated Slowly or rapidly decreasing rate 121 or 49 4.5–11.1% / 1.6–4.0%

- Ignoring saturation overestimates potential by 53–81% (p. 4).
- Historical soil carbon loss estimates range from 40 Gt C (148 Gt CO₂) to 537 Gt C (1,989 Gt CO₂); the latest is 116 Gt C (430 Gt CO₂) (p. 3).
- The input-based estimate of 0.52 Gt CO₂/yr (Janzen et al., 2022) implies an insignificant contribution (0–1%) (p. 5).
- The total net emission reduction needed for 1.5 °C is about 3000 Gt CO₂ (p. 5).
- SOC is reversible and shorter-lived than fossil carbon, so it cannot substitute for or delay emission cuts (p. 4). 4.2 Yields and measurement
- Across more than 21 meta-analyses, yield effects of more SOC range from negative to positive (p. 1, Table 1).
- Neutral or negative effects are found much more often when studies correct for N, P and K supply; most positive results come from studies where extra nutrients were included (p. 9).
- Benefits are larger on sandy soils, and one study found a positive effect in tropical climates (p. 9).
- The yield effect of SOC levels off at about 2% SOC (p. 9).
- Many studies report concentrations, not stocks; depth is reported inconsistently; equivalent soil mass methods are more accurate (p. 3).

## 5. Conclusions

The evidence does not justify global agendas that put SOC sequestration first. The authors call for 'soil- smart agriculture', adapted to each local context and measuring many soil functions together, and for moving away from global SOC targets in agricultural soils. SOC sequestration should be regarded as a co- benefit (p. 1). They also see better nitrogen use efficiency as a missed opportunity to cut N₂O, since agriculture causes about 70% of human N₂O emissions (p. 2).


## 6. Limitations

- Opinion paper; recalculations rely on published estimates and simple saturation assumptions.
- No new field data and no India-specific analysis.
- Yield evidence is summarised from meta-analyses, not re-analysed. PAGE NUMBERS This pack cites the early-view PDF (pp. 1–15). In the issue version (vol. 29(9)) the article runs from p. 2384 to p. 2398.

description: From 537 publications and more than 5,000 paired measurements, the authors found that in grasslands organic fertiliser raised aboveground biomass by 56% (inorganic 42%) and SOC by 19% (inorganic 2%), without the 18% loss of species richness seen with chemical fertiliser. # A global meta-analysis on the effects of organic and inorganic fertilization on grasslands and croplands


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

A global meta-analysis on the effects of organic and inorganic fertilization on grasslands and croplands Ting-Shuai Shi, Scott L. Collins, Kailiang Yu, Josep Peñuelas, Jordi Sardans, Hailing Li, Jian-Sheng Ye

**Authors:**
Ting-Shuai Shi, Scott L. Collins, Kailiang Yu, Josep Peñuelas, Jordi Sardans, Hailing Li, Jian-Sheng Ye

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 15, article 3411 (2024)

**Paper type:**
Research article (global meta-analysis)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47829-w

**Cite as:**
Shi, T.-S., Collins, S. L., Yu, K., Peñuelas, J., Sardans, J., Li, H., & Ye, J.-S. (2024). A global meta-analysis on the effects of organic and inorganic fertilization on grasslands and croplands. Nature Communications, 15, Article 3411. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467- 024-47829-w Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF. SOC = soil organic carbon; MAT = mean annual temperature.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

From 537 publications and more than 5,000 paired measurements, the authors found that in grasslands organic fertiliser raised aboveground biomass by 56% (inorganic 42%) and SOC by 19% (inorganic 2%), without the 18% loss of species richness seen with chemical fertiliser. In croplands (SOC only), organic inputs also raised SOC: by 32% in cooler areas (more than grasslands) and 34% in warmer areas (less than grasslands' 62%). Tillage may explain the weaker warm-climate cropland response.


## 1. Background

Inorganic fertiliser increases plant biomass but often reduces plant diversity in grasslands, a well-known trade-off (pp. 1–2). Organic fertilisers such as manure and compost may be a nature-based alternative. Grasslands cover about 41% of the land surface (excluding Greenland and Antarctica) and store about 34% of terrestrial carbon (p. 2). It was unclear whether croplands and grasslands differ in SOC response at comparable organic rates (p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To compare organic and inorganic fertilisation effects on aboveground biomass, plant diversity and SOC, and to find which climate and soil factors change these effects. One hypothesis was that croplands would show SOC gains comparable to grasslands (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

The search yielded 537 publications (described as 537 experiments in the abstract) on all continents except Antarctica (pp. 1, 7).

Table A. Paired measurements compiled (p. 7) Variable Inorganic (grassland) Organic (grassland) Organic (cropland) Aboveground biomass 1540 350 – Species richness 1625 155 – Pielou evenness 191 89 – SOC 799 388 367 Effects were calculated as weighted log response ratios and related to mean annual temperature (MAT), soil water content, soil properties and fertiliser rate with mixed-effects models. Organic inputs were livestock manure or compost (88% of experiments) or industrial organic fertiliser (12%); 12% of organic trials also added inorganic NPK. Trials where manure brought exotic seeds were excluded. About 97% of grassland experiments lasted under 10 years, while 74% of cropland experiments lasted over 10 years (pp. 5, 7).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Grasslands

- Inorganic fertiliser raised biomass by 42% but cut species richness by 18% and evenness by 6% (p. 2).
- Organic fertiliser raised biomass by 56% with no diversity loss; compared with inorganic it gave 10% more richness and evenness (p. 2).
- Organic fertiliser raised SOC by 19% vs unfertilised and 15% vs inorganic; inorganic raised SOC by 2% (p. 2).
- Organic fertiliser raised richness more in wetter grasslands; higher inorganic rates caused larger species losses (pp. 2–3). 4.2 Grasslands vs croplands (SOC) Table B. SOC change under organic fertilisation by climate (p. 3, Fig. 5a) Climate Croplands Grasslands MAT under 15 °C +32% +14% Warmer regions +34% +62%
- At comparable organic rates, SOC increases were equal in grasslands and croplands (p. 3).
- The SOC gain rose with organic rate and fell as initial SOC rose, more strongly in croplands (p. 3).
- With warming, the SOC response rose in grasslands but fell in croplands; the authors suggest tillage in warm regions speeds SOC decay (pp. 3, 5).

## 5. Conclusions

Organic fertilisation is a potential nature-based solution that raises forage production and soil carbon in grasslands without the diversity loss caused by inorganic fertiliser. Locally sourced, non-contaminated manure or industrial organic fertiliser should be used to avoid exotic species and other side effects (pp. 1, 5).


## 6. Limitations

- Biomass and diversity results are for grasslands only; croplands were analysed for SOC only (p. 7).
- Grassland trials were mostly short (under 10 years) (p. 7).
- SOC is expressed as percent change, not as stock per hectare.
- GHG emissions from manure (N₂O, CH₄) and crop yields were not assessed.
- Few experiments come from South Asian croplands (thesis author's assessment). CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The 56%, 42%, 19%, 15% and 2% figures apply to grasslands. Croplands are not simply 'weaker': they gained more SOC than grasslands in cooler climates and less only in warmer ones.

# Important role of Fe oxides in global soil carbon stabilization and stocks


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Important role of Fe oxides in global soil carbon stabilization and stocks Nan Jia, Lei Li, Hui Guo, Mingyu Xie

**Authors:**
Nan Jia, Lei Li, Hui Guo, Mingyu Xie

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 15, article 10318 (2024)

**Paper type:**
Research article (global meta-analysis and mapping)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-54832-8

**Cite as:**
Jia, N., Li, L., Guo, H., & Xie, M. (2024). Important role of Fe oxides in global soil carbon stabilization and stocks. Nature Communications, 15, Article 10318. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-54832-8 Open access article under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF. OC-Fe = iron-bound organic carbon; MAOC = mineral-associated organic carbon; POC = particulate organic carbon.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using 3,395 observations from 178 publications and a random forest model, the authors mapped iron- bound organic carbon (OC-Fe) in the top 30 cm of soil. The global stock is 233 Pg C, about 33% of topsoil SOC. Soils hold on average 33% of their modelled iron-bound maximum; croplands are lowest at 25.5%, with a 143 Pg C deficit. Croplands also have the lowest mean SOC (17.2 g/kg). Soil pH is the top control. The authors call for mineral factors in soil carbon models.


## 1. Background

Soil organic carbon (SOC) is the largest continuously cycling carbon pool on land. It includes particulate organic carbon (POC), partly decomposed plant material with a short residence time, and mineral- associated organic carbon (MAOC), protected by bonds with minerals (p. 1). Fe-Al oxides are the primary minerals bound to SOC (p. 4), but the global amount of iron-bound carbon (OC-Fe), its maximum capacity (OC-Femax) and its controls were unclear (p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To map Fe-Al oxides and use them to estimate global stocks of SOC, MAOC and OC-Fe; to find the factors controlling OC-Fe; and to estimate the contribution of OC-Fe to SOC and MAOC (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors compiled 3,395 observations from 178 publications that reported SOC and at least one mineral factor, with OC-Fe extracted by the citrate-bicarbonate-dithionite method; pot, lab and model studies were excluded (p. 7). A random forest model (R² = 0.90 in five-fold cross-validation) predicted OC-Fe and OC-Femax for 0–5, 5–15 and 15–30 cm across croplands, forests, grasslands, shrublands and wetlands (130.1 million km²; tundra and deserts excluded) (pp. 3–5).


## 4. Main findings

- The global topsoil OC-Fe stock is 232.9 Pg C, 33.5 ± 15.6% of SOC (pp. 3, 6).
- Mean SOC was highest in wetlands (117.9 g/kg) and permafrost (117.6 g/kg) and lowest in croplands (17.2 ± 19.7 g/kg); in topsoil, croplands were also lowest (19.5 ± 10.8 g/kg) (p. 2).
- Soils hold on average 33.0% of their modelled OC-Fe maximum, leaving a global deficit of 995 Pg C (Table 1).
- Large deficits occur at the equator and mid-latitudes (p. 1).
- Soil pH is the most important control: lower pH raises Fe and Al in solution and increases SOC adsorption onto Fe oxides. Oxalate-extractable Fe, clay and silt, and total N follow (pp. 3, 5). Table A. OC-Fe stocks by ecosystem, 0–30 cm (Table 1, p. 5) Ecosystem Area (M km²) OC-Fe (Pg C) Saturation (%) Deficit (Pg C) Cropland 13.6 20.2 25.5 143.0 Forest 49.2 118.2 27.8 516.9 Grassland 37.7 68.3 37.1 247.5 Shrubland 14.1 22.3 42.7 80.6 Wetland 2.2 3.9 48.5 7.0 Global 130.1 232.9 33.0 995.0

## 5. Conclusions

Iron oxides play an important role in stabilising soil carbon worldwide. Mineral factors should be added to soil carbon models to improve predictions. The global maps of OC-Fe and OC-Femax can guide soil carbon sequestration, although OC-Fe extraction methods carry uncertainty and OC-Femax comes from an idealised model (pp. 1, 7).


## 6. Limitations

- Sparse data in northern Canada, central and western Australia, Russia and western Europe (p. 7).
- Few subsoil observations, so only 0–30 cm was mapped with confidence (p. 7).
- Part of the variation remains unexplained (p. 7).
- No management practices were tested; the maps are global and not specific to Indian alluvial soils.

# Microbial necromass in cropland soils: A global meta‐analysis of management effects


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Microbial necromass in cropland soils: A global meta-analysis of management effects Ranran Zhou, Yuan Liu, Jennifer A. J. Dungait … Jing Tian (9 authors)

**Authors:**
Ranran Zhou, Yuan Liu, Jennifer A. J. Dungait, Amit Kumar, Jinsong Wang, Lisa K. Tiemann, Fusuo Zhang, Yakov Kuzyakov, Jing Tian

**Journal:**
Global Change Biology, vol. 29, issue 7, pp. 1998–2014 (2023)

**Paper type:**
Research article (global meta-analysis); accepted manuscript used

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16613

**Cite as:**
Zhou, R., Liu, Y., Dungait, J. A. J., Kumar, A., Wang, J., Tiemann, L. K., Zhang, F., Kuzyakov, Y., & Tian, J. (2023). Microbial necromass in cropland soils: A global meta- analysis of management effects. Global Change Biology, 29(7), 1998–2014. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16613 Page numbers refer to the accepted manuscript PDF ('AM p.'), which differs from the published pages 1998–2014. NT/RT = no or reduced tillage.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Across 481 paired observations from 61 articles, cropland management raised microbial necromass carbon by 12% (N fertiliser), 14% (cover crops), 20% (no or reduced tillage), 21% (manure) and 21% (straw); biochar had no effect. Straw worked best in semi-arid and cool climates and soils with pH < 8; NT/RT in warm, humid areas; manure everywhere. Effects were absent in sandy soils and short trials (≤3 years). Necromass made up 45–52% of the SOC gain under the main practices.


## 1. Background

Microbial necromass, the remains of dead bacteria and fungi, is a large and persistent part of soil organic carbon (SOC); in this dataset it was about 52% of SOC (AM p. 26). It is measured with amino sugar biomarkers: muramic acid comes only from bacteria, while glucosamine comes mainly from fungi (AM pp. 7, 11). Management effects had been measured in single studies but not summarised globally (AM p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To find how N fertiliser, manure, straw, biochar, no or reduced tillage (NT/RT) and cover crops change microbial necromass C, its contribution to SOC and its accumulation efficiency (necromass gain per unit SOC gain), and which climate and soil conditions favour accumulation (AM p. 7).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors selected 61 articles giving 481 paired observations, mostly from East Asia, North America and Western Europe (AM p. 10). Fungal and bacterial necromass C were calculated from glucosamine and muramic acid with standard conversion factors (AM p. 11). They calculated response ratios and

tested climate, soil pH, texture, initial SOC, straw amount and experiment duration with Random Forest and structural equation models (AM pp. 15–18).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Effect of management on total microbial necromass C (AM p. 15, Fig. 2a) Practice Change Notes Manure +21% Bacterial necromass +29%; works in all climates and soil pH Straw amendment +21% Fungal necromass +26%; best at pH < 8, semi-arid and cool climates No or reduced tillage +20% Mainly in warm and humid climates Cover crops +14% Humid and warm areas N fertiliser +12% Only in alkaline soils Biochar no effect Raised SOC but lowered the necromass share

- Only straw and NT/RT raised the share of SOC that is necromass (fungal share); manure raised the bacterial share but not the total share (AM p. 15).
- Manure raised necromass by 42% in warm climates, 28% in humid and 25% in semi-arid climates (AM p. 16).
- Manure and straw effects were larger when initial SOC was above 12 g/kg (AM p. 16).
- Effects were strongest in loam and clay soils and absent in sandy soils (AM p. 17).
- No significant effects in trials of 3 years or less, except manure; medium- to long-term trials showed the gains (AM p. 17).
- SOC rose 13–24% under these practices, and necromass made up 45–52% of the SOC increase, 9– 16% more than under N fertiliser (AM pp. 3, 26).

## 5. Conclusions

Long-term cropland management increases SOC by increasing microbial necromass. Getting the most necromass and SOC requires site-specific management matched to climate and soil (AM pp. 3, 28).


## 6. Limitations

- Amino sugar conversion factors give approximate necromass values (AM p. 11).
- Studies are concentrated in East Asia, North America and Western Europe (AM p. 10); few come from Indian rice-wheat systems (thesis author's assessment).
- Results are percentage changes, not sequestration rates per hectare.
- This pack uses the accepted manuscript; page numbers differ from the published version.

# Tree functional traits, forest biomass, and tree species diversity interact with site properties to drive forest soil carbon


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Tree functional traits, forest biomass, and tree species diversity interact with site properties to drive forest soil carbon Laurent Augusto, Antra Boča

**Authors:**
Laurent Augusto, Antra Boča

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 13, article 1097 (2022)

**Paper type:**
Research article (global data compilation)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-28748-0

**Cite as:**
Augusto, L., & Boča, A. (2022). Tree functional traits, forest biomass, and tree species diversity interact with site properties to drive forest soil carbon. Nature Communications, 13, Article 1097. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-28748-0 Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF. Amax = leaf maximum photosynthetic capacity.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

From 454 mature single-species stands in 136 sites, tree traits (mainly leaf photosynthetic capacity, Amax) and standing biomass explained about half (48.5%) of local variation in forest SOC. Trait effects were strongest in boreal climates and on acidic, poor, coarse soils, and weak in the warm-wet tropics. Mixed forests stored more SOC only when they also produced more biomass (r = +0.61). The authors recommend more biomass, more species and traits matched to the site, and protecting natural forests in the tropics.


## 1. Background

Forests store carbon in trees and soils in similar amounts. Tree biomass reaches limits in many regions and is vulnerable to windthrow, drought, wildfire, pests and disease, so storing carbon in forest soils is less risky (p. 2). How tree species influence soil organic carbon (SOC) was unclear and hotly debated (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To test how tree functional traits, standing biomass and species diversity interact with climate and soil to control forest SOC, and to suggest how to manage forests for more soil carbon (pp. 1–2).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors compiled 114 articles covering 454 mature single-species stands in 136 sites, comparing 178 species from 35 families growing under comparable conditions; stands were at least 30 years old and peat soils were excluded (pp. 2, 6). SOC was compared on an equivalent soil mass basis. Data on two- species mixtures and on SOC stability were extracted for 29 and 30 sites (p. 2).


## 4. Main findings

- A model based on Amax and standing biomass explained 48.5% of SOC variance (37.0% Amax, 11.5% biomass) (p. 2).
- Conservative species (low Amax, often ectomycorrhizal gymnosperms) had larger SOC pools than acquisitive species (often arbuscular-mycorrhizal angiosperms); gymnosperms stored more SOC on average (p. 3).
- Trait effects were strongest under boreal climate and on acidic, nutrient-poor, coarse-textured soils (p. 1).
- In warm-wet tropical regions, traits did not play an important role in SOC storage (p. 5).
- Mixtures increased SOC only when they overyielded in biomass; SOC gain correlated with biomass gain (r = +0.61, P = 0.016) (p. 5, Fig. 5).
- Mycorrhizal type and root traits influenced SOC decomposability (p. 4, Fig. 4).

## 5. Conclusions

The forest carbon sink can be optimised by (1) increasing standing biomass, (2) increasing tree species richness, and (3) choosing composition by tree traits suited to local conditions (p. 1). In tropical areas the most urgent goal is to protect or restore natural forests. At mid-latitudes or on fertile soils broadleaf species are suggested, and at high latitudes or on poor soils needleleaf species (p. 5).


## 6. Limitations

- Data are scarce for Africa, Asia (except China), the tropics and Russia, where selection criteria were applied flexibly (p. 6).
- Mixed-stand evidence comes from 29 sites with two-species mixtures (pp. 2, 6).
- Mostly topsoil data; deep-soil data were rarely available (p. 6).
- Results concern forest stands, not farm trees or agroforestry. CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The paper links broadleaf species to mid-latitudes or fertile soils and needleleaf species to high latitudes or poor soils (p. 5); it does not recommend both at the same latitudes.

# Unprotected carbon dominates decadal soil carbon increase


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Unprotected carbon dominates decadal soil carbon increase Minglong Liu, Shilu Zheng, Elise Pendall … Ming Nie (9 authors)

**Authors:**
Minglong Liu, Shilu Zheng, Elise Pendall, Pete Smith, Jiajia Liu, Jinquan Li, Changming Fang, Bo Li, Ming Nie

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 16, article 2008 (2025)

**Paper type:**
Research article (global data synthesis)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57354-z

**Cite as:**
Liu, M., Zheng, S., Pendall, E., Smith, P., Liu, J., Li, J., Fang, C., Li, B., & Nie, M. (2025). Unprotected carbon dominates decadal soil carbon increase. Nature Communications, 16, Article 2008. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57354-z Open access article under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the 8-page article PDF. POC = particulate organic carbon; MAOC = mineral-associated organic carbon.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

From 7,219 soil samples on six continents (2000–2022), particulate organic carbon (POC) rose by 21.8% while mineral-associated carbon (MAOC) fell by 5.3% (not significant), giving an 11.0% rise in total SOC and a 29.1% rise in the POC:MAOC ratio. Soil carbon is growing but becoming less stable. Planted forests and grazed grasslands lost POC, and Asian croplands lost POC while North American croplands gained it. The authors call for strategies that protect POC and help convert it to MAOC.


## 1. Background

Soil organic carbon (SOC) splits into particulate organic carbon (POC), which comes mainly from plants, is easy for microbes to reach and lasts years to decades, and mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC), which comes mainly from microbial by-products bound to clay and silt and lasts decades to centuries (p. 1). Global SOC storage appears to have risen, but how the two fractions changed over time was unquantified (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate global trends in POC and MAOC from 2000 to 2022 and to test how human disturbance and land management (planted forests, grazing, cropland practice) affect them (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors screened 1,826 articles, kept 456, and added data from databases such as ESDAC and SCaRP (p. 5). Only field samples from 0–40 cm depth separated with standard physical fractionation were used: POC was the light (< 1.6–1.85 g/cm³) or coarse (> 20–63 μm) fraction and MAOC the rest (pp. 5–6). This gave 7,219 samples: 3,614 cropland (1,533 Asia, 736 North America), 2,130 forest and 1,475 grassland (p. 6). Linear mixed-effects models estimated trends over sampling year, with depth, continent and land type as random effects weighted by land area (p. 6).

CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The earlier notes gave 3,603 cropland, 2,149 forest and 1,547 grassland samples. These come from the Fig. 1 caption (p. 2) and sum to 7,299; the Methods counts (p. 6) sum to the stated 7,219 and are used here.


## 4. Main findings

- POC was 27.4% and MAOC 70.0% of total SOC on average (p. 2).
- From 2000 to 2022 POC rose by 21.8% (P < 0.001), MAOC fell by 5.3% (P = 0.163, not significant) and total SOC rose by 11.0% (P = 0.003) (p. 2).
- The POC:MAOC ratio rose by 29.1% (p. 1), signalling falling SOC stability.
- POC fell in planted forests (P = 0.015) and grazed grasslands (P = 0.003) and rose in ungrazed grasslands (P < 0.001) (pp. 2–3).
- Across all croplands POC was stable (P = 0.870), but it fell in Asia and rose in North America (P < 0.001 for both); MAOC followed the same pattern (p. 3).
- MAOC rose in grazed grasslands, but total SOC did not change because POC fell (p. 4).

## 5. Conclusions

The global SOC increase is mainly driven by unprotected POC, so SOC stability is decreasing under climate change and human activity (p. 1). Maintaining soil carbon sinks needs strategies focused on POC, such as reducing grazing intensity, protecting forests and conservation agriculture, while helping POC convert to MAOC through less disturbance, deep-rooted plants and nitrogen-rich inputs (pp. 4–5).


## 6. Limitations

- Trends compare different sites sampled in different years rather than repeat sampling (thesis author's assessment; the paper does not discuss this).
- Only surface soils (0–40 cm) were included (p. 5).
- Results for Asian croplands are pooled; there is no South Asian or Indo-Gangetic result.
- Sample size varies across years; random-subsample checks did not change the conclusions (p. 6). CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The earlier notes said fractionation methods may differ between labs. The paper used only standard methods and reports that the choice of method does not alter its conclusions (p. 6, Suppl. Table 7).

# The positive effect of plant diversity on soil carbon depends on climate


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

The positive effect of plant diversity on soil carbon depends on climate Marie Spohn, Sumanta Bagchi, Lori A. Biederman … Laura Yahdjian (30 authors)

**Authors:**
Marie Spohn, Sumanta Bagchi, Lori A. Biederman, Elizabeth T. Borer, Kari Anne Bråthen, Miguel N. Bugalho, Maria C. Caldeira, Jane A. Catford, Scott L. Collins, Nico Eisenhauer, Nicole Hagenah, Sylvia Haider, Yann Hautier, Johannes M. H. Knops, Sally E. Koerner, Lauri Laanisto, Ylva Lekberg, Jason P. Martina, Holly Martinson, Rebecca L. McCulley, Pablo L. Peri, Petr Macek, Sally A. Power, Anita C. Risch, Christiane Roscher, Eric W. Seabloom, Carly Stevens, G. F. Veen, Risto Virtanen, Laura Yahdjian

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 14, article 6624 (2023)

**Paper type:**
Research article (global observational network study)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42340-0

**Cite as:**
Spohn, M., Bagchi, S., Biederman, L. A., Borer, E. T., Bråthen, K. A., Bugalho, M. N., Caldeira, M. C., Catford, J. A., Collins, S. L., Eisenhauer, N., Hagenah, N., Haider, S., Hautier, Y., Knops, J. M. H., Koerner, S. E., Laanisto, L., Lekberg, Y., Martina, J. P., Martinson, H., … Yahdjian, L. (2023). The positive effect of plant diversity on soil carbon depends on climate. Nature Communications, 14, Article 6624. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42340-0 Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF. MAT = mean annual temperature; MAP = mean annual precipitation; AI = aridity index (lower = drier).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Across 84 grasslands on six continents, plant diversity (Shannon index) was positively related to soil carbon content and to the soil C:N ratio. The links were weak across all sites (R² = 0.09) but strong in the warmest, driest and most arid quartiles (R² 0.38–0.56), and absent in cooler, moister sites. Plant biomass was related to SOC but not to diversity, so diversity seems to act through organic matter quality, not quantity. Restoring plant diversity likely enhances SOC sequestration, especially in warm and arid climates.


## 1. Background

Plant diversity is positively related to SOC in many ecosystems, usually explained by higher productivity and so more carbon input (p. 1). Most evidence comes from short, small-scale experiments at single sites, which may underestimate slow soil effects, and little is known about how climate changes the relationship (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To test how plant diversity relates to SOC and soil C:N ratio across grasslands spanning wide climate gradients, and whether the link works through plant biomass (quantity) or organic matter quality (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors used pre-treatment data from 84 natural and semi-natural Nutrient Network grassland sites (19 grassland types), collected 2007–2020 with one protocol (pp. 2, 7). Each site had about 30 plots of 5 × 5 m; plant cover was recorded in a 1 × 1 m subplot to compute the Shannon index, aboveground biomass was clipped (74 sites), and three soil cores from 0–10 cm were pooled per plot and analysed in one laboratory (p. 7). Regressions used site means, across all sites and within quartiles of temperature, precipitation and aridity (21 sites each), and structural equation models compared pathways (p. 8). CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The earlier notes said diversity was measured as species richness and the Shannon index. All analyses in the paper use the Shannon index only (pp. 7–8).


## 4. Main findings

- SOC was positively correlated with the Shannon index across all sites (R² = 0.09, P = 0.005) and rose by a factor of 2.6 from one species to a Shannon index of 2.5 (p. 3).
- Soil C:N ratio was also positively correlated with diversity (R² = 0.09, P = 0.006) (p. 3).
- The diversity–SOC link was significant only in the warmest (MAT > 15.58 °C, R² = 0.38), driest (MAP < 523 mm, R² = 0.46) and most arid (AI < 0.50, R² = 0.42) quartiles (p. 5, Table 2).
- Diversity was not correlated with plant biomass (P = 0.119), while biomass was correlated with SOC (R² = 0.09, P = 0.008) (pp. 2, 6).
- A model with diversity acting through C:N ratio fitted better than one acting through biomass (p. 7, Fig. 1).
- Across sites, SOC fell with temperature (R² = 0.19) and rose with the aridity index (R² = 0.38); clay content had no effect (P = 0.864) (p. 6).

## 5. Conclusions

Plant  diversity  affects  SOC  through  organic  matter  quality,  in  a  climate-dependent  way,  so  the biodiversity–ecosystem relationship depends on climate (p. 7). Because grasslands hold about one third of global terrestrial carbon, diversity loss could jeopardise SOC storage, particularly in warm and arid climates, and management that restores diversity likely enhances SOC sequestration (pp. 1, 7).


## 6. Limitations

- Observational: shows correlations; the authors note soil organic matter may also influence plant diversity (p. 7).
- Only the top 10 cm was sampled, and SOC is a content (g/kg), not a stock (p. 7).
- Grasslands only; no Indian sites named in the main text.
- One sampling per site, so no change over time is measured.

# Potential Role of Biochar on Capturing Soil Nutrients, Carbon Sequestration and Managing Environmental Challenges: A Review


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Potential role of biochar on capturing soil nutrients, carbon sequestration and managing environmental challenges: A review Zouhair Elkhlifi, Jerosha Iftikhar, Mohammad Sarraf … Zhuqi Chen (13 authors)

**Authors:**
Zouhair Elkhlifi, Jerosha Iftikhar, Mohammad Sarraf, Baber Ali, Muhammad Hamzah Saleem, Irshad Ibranshahib, Mozart Daltro Bispo, Lucas Meili, Sezai Ercisli, Ehlinaz Torun Kayabasi, Naser Alemzadeh Ansari, Alžbeta Hegedűsová, Zhuqi Chen

**Journal:**
Sustainability, vol. 15, issue 3, article 2527 (2023)

**Paper type:**
Review article

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3390/su15032527

**Cite as:**
Elkhlifi, Z., Iftikhar, J., Sarraf, M., Ali, B., Saleem, M. H., Ibranshahib, I., Bispo, M. D., Meili, L., Ercisli, S., Torun Kayabasi, E., Alemzadeh Ansari, N., Hegedűsová, A., & Chen, Z. (2023). Potential role of biochar on capturing soil nutrients, carbon sequestration and managing environmental challenges: A review. Sustainability, 15(3), Article 2527. https://doi.org/10.3390/su15032527 Open access article under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Page numbers refer to the article PDF (pp. 1–18). BC = biochar. Most numbers are from single cited studies, not new data.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This review summarises how feedstock and pyrolysis conditions shape biochar and its effects on soil nutrients, carbon and pollutants. High pyrolysis temperatures make biochar more aromatic and alkaline but may reduce nutrient availability, and different biochars release nutrients at different rates. Biochar can improve soil quality and store carbon, but effects are soil- and crop-specific and can be negative. The authors call for cheaper, better-controlled engineered biochar and testing with local farming communities.


## 1. Background

Biochar (BC) is a carbon-rich solid made by pyrolysis of biomass, usually at 300–800 °C with little or no oxygen (p. 6). It is studied as a soil amendment and as an adsorbent of pollutants (p. 2). Its properties depend on feedstock, residence time and pyrolysis conditions, and reported crop responses conflict: one cited review found yield changes from −36% to +31% (p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To summarise recent studies on the biochar composition that controls carbon in soil, and on biochar's role in soil fertility, nutrient capture, carbon sequestration and remediation of contaminated soils (p. 1).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors reviewed literature on how feedstock and pyrolysis conditions shape biochar, how biochar holds and releases nutrients, how it stores carbon, how engineered biochar removes contaminants, and

its reported drawbacks. Results of individual studies are summarised in tables (pp. 3–11). No systematic search or meta-analysis was reported.


## 4. Main findings

- Higher pyrolysis temperatures raise aromatic carbon, pH and ash but lower yield, CEC and volatile matter; at 500–800 °C nutrient availability may fall (pp. 3–4).
- Nutrient release differs by feedstock and process; most biochars release little N, so N fertiliser should accompany biochar (p. 6).
- Wood biochar is more stable than crop-residue biochar because of its higher lignin content (p. 7).
- Biochar can immobilise heavy metals and adsorb organic and inorganic pollutants, though it is selective (pp. 7, 9).
- A cited study (Woolf et al.) estimated that scaling up biochar could cut net human GHG emissions by up to 12% through fossil-fuel substitution (p. 10).
- Cited single-study results include up to twofold root and plant biomass at a 20% biochar rate (p. 11) and 18–24% more legume nodulation (p. 3).

## 5. Conclusions

Biochar can help maintain soil health sustainably, but research should focus on standardising production, predicting field decay, rhizosphere interactions and adsorption–desorption capacities (pp. 11–12). An economically  feasible  method  of  producing  engineered  biochar  with  better-controlled  pyrolysis  is needed, and applications should be optimised with local farming communities (p. 1).


## 6. Limitations

- Reported drawbacks include about 200% more weeds at 15 t/ha, fungal declines of 11% and 66%, harm to earthworms from aged biochar, and soil- and crop-specific effects (p. 9).
- Many numbers come from single studies with different feedstocks and doses; the 20% rate is far above normal field rates.
- The review says low-temperature biochar shows lower soil degradability (p. 7), which conflicts with its statement that high-temperature biochar is more aromatic and recalcitrant (p. 4).
- No Indian field trials. CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The earlier notes said the review gives no costs. It cites one estimate of £148–389 per tonne of biochar (Shackley et al.) and notes that regulation and feedstock testing could raise costs (p. 9); there is no cost analysis of its own.

description: This review compares life cycle assessments (LCAs) of biochar made from agro-residues. Results are hard to compare because studies use different functional units and boundaries, but the net carbon benefit is promising. For rice straw, one cited LCA found savings of 1.10–1.64 t CO₂-eq per tonne depending on pyrolysis type. The authors call for locally designed pyrolysis and for linking LCA with circular-economy and cost analysis.

**Authors:**
Xiefei Zhu, Claudia Labianca, Mingjing He, Zejun Luo, Chunfei Wu, Siming You, Daniel C. W. Tsang

**Journal:**
Bioresource Technology, vol. 360, article 127601 (2022)

**Paper type:**
Review article (accepted manuscript)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2022.127601

**Cite as:**
Zhu, X., Labianca, C., He, M., Luo, Z., Wu, C., You, S., & Tsang, D. C. W. (2022). Life-cycle assessment of pyrolysis processes for sustainable production of biochar from agro- residues. Bioresource Technology, 360, Article 127601. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2022.127601 Page numbers refer to the accepted manuscript PDF ('AM p.' = manuscript page number), which differs from the published version. Negative values = net CO₂-eq reduction.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This review compares life cycle assessments (LCAs) of biochar made from agro-residues. Results are hard to compare because studies use different functional units and boundaries, but the net carbon benefit is promising. For rice straw, one cited LCA found savings of 1.10–1.64 t CO₂-eq per tonne depending on pyrolysis type. Soil use beat energy use in one comparison, wet feedstocks gave little benefit, and village brick kilns saved less than stoves or large plants. The authors call for locally designed pyrolysis and for linking LCA with circular-economy and cost analysis.


## 1. Background

Agro-residues are primary field wastes (rice, wheat and cotton straw) or secondary processing wastes (rice husks, peanut shells, cobs) (AM p. 6). In many regions they are abandoned or burned, releasing CO₂, smog and particulate matter (AM p. 3). Pyrolysis at 300 °C and above converts them into biochar, bio-oil and syngas, and LCA tests whether this gives a real net carbon benefit (AM pp. 3, 8).


## 2. Aim of the study

To critically analyse recent LCAs of biochar production from different agro-residues, compare pyrolysis technologies, and assess biochar's net carbon benefit as an energy source, soil amendment or activated- carbon substitute (AM p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

The authors described residue properties, pre-treatment, pyrolysis routes and reactor types (AM pp. 6– 10), explained LCA goal and scope, functional units, system boundaries and inventories (AM pp. 11–20),

and compared impact results and sensitivity analyses from published LCAs summarised in Tables 2–3 (AM pp. 20–25, 45–48).


## 4. Main findings

- Righi et al. found −386 to −933 kg CO₂-eq per t feedstock for soil amendment versus −240 to −787 for energy supply (AM p. 21).
- For rice straw, Gong et al. found reductions of 1.14, 1.64 and 1.10 t CO₂-eq per t with fast, intermediate and slow pyrolysis; for corn stover 1.75, 1.12 and 1.84 (AM pp. 22–23).
- Crop residues pyrolysed at 400–700 °C avoided 200–470 kg CO₂-eq per t (AM p. 22); Clare et al. reported −1.06 t CO₂-eq per t, and Dai et al. a potential of 1.41 million t CO₂-eq for Chinese crop residues (AM p. 21).
- Wet orange peel gave only −5.5 kg CO₂-eq per t because of drying energy (AM p. 22).
- For rice husk, a brick kiln gave −229, a stove −318 and a large plant −360 kg CO₂-eq per t (AM p. 24).
- Extending the boundary to soil application makes CO₂-eq sequestration achievable (AM p. 21).

## 5. Conclusions

Available studies show good carbon reduction potential for biochar as an energy source, soil amendment and activated-carbon substitute, and pyrolysis design should be customised to the local context (AM p. 27). Biochar is not a silver bullet; co-products, economics and circular-economy modelling should be included in future LCAs (AM pp. 26–27).


## 6. Limitations

- Numbers are ranges from studies with different functional units, boundaries and assumptions (AM p. 2).
- Cases come from China, Southeast Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas; none from India (Tables 2–3).
- Manpower is usually left out of the system boundary, which favours labour-intensive small reactors (AM p. 23).
- This is the accepted manuscript version. CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The earlier notes said small village kilns were not assessed. The review does report them: for rice husk, a brick kiln gave −229, a stove −318 and a large plant −360 kg CO₂-eq per t (Mohammadi et al., AM p. 24). The earlier note that cases come mostly from China, Europe or North America also missed the Southeast Asian, Australian, Latin American and African cases.

# Maximizing carbon sequestration potential in Chinese forests through optimal management


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Maximizing carbon sequestration potential in Chinese forests through optimal management Zhen Yu, Shirong Liu, Haikui Li … Evgenios Agathokleous (14 authors)

**Authors:**
Zhen Yu, Shirong Liu, Haikui Li, Jingjing Liang, Weiguo Liu, Shilong Piao, Hanqin Tian, Guoyi Zhou, Chaoqun Lu, Weibin You, Pengsen Sun, Yanli Dong, Stephen Sitch, Evgenios Agathokleous

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 15, article 3154 (2024)

**Paper type:**
Research article (national modelling study)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47143-5

**Cite as:**
Yu, Z., Liu, S., Li, H., Liang, J., Liu, W., Piao, S., Tian, H., Zhou, G., Lu, C., You, W., Sun, P., Dong, Y., Sitch, S., & Agathokleous, E. (2024). Maximizing carbon sequestration potential in Chinese forests through optimal management. Nature Communications, 15, Article 3154. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47143-5 Open access (Nature Communications). Page numbers refer to the article PDF (pp. 1–12). Biomass carbon excludes dead wood, litter and soil carbon. 1 Pg = 1,000 Tg.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The authors drive a process-based model (DLEM) with China's national forest inventory to project forest biomass carbon from 2020 to 2100, including wood harvest, forest age and the official planting plan. Biomass carbon rises by 13.6 ± 1.5 Pg C, a mean sink of 172.3 ± 16.9 Tg C per year, mostly in natural non- timber forests. Ignoring how harvest changes forest age puts the sink peak 1–3 decades too early. Wood products add 0.6–2.0 Pg C, and optimal management (longer rotations and replacing unsuitable species) adds 2.3 ± 0.03 Pg C, but only if started quickly.


## 1. Background

China has the largest planted forest area in the world and pledged to expand it by 49.5 Mha from 2021, after 15 Mha planned for 2016–2020 (pp. 1, 9–10). Published estimates of its future forest carbon sink diverge because long-term data are limited, accounting methods differ, and most studies leave out forest demography (age structure) and wood harvest (pp. 1–2). The spread of reported stocks rises from 9% in 2020 to 25% in 2060 (p. 3).


## 2. Aim of the study

To project China's forest biomass carbon stock and sink from 2020 to 2100 with tree demography, harvest, species choice and forest structure considered together, and to assess how much improved management could add (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

The study uses more than 18 million tree records from about 415,000 permanent inventory plots (1999– 2018); the 9th inventory (2014–2018) gives the validated starting stock, and over 50,000 plots give age

dynamics (pp. 2–3, 6). DLEM runs on a 0.5° grid with harvest limited to timber forests and set by species and age, under four SSP climate and CO₂ scenarios and tree survival of 47% or 85% for new plantings (pp. 3, 8, 10). New plantations follow the national plan to 2050 on grassland and shrubland only, with species chosen from habitat-suitability maps (p. 10). A statistical model is used for comparison. Biomass carbon excludes dead wood, litter and soil (p. 2).


## 4. Main findings

- Biomass carbon stock rises by 13.6 ± 1.5 Pg C from 2020 to 2100, to 21.6–24.3 Pg C in 2100; raising survival of new plantings from 47% to 85% adds 1.0–1.1 Pg C (p. 3).
- The mean sink is 172.3 ± 16.9 Tg C per year over 2020–2100: 0.201 Pg C per year in 2020–2060 and 0.143 in 2060–2100 (pp. 4–5).
- Natural non-timber forests provide 57.7% of the stock increase, planted non-timber forests 34.2% and timber forests 8.1%; existing forests give 70.4 ± 3% and new forests 29.6 ± 2% (p. 4).
- The statistical model puts the sink peak in the 2020s–2040s; the process model, with harvest and real age change, in the 2050s. Ignoring harvest effects on age shifts the peak 1–3 decades too early (pp. 1, 5).
- Harvest removes 7.8 ± 0.3 Pg C from timber forests in 2020–2100; the wood product pool reaches 1.9 ± 0.1 Pg C in 2100, limited by the 61.5% share of short-lived paper. More long-lived products would raise the pool by 75.3% (1.4 ± 0.08 Pg C) (p. 5).
- Postponing harvest by 5 years after the key year adds 4.3–5.6 Tg C per year in timber forests; replacing ~4.13 Mha of unsuitable species adds 0.17–1.1 Tg C per year. Each year of delay loses 11– 17 Tg C (p. 5, Table 1). Together the paper reports an extra 28.1 ± 0.4 Tg C per year, 2.3 ± 0.03 Pg C in total (p. 5).

## 5. Conclusions

China's forests will remain a substantial net sink to 2100, but projections must include harvest and forest demography. Long-lived wood products and optimal management can raise the sink, and the authors urge swift implementation because delayed action gives little benefit (pp. 5–6).


## 6. Limitations

- China-wide modelling of national forestry; no village-scale or farm-tree data (0.5° grid).
- Biomass carbon only; soil, litter and dead wood are excluded (p. 2).
- Results depend on assumed survival, harvest rules and SSP scenarios.
- Thesis author's assessment: the process model is not directly usable in an M.Tech study, and species and climate differ from the Varuna basin. CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The earlier notes cited the paper without volume or article number and listed the authors only as 'Yu et al.'; the full citation is Nature Communications 15, 3154 (2024), 14 authors. The earlier notes also did not say that the carbon figures cover biomass only (no soil, litter or dead wood). All their numbers (415,000 plots, 13.6 ± 1.5, 0.6–2.0, 2.3 ± 0.03 Pg C, 1–3 decades, 49.5 Mha, 15 Mha) were confirmed.
INCONSISTENCIES IN THE PAPER (1) p. 4 gives the mean sink as 0.172 ± 0.017 Tg C per year, but p. 5 gives 172.3 ± 16.9 Tg C per year, so the unit on p. 4 should be Pg. (2) p. 3 calls the 13.6 ± 1.5 Pg C increase 'a sink potential of 11.2–14.8 Pg C', which is not the same range. (3) Table 1 gives 4.3–5.6 plus 0.17–1.1 Tg C per year for the two practices, but the text reports 28.1 ± 0.4 Tg C per year for both together; the paper does not explain the gap. These are flagged, not resolved.

#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

In 2023 fossil CO₂ emissions reached 10.1 ± 0.5 GtC (+1.3%) and land-use change added 1.0 ± 0.7 GtC, a total of 11.1 ± 0.9 GtC (40.6 GtCO₂). Fossil emissions were projected to rise a further 0.8% in 2024, with CO₂ reaching 422.45 ppm, 52% above pre- industrial. Only 65 GtC remain for a 50% chance of 1.5 °C, about 6 years at 2024 emissions.


## 1. Background

Knowing how much CO₂ humans emit and where it goes (atmosphere, ocean, land) is needed to understand the carbon cycle, support climate policy and project future climate change (p. 968). The Global Carbon Budget is the Global Carbon Project's annual update. The 2024 edition gives final data for 2023, a projection for 2024, cumulative emissions since 1750 and 1850, and an updated remaining carbon budget (p. 969).


## 2. Aim of the study

To describe and synthesise the data sets and methods that quantify the five major components of the global carbon budget and their uncertainties, and to document changes in methods and data since the previous edition (p. 968).


## 3. What the authors did

Fossil CO₂ emissions (EFOS) come from energy statistics and cement production data; land-use change emissions  (ELUC,  mainly  deforestation)  from  land-use  data  and  four  bookkeeping  models;  the atmospheric growth rate (GATM) from direct CO₂ measurements; the ocean sink (SOCEAN) from ocean biogeochemistry models and fCO₂-based data products; and the land sink (SLAND) from dynamic global vegetation  models.  Atmospheric  inversions,  atmospheric  oxygen  measurements  and  Earth  system models give extra lines of evidence on the land and ocean sinks. The budget imbalance BIM = EFOS + ELUC − (GATM + SOCEAN + SLAND) measures imperfect data and understanding. Uncertainties are ±1σ (p. 968). Units: 1 ppm = 2.124 GtC and 1 GtC = 3.664 GtCO₂ (p. 970).


## 4. Main findings

- In 2023, EFOS was 10.1 ± 0.5 GtC per year (10.3 ± 0.5 without the cement carbonation sink), +1.3% on 2022; ELUC was 1.0 ± 0.7, for a total of 11.1 ± 0.9 GtC per year (40.6 ± 3.2 GtCO₂) (p. 968).
- In 2023, GATM was 5.9 ± 0.2 GtC per year (2.79 ± 0.1 ppm), SOCEAN 2.9 ± 0.4 and SLAND 2.3 ± 1.0, with a budget imbalance of −0.02 GtC per year; CO₂ averaged 419.31 ± 0.1 ppm (p. 968).
- The 2023 land sink was 1.6 GtC lower than in 2022 and the lowest since 2015, driven by tropical ecosystems at the onset of El Niño and large Canadian wildfires (p. 969).
- Preliminary 2024: fossil CO₂ +0.8% (−0.2% to 1.7%) to 10.2 GtC; total 11.4 GtC (41.6 GtCO₂); CO₂ 422.45 ppm, 52% above about 278 ppm in 1750 (pp. 968–969).
- Over 2014–2023, fossil CO₂ grew 0.6% per year; India +3.6%, China +1.9%, EU27 −2.1%, USA −1.2% per year (p. 985; Table 9, p. 1012). Total emissions (fossil plus land use) showed zero growth over the decade (p. 969).
- Cumulative fossil CO₂ 1850–2023: USA 120 GtC (24%), EU 80 GtC (16%), China 75 GtC (15%), India 15 GtC (3%) (p. 985).
- Land use: 1.1 ± 0.7 GtC per year over 2014–2023; deforestation about 1.7 GtC per year, of which re-/afforestation and regrowth offset 1.2 GtC (p. 969).
- Remaining carbon budget from January 2025 (50% likelihood): 65, 160 and 305 GtC (235, 585, 1110 GtCO₂) for 1.5, 1.7 and 2 °C, about 6, 14 and 27 years at 2024 emissions (p. 1011).

## 5. Conclusions

The mean and trend of the budget components are consistently estimated over 1959–2023 with a near- zero overall imbalance, although discrepancies of up to about 1 GtC per year remain for annual to semi- decadal variability (p. 968). Total emissions have plateaued over the last decade but are not falling (p. 969). The 1.5 °C budget is about six years of current emissions, and even net zero by 2040 would emit 90 GtC, more than the 65 GtC left, unless emissions turn net negative afterwards (p. 1013).


## 6. Limitations

- Global and national data only; no district or village values.
- CO₂ only; CH₄ and N₂O are covered by papers 2 and 11.
- 2024 figures are projections and every edition revises earlier years, so use the latest edition when citing numbers.
- Land-use change emissions remain the most uncertain flux; values are in GtC (× 3.664 for GtCO₂). P., Peters, W., Pongratz, J., Schwingshackl, C., Sitch, S., Canadell, J. G., Ciais, P., Jackson, R. B., Alin, S. R., Alkama, R., … Zheng, B. (2022). Global Carbon Budget 2022. Earth System Science Data, 14, 4811–4900. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-14-4811-2022 Open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License (CC BY 4.0). Units: GtC; 1 GtC = 3.664 GtCO₂; 1 ppm CO₂ = 2.124 GtC; ±1σ uncertainties. Page numbers are journal pages.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

In 2021 fossil CO₂ emissions rebounded by 5.1% to 9.9 ± 0.5 GtC, the 2019 level, and land-use change added 1.1 ± 0.7 GtC, a total of 10.9 ± 0.8 GtC (40.0 GtCO₂). Of this, 5.2 GtC stayed in the atmosphere, the ocean took 2.9 GtC and the land 3.5 GtC. Fossil emissions were projected to rise a further 1.0% in 2022, with CO₂ reaching 417.2 ppm, 51% above pre-industrial. India's fossil emissions grew fastest among the big emitters (+3.8% per year over 2012–2021). 105 GtC remain for a 50% chance of 1.5 °C, about 9 years at 2022 emissions and 32 GtC less than in the IPCC AR6 assessment.


## 1. Background

Knowing how much CO₂ humans emit and where it goes (atmosphere, ocean, land) is needed to understand the carbon cycle, support climate policy and project future climate change (p. 4813–4814). The Global Carbon Budget is the Global Carbon Project's annual update. The 2022 edition gives final data for 2021, a projection for 2022, cumulative emissions since 1750 and 1850, and an updated remaining carbon budget (p. 4815).


## 2. Aim of the study

To describe and synthesise the data sets and methods that quantify the five major components of the global carbon budget and their uncertainties, and to document changes in methods and data since the previous edition (p. 4813–4814).


## 3. What the authors did

Fossil CO₂ emissions (EFOS) come from energy statistics and cement production data; land-use change emissions  (ELUC,  mainly  deforestation)  from  land-use  data  and  three  bookkeeping  models;  the atmospheric growth rate (GATM) from direct CO₂ measurements; the ocean sink (SOCEAN) from ocean biogeochemistry models and fCO₂-based data products; and the land sink (SLAND) from dynamic global vegetation models. Atmospheric inversions, which close the global carbon balance by design, are assessed as an independent check (p. 4815). The budget imbalance BIM = EFOS + ELUC − (GATM + SOCEAN + SLAND) measures imperfect data and understanding. Uncertainties are ±1σ (p. 4813–4814). Units: 1 ppm = 2.124 GtC and 1 GtC = 3.664 GtCO₂ (p. 4816).


## 4. Main findings

- In 2021, EFOS was 9.9 ± 0.5 GtC per year (10.1 ± 0.5 without the cement carbonation sink), +5.1% on 2020; ELUC was 1.1 ± 0.7, for a total of 10.9 ± 0.8 GtC per year (40.0 ± 2.9 GtCO₂) (p. 4813).
- In 2021, GATM was 5.2 ± 0.2 GtC per year (2.5 ± 0.1 ppm), SOCEAN 2.9 ± 0.4 and SLAND 3.5 ± 0.9, with a budget imbalance of −0.6 GtC per year; CO₂ averaged 414.71 ± 0.1 ppm (pp. 4813–4814).
- Preliminary 2022: fossil CO₂ +1.0% (0.1% to 1.9%) to 10.0 GtC (36.6 GtCO₂), slightly above 2019; total 11.1 GtC (40.5 GtCO₂); CO₂ 417.2 ppm, 51% above pre-industrial (p. 4814).
- Over 2012–2021, fossil CO₂ grew 0.5% per year; India +3.8%, China +1.5%, EU27 −1.8%, USA −1.1% per year (p. 4826). Fossil CO₂ fell in 24 countries, together about a quarter of world fossil emissions (p. 4814).
- Cumulative fossil CO₂ 1850–2021: USA 115 GtC (24%), EU 80 GtC (17%), China 70 GtC (14%); no share is given for India (p. 4826).
- Land use: 1.2 ± 0.7 GtC per year over 2012–2021; deforestation 1.8 ± 0.4 GtC per year, of which afforestation, reafforestation and forestry offset 0.9 ± 0.3 GtC (p. 4814).
- The ocean sink trend since 2010 differs by a factor of 3 between data products (+0.7 GtC per year per decade) and models (+0.2) (p. 4814).
- Remaining carbon budget from January 2023 (50% likelihood): 105, 200 and 335 GtC (380, 730, 1230 GtCO₂) for 1.5, 1.7 and 2 °C, about 9, 18 and 30 years at 2022 emissions; net zero by 2050 needs cuts of about 0.4 GtC (1.4 GtCO₂) per year (pp. 4814, 4847).
