## 5. Conclusions

The mean and trend of the budget components are consistently estimated over 1959–2021, but discrepancies of up to 1 GtC per year persist for annual to semi-decadal variability (p. 4814). Year-to-year variability in the land sink, about 1 GtC per year, makes small annual changes in emissions hard to detect in atmospheric CO₂ (p. 4815). Reaching zero CO₂ by 2050 needs a linear cut of about 0.4 GtC per year, comparable to the 2020 COVID-19 drop, which shows the scale of action needed (p. 4814).


## 6. Limitations

- Global and national data only; no district or village values.
- CO₂ only; CH₄ and N₂O are covered by papers 2 and 11.
- 2022 figures are projections and every edition revises earlier years, so use the latest edition when citing numbers.
- Land-use change emissions remain the most uncertain flux; values are in GtC (× 3.664 for GtCO₂). CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER NOTES The earlier notes listed the authors as 'Friedlingstein, O'Sullivan, Jones, Andrew, Bakker, Hauck, Landschützer, Le Quéré, Luijkx, Peters, et al.', copied from the 2023 edition. Bakker is not an author of this edition and Landschützer is not among the first ten; the first ten are Friedlingstein, O'Sullivan, Jones, Andrew, Gregor, Hauck, Le Quéré, Luijkx, Olsen and Peters (106 authors; vol. 14, pp. 4811–4900). The Relevance notes planned to use 'India's cumulative share', but this edition gives cumulative fossil shares only for the USA (24%), EU (17%) and China (14%), not for India (p. 4826); India's 3% comes from the 2023 and 2024 editions. 'Largest uncertainty: land-use change emissions' was widened to the paper's three named gaps. All other old numbers were confirmed. INCONSISTENCIES IN THE PAPER (1) Total 2021 emissions are 10.9 ± 0.8 GtC (40.0 ± 2.9 GtCO₂) in the abstract (p. 4813), 11.0 GtC (40.2 GtCO₂) in the executive summary (p. 4814), and 10.9 ± 0.9 GtC (40.0 ± 3.3 GtCO₂) in Sect. 3.4 and Table 6 (pp. 4834–4835). (2) Sect. 3.4.2 gives the atmospheric growth 'during 2012–2022' although the decade is 2012–2021 (p. 4834). This summary uses the abstract and table values and flags the differences.

Nabel, Shin- Ichiro Nakaoka, Yosuke Niwa, Tsuneo Ono, Denis Pierrot, Benjamin Poulter, Gregor Rehder, Laure Resplandy, Eddy Robertson, Christian Rödenbeck, Thais M. Rosan, Jörg Schwinger, Clemens Schwingshackl, Roland Séférian, Adrienne J. Sutton, Colm Sweeney, Toste Tanhua, Pieter P. Tans, Hanqin Tian, Bronte Tilbrook, Francesco Tubiello, Guido R. van der Werf, Nicolas Vuichard, Chisato Wada, Rik Wanninkhof, Andrew J. Watson, David Willis, Andrew J. Wiltshire, Wenping Yuan, Chao Yue, Xu Yue, Sönke Zaehle, Jiye Zeng (94 authors)

**Journal:**
Earth System Science Data, vol. 14, pp. 1917–2005 (2022)

**Dates:**
Received 28 October 2021 · Accepted 15 March 2022 · Published 26 April 2022

**Paper type:**
Data description paper (annual 'living data' update of the Global Carbon Project); open access, CC BY 4.0

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-14-1917-2022

**Cite as:**
Friedlingstein, P., Jones, M. W., O'Sullivan, M., Andrew, R. M., Bakker, D. C. E., Hauck, J., Le Quéré, C., Peters, G. P., Peters, W., Pongratz, J., Sitch, S., Canadell, J. G., Ciais, P., Jackson, R. B., Alin, S. R., Anthoni, P., Bates, N. R., Becker, M., Bellouin, N., . . . Zeng, J. (2022). Global Carbon Budget 2021. Earth System Science Data, 14, 1917–2005. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-14-1917-2022 Open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License (CC BY 4.0). Units: GtC; 1 GtC = 3.664 GtCO₂; ±1σ uncertainties.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

In 2020, humans emitted 10.2 ± 0.8 GtC of CO₂ (37.4 GtCO₂), even though fossil emissions fell 5.4% in the COVID year; preliminary data show a +4.8% rebound in 2021. About half of the emissions stay in the atmosphere, with the rest taken up roughly equally by the ocean and land. From January 2022, the remaining carbon budget for 1.5 °C (50% likelihood) is 120 GtC, about 11 years of 2021 emissions.


## 1. Background

Knowing how much CO₂ humans emit, and where it goes (atmosphere, ocean or land), is critical for understanding the carbon cycle, setting climate policy and projecting future climate change. Atmospheric CO₂ rose from about 277 ppm in 1750 to 412.4 ± 0.1 ppm in 2020 (p. 1920). The Global Carbon Budget is an annual update by the Global Carbon Project. The 2021 edition gives final data for 2020, preliminary data for 2021 and an updated remaining carbon budget. THE BUDGET EQUATION EFOS + ELUC = GATM + SOCEAN + SLAND + BIM. Emissions from fossil fuels and land-use change equal the growth in atmospheric CO₂ plus the ocean and land sinks; the budget imbalance (BIM) is what is left over and measures imperfect data and understanding.


## 2. Aim of the study

To describe and synthesise the datasets and methods that quantify the five major components of the global carbon budget and their uncertainties, and to document changes in methods and data since the previous editions.


## 3. What the authors did

- EFOS: energy statistics and cement production data, with the cement carbonation sink subtracted.
- ELUC: land-use data and three bookkeeping models (H&N2017, BLUE, OSCAR); 17 DGVMs as an independent estimate.
- GATM: direct measurements of atmospheric CO₂ (1 ppm = 2.124 GtC).
- SOCEAN: eight global ocean biogeochemistry models and seven observation-based fCO₂ data products.
- SLAND: 17 dynamic global vegetation models.
- Checks: six atmospheric inversions, atmospheric O₂ data and Earth system models.
- New in this edition: the first approach to reconcile the ELUC estimate with national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs). All uncertainties are reported as ±1σ. Values are in GtC; multiply by 3.664 to get GtCO₂.

## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 The 2020 budget

Table A. Global carbon budget for 2020 (Abstract, p. 1919) Component 2020 value (GtC/yr) Note Fossil CO₂ (EFOS) 9.3 ± 0.5 Includes cement carbonation sink; 9.5 ± 0.5 without it; −5.4% vs 2019 Land-use change (ELUC) 0.9 ± 0.7 Mainly deforestation Total emissions 10.2 ± 0.8 37.4 ± 2.9 GtCO₂ Atmospheric growth (GATM) 5.0 ± 0.2 2.4 ± 0.1 ppm/yr; mean CO₂ 412.45 ppm Ocean sink (SOCEAN) 3.0 ± 0.4 Land sink (SLAND) 2.9 ± 1 Budget imbalance (BIM) −0.8 Sources underestimated or sinks overestimated


### 4.2 The last decade (2011–2020)

Fossil emissions averaged 9.5 ± 0.5 GtC/yr (90% of total emissions) and land-use change 1.1 ± 0.7 GtC/yr (10%). Of the total of 10.6 ± 0.8 GtC/yr, the atmosphere kept 47% (5.1 GtC/yr), the ocean took 26% (2.8 GtC/yr) and the land 29% (3.1 GtC/yr), with an imbalance of about 3% (pp. 1920, 1949–1950). Fossil emission growth slowed to 0.6% per year, from 3.0% per year in the 2000s (p. 1932).


### 4.3 Countries

Over the last 10 years, China's fossil emissions rose +1.0% per year (dominating the global trend) and India's +3.9% per year, while the EU27 fell −1.9% and the USA −1.1% per year (p. 1932). Over 1850–2020 the USA emitted the most, 110 GtC (25%), followed by the EU (80 GtC, 18%) and China (60 GtC, 14%). Coal supplied 46% of cumulative fossil CO₂, oil 35% and gas 14%.


### 4.4 The 2021 projection

Fossil CO₂ rebounded by +4.8% (4.2% to 5.4%) to about 9.9 GtC (36.4 GtCO₂), close to the 2019 level. Compared with 2019, emissions were 5.7% higher in China (3.0 GtC) and 3.2% higher in India (0.74 GtC), but 4.5% lower in the USA, 5.3% lower in the EU and 4.0% lower in the rest of the world (p. 1920). Atmospheric CO₂ was set to reach 414.7 ppm, 50% above pre-industrial levels.


### 4.5 Land-use change

Net ELUC is the small difference between near-constant gross emissions (3.8 ± 0.6 GtC/yr in 2011–2020) and growing gross removals (2.7 ± 0.4 GtC/yr). Cumulative ELUC for 1850–2020 was 200 ± 65 GtC, with model estimates from 140 to 270 GtC (pp. 1920, 1936). Accounting for the part of the natural sink that national inventories assign to managed land makes the two approaches consistent.


### 4.6 Cumulative emissions and remaining budget

Emissions in 1850–2020 totalled 660 ± 65 GtC, partitioned among the atmosphere (41%), ocean (26%) and land (30%), with a 25 GtC (4%) imbalance (p. 1949).

Table B. Remaining carbon budget from January 2022, 50% likelihood (p. 1951) Warming limit GtC GtCO₂ Years at 2021 emissions 1.5 °C 120 420 about 11 1.7 °C 210 770 about 20 2 °C 350 1270 about 32 Reaching net-zero CO₂ by 2050 requires cutting total emissions by about 0.4 GtC (1.4 GtCO₂) each year, comparable to the 2020 decrease.


## 5. Conclusions

1. The mean and trend of the budget are consistently estimated over 1959–2020; the mean imbalance since 1960 is only 0.03 GtC/yr. 2. Discrepancies of up to about 1 GtC/yr remain in annual to semi-decadal variability. 3. Three main uncertainties: land-use change emissions; the land CO₂ flux in the northern extra-tropics; and the strength of the ocean sink over the last decade. 4. Human CO₂ emissions remain near record levels, and the 1.5 °C budget is only about 11 years of current emissions.


## 6. Limitations

- Global and national data only; no district or village values.
- Covers CO₂ only; CH₄ and N₂O are covered by other budgets (papers 2 and 11).
- Land-use change emissions are highly uncertain, and 2021 values are preliminary projections.
- Each edition revises earlier years, so cite the latest edition for current numbers (papers 26–28 are newer).

# The enduring world forest carbon sink


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

The enduring world forest carbon sink Yude Pan, Richard A. Birdsey, Oliver L. Phillips, Richard A. Houghton, Jingyun Fang, Pekka E. Kauppi, Heather Keith, Werner A. Kurz and 9 co-authors

**Authors:**
Yude Pan, Richard A. Birdsey, Oliver L. Phillips, Richard A. Houghton, Jingyun Fang, Pekka E. Kauppi, Heather Keith, Werner A. Kurz, Akihiko Ito, Simon L. Lewis, Gert-Jan Nabuurs, Anatoly Shvidenko, Shoji Hashimoto, Bas Lerink, Dmitry Schepaschenko, Andrea Castanho, Daniel Murdiyarso

**Journal:**
Nature, vol. 631, pp. 563–569 (2024) Version read Authors' accepted manuscript (White Rose Research Online); page numbers in this report are manuscript pages

**Paper type:**
Research article: global synthesis of ground-based forest inventory data

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07602-x

**Cite as:**
Pan, Y., Birdsey, R. A., Phillips, O. L., Houghton, R. A., Fang, J., Kauppi, P. E., Keith, H., Kurz, W. A., Ito, A., Lewis, S. L., Nabuurs, G.-J., Shvidenko, A., Hashimoto, S., Lerink, B., Schepaschenko, D., Castanho, A., & Murdiyarso, D. (2024). The enduring world forest carbon sink. Nature, 631, 563–569. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07602-x Read from the authors' accepted manuscript (White Rose Research Online); page numbers below are the manuscript's printed page numbers, not the journal pages. ± values are 95% confidence ranges.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using forest inventory data for about 95% of the world's forests, the authors find that forests took up a steady 3.6 Pg C per year from 1990 to 2019 (3.5 in the 2010s), equal to almost half of fossil fuel emissions. The total hides big shifts: temperate and tropical regrowth sinks rose by about 30%, while boreal and intact tropical sinks fell by a third. Tropical deforestation (2.2 Pg C per year) cancelled about two-thirds of the benefit. Stopping deforestation is the most important way to keep the sink.


## 1. Background

Carbon dioxide uptake by land ecosystems is critical for moderating climate change, and forests are its main part. Atmospheric CO₂ passed 420 ppm in 2023. Reaching net zero by 2050 will need large-scale negative emissions of up to 6 Pg C per year, and land has historically lost 180 Pg C to land-use change, part of which can be restored (ms pp. 1–2). Remote sensing and models can map land sinks at high resolution but struggle to give long-term baselines  and  often  disagree.  Forest  inventories,  based  on  tree-by-tree  measurements,  give  an independent, ground-based view.


## 2. Aim of the study

To give a ground-based, long-term assessment of how much carbon the world's forests took up over three decades (1990–2019), where it is stored, and how the sink changed by biome and carbon pool.


## 3. What the authors did

- Synthesised forest inventory and long-term monitoring data for boreal, temperate and tropical biomes, 1990–2019, combined with remote-sensing-based forest areas.
- Covered about 4.0 billion ha, 95% of global forest; remote unmanaged northern forests, some sparse Asian forests, mangroves and non-forest peatlands were not included (ms p. 21).
- Estimated stocks and stock changes in five pools: living biomass, dead wood, litter, soil and harvested wood products.
- Split boreal and temperate forests into remaining and new (afforested or reforested) forests, and tropical forests into intact and regrowth forests.
- Subtracted tropical deforestation emissions to get the net forest sink, and compared the results with the Global Carbon Budget, DGVMs and inversions.
- Reported ± values as 95% confidence ranges (ms p. 27).

## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Forest area and carbon stock

World forest area fell by 5% from 1990 to 2020, from 4,022 to 3,812 Mha. Tropical forests lost 273 Mha (13%), including 467 Mha (26%) of intact forest, while regrowth forests expanded by 194 Mha (56%). Temperate forests gained 52 Mha (7%) and boreal forests were stable (+12 Mha). The 2020 forest carbon stock was 870 ± 61 Pg C: 43% in living biomass, 45% in soil, 8% in dead wood and 4% in litter (ms p. 3).


### 4.2 The sink by biome

Table A. Forest carbon sinks (Pg C per year) from Table 1 of the paper (ms p. 33) Biome 1990s 2000s 2010s Change Boreal 0.51 0.49 0.32 −36% Temperate 0.53 0.59 0.68 +30% Tropical intact 1.28 1.03 0.88 −31% Tropical regrowth 1.27 1.46 1.64 +29% World forests (gross sink) 3.59 3.57 3.53 stable Tropical deforestation emissions −2.66 −1.91 −2.13 Global forest net sink 0.93 1.66 1.39 no significant trend Temperate sinks rose mainly because China's large planting programmes of the late 1980s and early 1990s reached their most productive stage. Tropical regrowth forests, with only 20% of the intact area in the 1990s, had a similar sink because they sequester carbon about five times faster. Boreal sinks fell because of more severe wildfires, insect outbreaks and logging, especially in Asian Russia (−42%); Canada's managed forests became small sources. Intact tropical sinks fell mainly because deforestation reduced their area, with Amazon droughts adding tree mortality (ms pp. 5–8).


### 4.3 Necromass and wood products

Necromass (dead wood, litter and soil) holds 58% of forest carbon, from 45% in tropical to 80% in boreal forests. Only about 10% of the carbon in harvested timber is stored in wood products, which supply just 6% of the global sink (0.21 Pg C per year in the 2010s) (ms pp. 8–9).


### 4.4 Comparison with fossil emissions and other estimates

Forests took up 107 Pg C since 1990, equal to 46% of fossil fuel emissions (7.8 ± 0.4 Pg C per year), but 63% of this was negated by tropical deforestation. The net forest sink (1.3 Pg C per year) is only 17% of fossil emissions but 91% of the land net sink. Because the land gross sink grew while the forest sink did not, the forest share of the land gross sink fell from 75% to 65%, and models that show rising forest uptake may overestimate future uptake (ms pp. 12, 15).


## 5. Conclusions

1. The global forest sink has endured, undiminished, for three decades, despite large regional changes. 2. It may weaken because of ageing forests, continuing deforestation and more intense disturbance. 3. The single most important action is to stop deforestation and degradation and protect old carbon stocks. 4. Reforestation, afforestation, climate-smart management and long-lived wood products can add to the sink. 5. The forest sequestration rate (~3.56 Pg C, ~13 Gt CO₂-eq per year) is a baseline for IPCC's estimate that land sectors could mitigate an extra 8–14 Gt CO₂-eq per year in 2020–2050.


## 6. Limitations

- Data quality varies across countries; uncertainty is largest in the tropics (±27%) and boreal forests (±13%).
- Soils, dead wood and forest area estimates are the least certain parts.
- Results are global and biome-level; there are no India-specific values.
- Non-forest peatlands, wetlands and mangroves are excluded.

# Sustainable Energy Transition for Renewable and Low Carbon Grid Electricity Generation and Supply


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Sustainable Energy Transition for Renewable and Low Carbon Grid Electricity Generation and Supply Moses Jeremiah Barasa Kabeyi, Oludolapo Akanni Olanrewaju

**Authors:**
Moses Jeremiah Barasa Kabeyi, Oludolapo Akanni Olanrewaju (Industrial Engineering Department, Durban University of Technology, South Africa)

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Energy Research, vol. 9, article 743114 (45 pages)

**Dates:**
Received 17 July 2021 · Accepted 28 December 2021 · Published 24 March 2022

**Paper type:**
Review article (open access)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/fenrg.2021.743114

**Cite as:**
Kabeyi, M. J. B., & Olanrewaju, O. A. (2022). Sustainable energy transition for renewable and low carbon grid electricity generation and supply. Frontiers in Energy Research, 9, 743114. https://doi.org/10.3389/fenrg.2021.743114 Open access review (Frontiers). Figures in this summary are quoted from the review; most come from the IEA, BP, UN and other sources it cites.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Fossil fuels still supplied 61.3% of the world's electricity in 2020. This review proposes a roadmap to a low-carbon grid built on three technological changes: saving energy on the demand side, generating more efficiently, and substituting fossil fuels with renewables and low-carbon nuclear. It argues that energy options must be judged on five dimensions (technical, environmental, economic, social and political-institutional) and that smart grids, storage, finance and policy are needed to make renewable electricity reliable and affordable.


## 1. Background

The energy sector produces about two-thirds of global CO₂, and electricity generation about 26% of total greenhouse gas emissions (pp. 2, 5). Global primary energy use grew from 155 EJ in 1965 to 557 EJ in 2020, and fossil fuels supply about 85% of it. In 2020, coal, gas and oil produced  61.3% of global electricity (p. 11). The Stockholm, Rio and Johannesburg conferences linked energy to the environment, the economy and society, making sustainable energy development a key part of sustainable development. The Paris Agreement aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C.


## 2. Aim of the study

To review energy transition strategies and propose a roadmap for sustainable, low-carbon grid electricity generation, transmission, distribution and use, in line with the Paris Agreement, that nations can adapt to their local conditions.


## 3. What the authors did

A literature review using critical discourse analysis. The authors cover greenhouse gases from power generation, global electricity generation, sustainable energy development, five dimensions of energy sustainability, and strategies for the transition (policy, planning, renewables, decentralised and smart grids, research and development, and Earth radiation management). They summarise energy options (Table 5) and strategies (Table 6). No new data were collected.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 The 2020 electricity mix

Table A. Global electricity generation by source, 2020 (review's Table 3, p. 36) Source Share Group Coal 35.1% Fossil (61.3%) Gas 23.4% Fossil Oil 2.8% Fossil Hydro 16.0% Renewable and low carbon (38%) Nuclear 10.1% Renewable and low carbon Wind 5.9% Renewable and low carbon Solar 3.2% Renewable and low carbon Geothermal and other renewables 2.8% Renewable and low carbon Others (unclassified) 0.7%


### 4.2 Three technological changes

Transition  strategies  consist  of  energy  savings  on  the  demand  side,  generation  efficiency  at  the production level, and substitution of fossil fuels by renewables and low-carbon nuclear. Large-scale renewables should go with efficiency gains in existing non-renewable plants, which still help reduce and stabilise costs.


### 4.3 Five dimensions of energy sustainability

Sustainable development has economic, social and environmental pillars; energy sustainability also needs technical and political-institutional dimensions (Table 4, p. 36). Environmental indicators include life-cycle GHG emissions in kg CO₂-eq per kWh; economic ones include generation cost, payback and affordability; social ones include acceptance and access.


### 4.4 Grid technologies

- About 10% of grid power is lost in transmission and distribution, 40% of it on the distribution side (p. 32).
- Smart grids allow two-way communication, consumers to sell power, variable pricing and peak shaving.
- Microgrids balance variable renewables with conventional units; storage and resilient grids absorb solar and wind.
- In 2019 about 37% of global electricity came from low-carbon sources; transport is about 14% of GHG emissions, so electrifying it matters (p. 33).
- IEA: efficiency could deliver over 40% of the targeted cut in energy-related GHG emissions between 2020 and 2040 (pp. 33–34). 4.5 Barriers and finance Renewables are competitive, especially for remote areas, but low- and middle-income people lack capital. Financing is needed for  solar PV, micro-hydro, wind pumps, biodigesters and biogas and improved woodstoves; higher initial investment is a key barrier (p. 31). 4.6 Technology routes Three groups of technology are needed: conventional mitigation, negative emission technologies that capture and store carbon, and technologies that change the Earth's radiative energy budget (solar radiation management).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Sustainable development cannot be achieved without sustainable energy. 2. Both renewable and cleaner non-renewable sources have a role in the short- and long-term transition. 3. A resilient grid with storage, smart grids and microgrids is needed for variable renewables. 4. Electrification of transport, industry and homes with renewable power, plus waste-to-energy, will cut emissions. 5. The transition needs supportive policy, finance, institutions and decision-support models.


## 6. Limitations

- A broad global review of grid electricity, not rural off-grid systems; no new data.
- Most numbers are secondary (IEA, BP, UN); some are inconsistent within the paper (for example the 2018 fuel shares on p. 3, and older GWP values in Table 1), so cite the primary sources.
- No village or Indian case data.

# Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO₂ Kevin Rennert, Frank Errickson, Brian C. Prest, Lisa Rennels, Richard G. Newell, William Pizer, Cora Kingdon, Jordan Wingenroth and 16 co-authors

**Authors:**
Kevin Rennert, Frank Errickson, Brian C. Prest, Lisa Rennels, Richard G. Newell, William Pizer, Cora Kingdon, Jordan Wingenroth, Roger Cooke, Bryan Parthum, David Smith, Kevin Cromar, Delavane Diaz, Frances C. Moore, Ulrich K. Müller, Richard J. Plevin, Adrian E. Raftery, Hana Ševčíková, Hannah Sheets, James H. Stock, Tammy Tan, Mark Watson, Tony E. Wong, David Anthoff

**Journal:**
Nature, vol. 610, pp. 687–692 (27 October 2022)

**Dates:**
Received 23 December 2021 · Accepted 11 August 2022 · Published online 1 September 2022

**Paper type:**
Research article (economic modelling; integrated assessment model)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05224-9

**Cite as:**
Rennert, K., Errickson, F., Prest, B. C., Rennels, L., Newell, R. G., Pizer, W., Kingdon, C., Wingenroth, J., Cooke, R., Parthum, B., Smith, D., Cromar, K., Diaz, D., Moore, F. C., Müller, U. K., Plevin, R. J., Raftery, A. E., Ševčíková, H., Sheets, H., . . . Anthoff, D. (2022). Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO₂. Nature, 610, 687–692. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05224-9 All dollar values are 2020 US dollars per metric tonne of CO₂; ranges are 5–95%.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using the new open-source GIVE model, the authors estimate a mean social cost of CO₂ of $185 per tonne ($44–$413, 5–95% range, 2020 US$) at a 2% near-term discount rate, 3.6 times the US government's $51. The lower discount rate explains most of the increase, and updated damage functions most of the rest; heat-related mortality ($90) and agriculture ($84) dominate. Because several damage types are still missing, the estimate is probably conservative.


## 1. Background

The social cost of CO₂ (SC-CO₂) is the money value of damages to society from one extra metric tonne of CO₂. In regulatory analysis, the climate benefit of a policy is usually the change in CO₂ emissions multiplied by the SC-CO₂. The US government has used it in more than 60 major regulations, and agencies in Germany, Canada and Mexico also use it (p. 687). A 2017 report of the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) found that existing estimates no longer reflected the latest research and recommended improvements in scientific basis, transparency and treatment of uncertainty.


## 2. Aim of the study

To produce an updated SC-CO₂ estimate that responds fully to the NASEM near-term recommendations, using improved socioeconomic projections, climate models, damage functions and discounting.


## 3. What the authors did

They built the open-source Greenhouse Gas Impact Value Estimator (GIVE) on the Mimi.jl platform. It has four steps: 1. Socioeconomics: RFF-SPs, probabilistic multi-century projections of country population and GDP per capita, and global CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O emissions. 2. Climate: the FaIR climate model and the BRICK sea-level model, with parameter uncertainty. 3. Damages: sectoral, regional damage functions for agriculture, temperature-related mortality, building energy use and sea-level rise (CIAM, with optimal coastal adaptation). 4. Discounting: a Ramsey-like discount rate linked to uncertain economic growth; preferred near-term rate 2% (ρ = 0.2%, η = 1.24). They compared results step by step with the DICE-2016R model and tested two meta-analysis-based global damage functions as a sensitivity analysis.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 The headline value

The preferred mean SC-CO₂ is $185 per tCO₂ ($44–$413, 5–95% range), 3.6 times the US government's $51 at a 3% constant discount rate (p. 689). Table A. Mean SC-CO₂ by near-term discount rate (2020 US$ per tCO₂; pp. 689–690) Near-term discount rate Mean 5–95% range 3.0% $80 $12–$197 2.5% $118 $23–$280 2.0% (preferred) $185 $44–$413 1.5% $308 $94–$626


### 4.2 Damages by sector

Temperature-related mortality is the largest driver (mean partial SC-CO₂ $90, range $39–$165), followed by agriculture ($84, range −$23 to $263, the widest because CO₂ fertilisation may bring benefits). Building energy use adds $9 (cooling offset by lower heating) and sea-level rise only $2, because its damages come late and are reduced by optimal coastal adaptation (p. 690).


### 4.3 Why the value rose

Table B. From DICE-2016R to this study (paper's Table 1, p. 690) Step Mean SC-CO₂ Share of change DICE-2016R $44 GIVE with DICE damage function, 3% rate $59 11% GIVE with sectoral damages, 3% rate $80 15% GIVE with sectoral damages, 2% rate (this study) $185 74% Two meta-analysis damage functions give means within −18% to +11% of the preferred estimate.


### 4.4 Socioeconomic outlook

In the RFF-SPs, median world population peaks at about 11 billion around 2130 and falls to 7.3 billion by 2300; median per-capita growth averages 0.88% a year over 2020–2300; and median net CO₂ emissions fall to 17 GtCO₂ in 2100, about 40% of today's level (p. 689).


## 5. Conclusions

5. Updated, comprehensive evidence implies a much higher SC-CO₂ than values used in policy today. 6. The lower near-term discount rate is the largest driver; updated damage functions are second. 7. Higher SC-CO₂ values substantially raise the estimated benefits of mitigation and the net benefits of stricter climate policy. 8. The estimate is probably conservative because several damage types and tipping points are missing. 9. The method can be extended to other years and to CH₄, N₂O and HFCs.


## 6. Limitations

- Only four damage sectors; biodiversity, labour productivity, conflict, migration and most non-market damages are missing; only one tipping point (rapid Antarctic ice loss) is approximated.
- Results are very sensitive to the discount rate.
- Values are global, in 2020 US dollars, with no equity weighting; one climate model (FaIR) is used.
- For Indian village work the value must be converted carefully and reported as a range.

# Cost, environmental impact, and resilience of renewable energy under a changing climate: a review


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Cost, environmental impact, and resilience of renewable energy under a changing climate: a review Ahmed I. Osman, Lin Chen, Mingyu Yang, Goodluck Msigwa, Mohamed Farghali, Samer Fawzy, David W. Rooney, Pow-Seng Yap

**Authors:**
Ahmed I. Osman, Lin Chen, Mingyu Yang, Goodluck Msigwa, Mohamed Farghali, Samer Fawzy, David W. Rooney, Pow-Seng Yap

**Journal:**
Environmental Chemistry Letters, vol. 21, pp. 741–764 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 21 September 2022 · Accepted 6 October 2022 · Published online 28 October 2022

**Paper type:**
Review article (open access, CC BY 4.0)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01532-8

**Cite as:**
Osman, A. I., Chen, L., Yang, M., Msigwa, G., Farghali, M., Fawzy, S., Rooney, D. W., & Yap, P.-S. (2023). Cost, environmental impact, and resilience of renewable energy under a changing climate: a review. Environmental Chemistry Letters, 21, 741–764. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-022-01532-8 Open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. Published online 28 October 2022 (often cited as 2022); issue year 2023. Cost data are mostly from IRENA (2022).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Renewable power has become much cheaper: solar PV electricity fell from $0.417 to $0.048 per kWh between 2010 and 2021 (−88%), and onshore wind fell 68%. Climate change may cut wind and hydropower output by up to about 40% in some regions, while solar is least affected. Hydropower is the most environmentally damaging renewable; wind and biomass have the smallest impacts. Renewables could decarbonise 90% of the power sector by 2050.


## 1. Background

Fossil-fuel energy causes more than  75% of global greenhouse gas emissions and about  90% of CO₂ emissions (p. 741). Energy demand is expected to rise 56% by 2040. Renewables are needed to decarbonise energy, but rising temperatures, extreme winds, sea-level rise and lower rainfall can affect their output, and their environmental effects are less studied (p. 742).


## 2. Aim of the study

To  review  the  costs  of  renewable  energy,  the  impact  of  climate  change  on  renewables,  the environmental and economic impacts of renewables, and decarbonisation in different countries, focusing on solar, wind, biomass, hydropower and geothermal energy.


## 3. What the authors did

A literature review. Cost data come mainly from IRENA (2022); the comparison of environmental effects is taken from Rahman et al. (2022); country studies are summarised in Table 4. No new data were collected.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Costs

Table A. Global levelised cost of electricity, 2010 vs 2021 (IRENA, review's Table 3, p. 747) Source 2010 ($/kWh) 2021 ($/kWh) Change Solar photovoltaics 0.417 0.048 −88% Onshore wind 0.102 0.033 −68% Concentrated solar power 0.358 0.114 −68% Offshore wind 0.188 0.075 −60% Bioenergy 0.078 0.067 −14% Hydropower 0.039 0.048 +24% Geothermal 0.050 0.068 +34% Installed PV cost fell 82%, from $4808 to $857 per kW. In Europe, solar and wind power in 2021 cost four to six times less than fossil power in 2022. A micro-hydropower plant's start-up cost is split into civil works (40%), turbine and generator (30%), control equipment (22%) and management (8%) (pp. 747– 749).


### 4.2 Climate impacts on renewables

- Wind: small overall changes in some regions, but up to −40% in northern Canada and Alaska under a high-emission scenario (p. 750).
- Hydropower: up to −41% generation by 2050 in Portugal; South America is the most vulnerable region (pp. 750–752).
- Solar: the least affected source; PV output may rise in some places and fall about 4% over much of Africa (p. 751).
- Biomass: climate can alter productivity, growth, chemical composition and soil microbes; +1 °C reduces global wheat yields by 6.0%, maize by 7.4% and rice by 3.2% (p. 751). 4.3 Environmental impacts Hydroelectric plants are the most damaging (greenhouse gases, eutrophication, sediment, drying rivers, floods, soil erosion, resettlement). Solar PV must be installed carefully. Wind turbines and biomass plants have negligible impact and are recommended for wide use. Most country studies since 2016 show renewables reduce life-cycle CO₂, but a study in a remote block of Uttaranchal, India (Akella et al. 2009) found a rise in emissions (pp. 753–756). 4.4 Economic impacts Fossil fuels were subsidised by $5.9 trillion in 2020. About $4 trillion per year of renewable investment is needed by 2030 for net zero, but avoided pollution and climate impacts could save up to $4.2 trillion per year by 2030, and the energy transformation could add $98 trillion to global GDP in 2016–2050 (pp. 756– 757).

### 4.5 Countries

China supplies about two-thirds of the world's solar panels and nearly half of its wind turbines; India uses auctions, private energy trading and procurement tracking; Japan sets yearly renewable obligations for utilities; Nigeria uses distributed generation and smart grids; South Africa uses green funds and carbon credits (pp. 757–759).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Except hydropower and geothermal, renewable costs have fallen sharply since 2010. 2. Climate change can cut wind and hydro output by up to about 40% regionally; solar is the most resilient. 3. Hydropower has the largest environmental impact; wind and biomass the smallest. 4. Renewables could supply 65% of world electricity by 2030 and decarbonise 90% of the power sector by 2050, helping limit warming to 1.5 °C.


## 6. Limitations

- Global review of studies of mixed quality; costs and impacts vary by location.
- Little detail on small rural or off-grid systems.
- Some numbers in the paper are garbled (for example, jobs written in dollars on p. 757), so check the primary sources.
- Often cited as 2022 (online date); the issue year is 2023.

# Monitoring global carbon emissions in 2022


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Monitoring global carbon emissions in 2022 Zhu Liu, Zhu Deng, Steve Davis, Philippe Ciais

**Authors:**
Zhu Liu (Tsinghua University), Zhu Deng (Alibaba Cloud), Steve Davis (University of California, Irvine), Philippe Ciais (LSCE, France; The Cyprus Institute)

**Journal:**
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, vol. 4, pp. 205–206 (April 2023)

**Dates:**
Published online 13 March 2023

**Paper type:**
Comment (near-real-time emissions data, Carbon Monitor)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00406-z

**Cite as:**
Liu, Z., Deng, Z., Davis, S., & Ciais, P. (2023). Monitoring global carbon emissions in


## 2022. Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, 4, 205–206.

https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00406-z Two-page Comment based on Carbon Monitor near-real-time data (fossil fuel combustion and cement CO₂).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Global CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and cement reached 36.1 ± 0.3 GtCO₂ in 2022, 1.5% more than in 2021 and 2.0% more than in 2019, so the COVID dip was short-lived and no peak is in sight. Power and industry gave two-thirds of the total. China's emissions fell for the first time (−1.5%), while India's rose 7%. At this pace the remaining 1.5 °C carbon budget could be used up within 2–7 years.


## 1. Background

COVID-19 caused a record fall in global CO₂ emissions in 2020 (−5.4%, 1.9 GtCO₂), but emissions rebounded by 6.3% (2.1 GtCO₂) in 2021. With little time left to meet the 1.5 °C or 2 °C goals, detailed, near-real-time tracking of emissions is crucial (p. 205).


## 2. Aim of the study

To present and analyse daily, national and sector-specific CO₂ emissions for 2022 using near-real-time data from the Carbon Monitor project, and to track the remaining carbon budget.


## 3. What the authors did

They used Carbon Monitor near-real-time data on fossil fuel combustion and cement production to estimate daily CO₂ emissions by sector and country for 2022, compared them with 2019–2021 and with the Global Carbon Project and IEA, and calculated how much of the IPCC and newer (Lamboll et al.) carbon budgets 2022 emissions used, including land-use change emissions.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Global total

Emissions were 35.3 GtCO₂ in 2019, 33.4 in 2020, 35.5 in 2021 and 36.1 ± 0.3 in 2022: +2.0%, +7.9% and +1.5% relative to those years. The 1.5% growth (0.9–2.6%) agrees with the GCP (1.0 ± 0.9%) and the IEA (<1%).


### 4.2 Sectors

Table A. Sector shares of global CO₂ in 2022 and growth rates (p. 205) Sector Share 2022 Growth 2021 Growth 2022 Power 39.3% +6.9% +0.8% Industry 28.9% +5.7% +1.1% Ground transport 17.9% +8.8% +2.5% Residential 9.9% International bunkers 3.1% international aviation +44% Domestic aviation 0.9% +25.5% −0.9% International aviation rose 44% in 2022 but stayed 25% below 2019.


### 4.3 Countries

The top five emitters produced 23.3 GtCO₂ (65% of the total). China's emissions fell 1.5%, its first reduction, perhaps because of the extended zero-COVID policy, but remained 5.6% above 2019. US and EU emissions rose 3.2% and 0.5%. India's emissions grew 7% (7.9% above 2019), on pace to pass the EU as the third largest emitter in 2023. Russia's fell 1.8%.


### 4.4 Carbon budget countdown

Table B. Share of remaining carbon budgets used by 2022 emissions (pp. 205–206) Budget Used in 2022 Remaining Years left IPCC 1.5 °C (67%), 400 GtCO₂ from 2020 10.0% 283 GtCO₂ 7.1 IPCC 2 °C (67%), 1,150 GtCO₂ from 2020 3.5% 1,033 GtCO₂ 25.8 Lamboll et al. 1.5 °C (66%), 110 GtCO₂ from 2022 36.5% 70 GtCO₂ 1.7 Lamboll et al. 2 °C (66%), 990 GtCO₂ from 2022 4.1% 950 GtCO₂ 23.7 Counting non-CO₂ gases (methane, nitrous oxide, fluorinated gases) would make the remaining budget even smaller.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Global emissions continue to rise despite efforts to cut fossil energy use; the peak has not yet been reached. 2. The 1.5 °C budget could be exhausted within 2–7 years (67% likelihood). 3. Power, transport and industry need deeper decarbonisation and more renewable energy.

4. Countries must act now on net-zero pledges, with international cooperation; near-real-time monitoring shows early whether mitigation works.


## 6. Limitations

- Covers fossil fuel and cement CO₂ (land-use change is added only for the budget countdown); no CH₄, N₂O or F-gases.
- Near-real-time data are preliminary and are revised later.
- National and sector totals only; no village or district values.

# Indicators of Global Climate Change 2023: annual update of key indicators of the state of the climate system and human influence


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Indicators of Global Climate Change 2023: annual update of key indicators of the state of the climate system and human influence Piers M. Forster, Chris Smith, Tristram Walsh, William F. Lamb, Robin Lamboll, Bradley Hall and 53 co- authors

**Authors:**
Piers M. Forster, Chris Smith, Tristram Walsh, William F. Lamb, Robin Lamboll, Bradley Hall, Mathias Hauser, Aurélien Ribes, Debbie Rosen, Nathan P. Gillett, Matthew D. Palmer, Joeri Rogelj, Karina von Schuckmann, Blair Trewin, Myles Allen, Robbie Andrew, Richard A. Betts, Alex Borger, Tim Boyer, Jiddu A. Broersma, Carlo Buontempo, Samantha Burgess, Chiara Cagnazzo, Lijing Cheng, Pierre Friedlingstein, Andrew Gettelman, Johannes Gütschow, Masayoshi Ishii, Stuart Jenkins, Xin Lan, Colin Morice, Jens Mühle, Christopher Kadow, John Kennedy, Rachel E. Killick, Paul B. Krummel, Jan C. Minx, Gunnar Myhre, Vaishali Naik, Glen P. Peters, Anna Pirani, Julia Pongratz, Carl- Friedrich Schleussner, Sonia I. Seneviratne, Sophie Szopa, Peter Thorne, Mahesh V. M. Kovilakam, Elisa Majamäki, Jukka-Pekka Jalkanen, Margreet van Marle, Rachel M. Hoesly, Robert Rohde, Dominik Schumacher, Guido van der Werf, Russell Vose, Kirsten Zickfeld, Xuebin Zhang, Valérie Masson-Delmotte and Panmao Zhai (59 authors)

**Journal:**
Earth System Science Data, vol. 16, pp. 2625–2658 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 24 April 2024 · Accepted 31 May 2024 · Published 5 June 2024

**Paper type:**
Data description paper (annual update of climate indicators)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-2625-2024

**Cite as:**
Forster, P. M., Smith, C., Walsh, T., Lamb, W. F., Lamboll, R., Hall, B., Hauser, M., Ribes, A., Rosen, D., Gillett, N. P., Palmer, M. D., Rogelj, J., von Schuckmann, K., Trewin, B., Allen, M., Andrew, R., Betts, R. A., Borger, A., Boyer, T., . . . Zhai, P. (2024). Indicators of Global Climate Change 2023: annual update of key indicators of the state of the climate system and human influence. Earth System Science Data, 16, 2625–2658. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-2625-2024 Open access under CC BY 4.0. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11388387.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

IPCC reports come only every 5–10 years, so this group updates the key AR6 climate indicators each year with the same methods. For 2014–2023, observed warming was 1.19 °C and all of it was human-induced (1.19 [1.0 to 1.4] °C). Human-induced warming reached 1.31 °C in 2023 and is rising at 0.26 °C per decade, driven by GHG emissions at a high of 53 ± 5.4 GtCO₂e per year and weaker aerosol cooling. Only about 200 GtCO₂ of the 1.5 °C budget (50% chance) remained at the start of 2024.


## 1. Background

IPCC assessments are the trusted source of evidence for UNFCCC negotiations, but successive reports come out 5–10 years apart, leaving an information gap. AR6 used data up to 2019. The Indicators of Global Climate Change (IGCC) project gives annual updates; this is the second (pp. 2626–2627).


## 2. Aim of the study

To update, to the end of 2023, the indicators that link cause to effect: GHG and short-lived climate forcer emissions, GHG concentrations, effective radiative forcing (ERF), Earth's energy imbalance, surface temperature, human-induced warming, the remaining carbon budget and land maximum temperature.


## 3. What the authors did

They followed IPCC AR6 WGI (and WGIII Ch. 2) methods as closely as possible. CO₂e uses AR6 GWP100 values. Human-induced warming was estimated with the three AR6 attribution methods: the Global Warming Index (GWI), regularised optimal fingerprinting (ROF) and kriging for climate change (KCC) (p. 2639). Remaining carbon budgets were updated with the MAGICC emulator, AR6 WGIII scenarios and the new warming estimate (p. 2644). All data are open on Zenodo.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Emissions

Table A. Global GHG emissions (GtCO₂e per year; Table 1, p. 2632) Period Total GHG CO₂ fossil and industry CO₂ land use CH₄ 1970–1979 30 ± 4.2 17.2 4.6 6.3 1990–1999 40 ± 5.2 23.3 5.8 7.5 2010–2019 53 ± 5.5 34.8 5.2 8.8 2013–2022 53 ± 5.4 35.3 4.7 8.8 2022 55 ± 5.3 36.4 4.3 9.0 In 2022, N₂O added 3.1 and F-gases 1.8 GtCO₂e. Total emissions in 2022 equalled the earlier highs of 2019 and 2021. Fossil CO₂ was projected at 36.8 GtCO₂ for 2023 (pp. 2629–2630). These totals are about 3 GtCO₂e below AR6 because land-use CO₂ and CH₄ estimates were revised down (Table 10, p. 2648).


### 4.2 Concentrations, forcing and energy imbalance

In 2023, CO₂ was 419.3 ppm, CH₄ 1922.5 ppb and N₂O 336.9 ppb. Total human ERF was 2.79 [1.78 to 3.61] W m⁻² relative to 1750 (AR6: 2.72 W m⁻² for 2019). The Earth's energy imbalance averaged 0.96 W m⁻² over 2010–2023, up from 0.79 W m⁻² for 2006–2018 (Table 10, p. 2648). NOTE ON THE SOURCE The paper gives the 2023 ERF upper bound as 3.61 W m⁻² in Sect. 4 (p. 2633) but 3.60 W m⁻² in Table 10 (p. 2648).


### 4.3 Warming

Observed warming for 2014–2023 was 1.19 [1.06 to 1.30] °C and human-induced warming 1.19 [1.0 to 1.4] °C. In 2023 human-induced warming was 1.31 [1.1 to 1.7] °C, below the observed record of 1.43 [1.32 to 1.53] °C, which points to a large role for El Niño. Human-induced warming rose at 0.26 [0.2 to 0.4] °C per decade (Table 6, p. 2642; p. 2644). Land maximum temperatures reached 1.81 °C above pre- industrial in 2014–2023 (p. 2646).


### 4.4 Remaining carbon budget

Table B. Remaining carbon budget from the start of 2024 (GtCO₂; Table 8, p. 2645) Limit 33% 50% 67% 83% 1.5 °C 300 200 150 100 1.7 °C 700 550 450 350 2.0 °C 1400 1100 900 750 The 1.5 °C (50%) budget fell from 500 GtCO₂ (start of 2020, AR6) to 200 GtCO₂ (start of 2024). About 164 GtCO₂ was emitted from 2020 to 2023, and updated emulators and scenarios removed about 100 GtCO₂ more (pp. 2644, 2648).


## 5. Conclusions

1. This is a critical decade: human-induced warming rates are at their highest, and 1.5 °C may be reached within about 10 years. 2. Emissions are at a long-term high, but there are signs that their growth has slowed compared with the 2000s. 3. Rapid and stringent emission cuts could halve warming rates over the next 20 years. 4. Annual updates traceable to IPCC methods can track whether the indicators change direction (pp. 2649–2650).


## 6. Limitations

- Global indicators only; no regional or national values.
- Large uncertainties remain in aerosol forcing and land-use CO₂ (±70%).
- Natural CH₄ changes are excluded while wildfire aerosol is included, which is inconsistent (p. 2649).
- 2023 non-CO₂ emissions were not yet available.

#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This third annual update of the IPCC AR6 climate indicators covers data to 2024. For 2015–2024, observed warming was 1.24 °C, of which 1.22 [1.0 to 1.5] °C was human-induced. Human-induced warming reached 1.36 °C in 2024 and is rising at 0.27 °C per decade, driven by record GHG emissions (53.6 ± 5.2 GtCO₂e per year, 2014–2023) and weaker aerosol cooling. The energy imbalance is 25% above AR6 and sea level is rising faster. A 2026 corrigendum puts the remaining 1.5 °C budget (50%) at 160 GtCO₂ from 2025, about four years of current emissions.


## 1. Background

IPCC reports come out 5–10 years apart, while the climate is changing fast. The Indicators of Global Climate Change (IGCC) project gives policymakers annual updates traceable to IPCC AR6 methods; this is its third edition (pp. 2641–2642).


## 2. Aim of the study

To update, to the end of 2024, the indicators of the state of the climate: GHG and short-lived climate forcer emissions, concentrations, effective radiative forcing (ERF), Earth's energy imbalance, surface temperature, human-induced warming, the remaining carbon budget and temperature extremes, adding land precipitation and sea-level rise this year.


## 3. What the authors did

They followed IPCC AR6 WGI methods as closely as possible. CO₂e uses AR6 GWP100 values, and the WGIII emissions convention was compared with national inventories. Human-induced warming used the three AR6 attribution methods; remaining carbon budgets used TCRE with emulators. All data are open on Zenodo. SOURCE USED The PDF in the folder is the discussion preprint. Numbers here follow the version of record (ESSD 17, 2641–2680), which differs slightly (e.g. human-induced warming 1.22 °C, not 1.23 °C), and the 2026 corrigendum to Table 8.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Emissions

Table A. Global GHG emissions (GtCO₂e per year; Table 1, p. 2649) Period Total GHG CO₂ fossil and industry CO₂ land use CH₄ N₂O 1970–1979 30.9 17.3 5.2 6.3 1.9 1990–1999 39.3 23.6 5.7 7.2 2.3 2010–2019 52.9 35.4 4.9 8.4 2.7 2014–2023 53.6 36.3 4.1 8.7 2.8 2023 55.4 37.8 3.6 9.2 2.9 F-gases added 1.9 GtCO₂e in 2023. Fossil CO₂ was projected at 38.2 GtCO₂ for 2024. National inventories gave 47.1 GtCO₂e for 2023, 8.3 GtCO₂e lower, mainly because they count about 7.5 GtCO₂ more land-use removals (p. 2646).


### 4.2 Concentrations, forcing and energy imbalance

In 2024, CO₂ was 422.8 ppm, CH₄ 1929.7 ppb and N₂O 337.9 ppb. Total human ERF was 2.97 [2.05 to 3.77] W m⁻² relative to 1750 (AR6: 2.72 W m⁻² for 2019; p. 2651). The energy imbalance averaged 0.99 W m⁻² over 2012–2024, 25% above the AR6 value for 2006–2018 (Table 11, p. 2667).


### 4.3 Warming, extremes and sea level

Observed warming for 2015–2024 was 1.24 [1.11 to 1.35] °C and human-induced warming 1.22 [1.0 to 1.5] °C. In 2024 observed warming was 1.52 [1.39 to 1.65] °C and human-induced 1.36 [1.1 to 1.7] °C (Table 6, p. 2660). The human-induced rate was 0.27 [0.2 to 0.4] °C per decade (Table 7, p. 2662). Land maximum temperatures reached 1.90 °C in 2015–2024. Sea level rose 228.0 mm from 1901 to 2024; since 1993 the rate is 3.46 mm per year (Table 10, p. 2666).


### 4.4 Remaining carbon budget

Table B. Remaining carbon budget from the start of 2025 (GtCO₂; corrigendum Table 8, 2026) Limit 33% 50% 67% 83% 1.5 °C 240 160 110 60 1.6 °C 460 350 260 190 1.7 °C 690 530 420 320 2.0 °C 1350 1080 890 720 The published paper gave 130 GtCO₂ for 1.5 °C (50%), exhausted in a little over 3 years at 2024 emissions of 42 GtCO₂ per year (p. 2663). The 2026 corrigendum recalculated budgets from human-induced rather than observed warming, giving 160 GtCO₂, a little over 4 years; the conclusions do not change.


## 5. Conclusions

1. This is a critical decade: human-induced warming rates are at their highest, and 1.5 °C may be reached in around 5 years. 2. Earth's energy imbalance has risen to about 1.0 W m⁻², 25% above AR6, with committed sea-level rise to follow. 3. Emissions are at a long-term high but their growth has slowed; rapid cuts could halve warming rates over 20 years. 4. Annual updates depend on open, well-supported monitoring networks (pp. 2669–2670).


## 6. Limitations

- Global indicators only; no regional or national values.
- Large uncertainties in aerosol forcing and land-use CO₂ (±70%).
- One of the three AR6 attribution methods is diverging (Table 11).
- Budget values changed after publication (2026 corrigendum); 2024 non-CO₂ emissions were not yet available.

# Mycorrhizal mycelium as a global carbon pool


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Mycorrhizal mycelium as a global carbon pool Heidi-Jayne Hawkins, Rachael I. M. Cargill, Michael E. Van Nuland, Stephen C. Hagen, Katie J. Field, Merlin Sheldrake, Nadejda A. Soudzilovskaia, E. Toby Kiers

**Authors:**
Heidi-Jayne Hawkins (University of Cape Town; Conservation International), Rachael I. M. Cargill, Michael E. Van Nuland, Stephen C. Hagen, Katie J. Field, Merlin Sheldrake, Nadejda A. Soudzilovskaia, E. Toby Kiers

**Journal:**
Current Biology, vol. 33, issue 11, pp. R560–R573 (5 June 2023)

**Paper type:**
Review with quantitative data synthesis (194 datasets)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2023.02.027

**Cite as:**
Hawkins, H.-J., Cargill, R. I. M., Van Nuland, M. E., Hagen, S. C., Field, K. J., Sheldrake, M., Soudzilovskaia, N. A., & Kiers, E. T. (2023). Mycorrhizal mycelium as a global carbon pool. Current Biology, 33(11), R560–R573. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2023.02.027 Open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7286515.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Mycorrhizal fungi trade soil nutrients for plant carbon. Pooling 194 datasets, the authors give the first global estimate of how much plant carbon goes to their underground mycelium: about 3.58 Gt C (13.12 Gt CO₂e) per year, equal to 36% of fossil fuel CO₂ emissions in 2021. Ectomycorrhizal fungi take the largest share of host NPP (13.1%), arbuscular fungi 6.2%. Crops give much less (3.3% on average; under 0.1% for wheat, barley and maize). How long this carbon stays in soil is not yet known.


## 1. Background

Plants and mycorrhizal fungi have formed partnerships for more than 400 million years. Up to 80% of plant phosphorus and 20% of nitrogen can come via the fungi. About 75% of land carbon is stored below ground, and the fungi sit at a key entry point of carbon into soil food webs, but their global role in moving carbon into soil was under-explored (p. R560).


## 2. Aim of the study

To give the first global quantitative estimate of carbon allocated from plants to mycorrhizal mycelium, and to review how these fungi add carbon to, and lose it from, soils.


## 3. What the authors did

They collected 194 datasets (mostly isotope labelling, plus mass balance, FACE and modelling) from forests, shrublands, heathlands, grasslands and croplands in Central Europe, the USA, South America and Asia; none were found from Southeast Asia, Oceania or Africa. External mycelium was used as a common proxy; where only hyphal-compartment labelling was available, values were cut by 7% to remove exudates (pp. R563–R564). Mean allocations by fungal type were applied to global NPP, masked by maps of mycorrhizal vegetation and plant functional groups (p. R565).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Allocation by fungal type

Table A. Mean share of host NPP allocated to mycorrhizal mycelium (p. R564) Fungal type Share of NPP Datasets (N) Ectomycorrhizal (EcM) 13.1% ± 0.22 63 Arbuscular (AM) 6.2% ± 0.11 89 Dark septate endophytes (DSE) 4.6% ± 0.29 7 Ericoid (ErM) 3.5% ± 0.14 28 Orchid (OM) 1.0% ± 0.47 3 Allocation differed significantly by type (P < 0.0001). Some AM and EcM experiments reached 50% of NPP. Only 30% of datasets covered more than one season or plant age (pp. R564–R565).


### 4.2 Crops and plant types

Crops allocated 3.3% ± 0.55 of NPP to AM fungi (N = 55), four times less than wild grasses and forbs. Medic and ryegrass gave about 5%, while  wheat, barley and maize gave less than 0.1%, possibly because of fine roots, breeding for fertiliser response and intensive cultivation. Herbaceous plants gave 6.5% and woody plants 2.3% (N = 6 only) (p. R565).


### 4.3 Global flux

Per year, plants send 1.07 Gt C (3.93 Gt CO₂e) to AM fungi, 2.47 Gt C (9.07 Gt CO₂e) to EcM fungi and


### 0.03 Gt C (0.12 Gt CO₂e) to ErM fungi:  3.58 Gt C or 13.12 Gt CO₂e in total, 36% of fossil fuel CO₂

emissions in 2021 (p. R565–R566). AM vegetation holds more biomass (241 Gt C vs 100 Gt C for EcM), but EcM fungi carry more carbon into soil.


### 4.4 Mechanisms

- Living hyphae draw carbon into soil and help create and stabilise soil aggregates.
- Dead fungal tissue (necromass) forms a scaffold that protects organic matter; melanin slows decay.
- Exudates feed microbes and can form stable mineral-associated organic matter.
- Losses: fungal respiration is 6–14% (AM) and 6–25% (EcM) of soil respiration; fungi can also increase priming (pp. R566–R568).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Mycorrhizal fungi are a major global carbon pool, drawing 3–13% (up to 50%) of host NPP below ground. 2. About 13 Gt CO₂e a year moves through plants into mycorrhizal mycelium; this may be an over- or underestimate. 3. Mycorrhizal fungi should be included in global climate and carbon-cycle models and in conservation policy and practice (p. R569).


## 6. Limitations

- Data mostly from single time points; few studies for ErM, OM and DSE fungi.
- No data from Southeast Asia, Oceania or Africa; tropical forests, savannas and the global south are under-represented (pp. R564, R568).
- Only external hyphae were counted, so the flux may be underestimated; losses through respiration were not assessed.
- How long the carbon stays in soil is unknown, so the flux is not the same as long-term storage (p. R569).

# Assessing the environmental impacts of renewable energy sources: A case study on air pollution and carbon emissions in China


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Assessing the environmental impacts of renewable energy sources: A case study on air pollution and carbon emissions in China Xihui Haviour Chen, Kienpin Tee, Marwa Elnahass, Rizwan Ahmed

**Authors:**
Xihui Haviour Chen (Heriot-Watt University), Kienpin Tee (James Cook University, Singapore), Marwa Elnahass (Newcastle University), Rizwan Ahmed (University of Kent)

**Journal:**
Journal of Environmental Management, vol. 345, article 118525 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 25 April 2023 · Accepted 25 June 2023 · Online 6 July 2023

**Paper type:**
Research article (national time-series econometrics)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.118525

**Cite as:**
Chen, X. H., Tee, K., Elnahass, M., & Ahmed, R. (2023). Assessing the environmental impacts of renewable energy sources: A case study on air pollution and carbon emissions in China. Journal of Environmental Management, 345, 118525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.118525 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using quarterly Chinese data for 1990–2022, the authors regress CO₂ and total GHG emissions on the shares of renewable and fossil energy in final energy use, with GDP, exports, population and coal rents as controls. A higher renewable share goes with lower emissions and a higher fossil share with higher emissions, and Granger tests show the direction runs from the energy mix to emissions, not back. China still relies on fossil fuels (79% of final energy on average). Note that the paper's 'air pollution' variable is CO₂ and GHG emissions, not air quality.


## 1. Background

Air pollution harms health and economies: 6.7 million deaths were linked to indoor and outdoor pollution in 2019, 4.3 million of them to outdoor pollution (p. 1). China, the second-largest economy, emitted about 30% of global CO₂ in 2020 and is the largest methane emitter (about 26%). Its 14th Five- Year Plan (2021–2025) uses 'dual control': a cap on energy use and a falling energy intensity of GDP (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To test how renewable and non-renewable energy affect China's carbon emissions, with two hypotheses: H1, renewable use is negatively related to pollution as the economy grows; H2, stricter regulation raises renewable use, which Granger-causes lower pollution (pp. 5–6).


## 3. What the authors did

They used quarterly World Bank and National Bureau of Statistics data for 1990–2022 (128 observations, winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles). Dependent variables were CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and cement (kt) and total GHG emissions (kt CO₂e). Independent variables were the renewable share and the non-renewable share of final energy consumption. Controls were coal rents, GDP, exports and population. ARIMA regressions gave baseline effects, and Granger causality tests with two lags tested the direction both ways (pp. 6–7). CORRECTION TO THE OLD SUMMARY ARIMA is used here as a regression with controls, not for forecasting, and 'air pollution' is measured only as CO₂ and GHG emissions (p. 6).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Baseline ARIMA results

Table A. Effect of energy shares on log emissions (Table 3, p. 9) Variable Log CO₂ Log GHG Renewable share −0.01035 (p < 0.01) −0.0155 (p < 0.01) Non-renewable share +0.00713 (p < 0.1) +0.00984 (p < 0.1) Observations 128 128 The authors read this as about a 1.0% fall in CO₂ (1.55% for GHG) per unit rise in renewable share, and a 0.71% rise (0.98%) per unit rise in fossil share (p. 8).


### 4.2 Granger causality

Lagged  renewable  and  fossil  shares  significantly  predicted  CO₂  and  GHG  emissions,  while  lagged emissions did not predict either energy share. The authors conclude that policy-driven renewables have reduced emissions, but rising pollution has not pushed policymakers to speed up renewables (Tables 4– 5, pp. 8–10).


### 4.3 Energy mix

Mean shares over the sample were 79.23% non-renewable and 18.79% renewable (p. 8). The renewable share rose from about 10% in 1990 to nearly 30% in 2021 (p. 11).


### 4.4 Points to read with care

- Coefficients are described 'per kiloton', but the energy variables are percentage shares (p. 8).
- The text gives −0.00529 for the renewable → CO₂ lag total, Table 4 gives −0.00629; for GHG the text says renewables 'increase' emissions by 0.00201, while Table 5 shows −0.00201 (pp. 8–10).
- The paper says China aims for 'carbon dioxide neutrality by 2030'; the 2020 pledge was a CO₂ peak before 2030 and neutrality before 2060 (p. 2).

## 5. Conclusions

1. Renewable energy use reduces, and fossil energy use increases, China's CO₂ and GHG emissions, with one-way causality.

2. China still relies heavily on fossil fuels, so the shift to cleaner energy must continue. 3. Results are consistent with the Environmental Kuznets Curve and the Porter Hypothesis. 4. Developed nations should help cut renewable costs and support developing countries (pp. 10–11).


## 6. Limitations

- China only, at national level; geography is not considered (p. 11).
- Statistical (Granger) causality, not physical causation; energy shares and emissions are highly correlated with GDP and exports (Table 2).
- No direct air-quality pollutant is modelled.
- Not applicable to rural or village scale without new data.

# Social, environmental, and economic consequences of integrating renewable energies in the electricity sector: a review


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Social, environmental, and economic consequences of integrating renewable energies in the electricity sector: a review Mohamed Farghali, Ahmed I. Osman, Zhonghao Chen, Amal Abdelhaleem, Ikko Ihara, Israa M. A. Mohamed, Pow-Seng Yap, David W. Rooney

**Authors:**
Mohamed Farghali (Obihiro University; Assiut University), Ahmed I. Osman (Queen's University Belfast), Zhonghao Chen, Amal Abdelhaleem, Ikko Ihara, Israa M. A. Mohamed, Pow-Seng Yap (Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University), David W. Rooney

**Journal:**
Environmental Chemistry Letters, vol. 21, pp. 1381–1418 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 10 February 2023 · Accepted 24 February 2023 · Online 24 March 2023

**Paper type:**
Review article

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-023-01587-1

**Cite as:**
Farghali, M., Osman, A. I., Chen, Z., Abdelhaleem, A., Ihara, I., Mohamed, I. M. A., Yap, P.-S., & Rooney, D. W. (2023). Social, environmental, and economic consequences of integrating renewable energies in the electricity sector: a review. Environmental Chemistry Letters, 21, 1381–1418. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-023-01587-1 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This review gathers case studies on adding solar, wind, hydro, bioenergy and storage to electricity systems. Hybrid systems are more reliable and more resilient to climate change than single sources; PV/wind/hydro systems gave 2.11–5.46% more power under climate change. CO₂ savings rise with the renewable share, and a PV/wind/battery/diesel desalination system cut water cost by 69% and environmental impacts by 90%. Rural Indian cases include a Punjab PV/biogas microgrid at $0.0735/kWh. Renewables still have impacts (hydropower most), and poor design raises costs.


## 1. Background

Hydrocarbons  still  provide  over  80%  of  the  world's  energy.  Moving  to  electricity  is  seen  as  an improvement, but power generation is a major CO₂ source and renewables also have impacts (p. 1381). By the end of 2020 the world had 2,799 GW of renewable capacity: hydropower 1,211 GW (43%), wind 733 GW (26%), solar 714 GW (26%), bioenergy 127 GW and geothermal 14 GW (p. 1382).


## 2. Aim of the study

To review the integration of renewable energy into the electricity sector from social, environmental and economic perspectives, including hybrid systems, water desalination and climate resilience.


## 3. What the authors did

A narrative review of published studies on solar PV, wind, hydropower, bioenergy, geothermal and battery storage, single and hybrid. It compiles tables of optimal hybrid designs, renewable fractions, costs of energy and CO₂ emissions from individual case studies; no new data or pooled analysis.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Social impacts

An extra 1 GWh a year of renewable power could offer 3.5 jobs; renewables employed 9.8 million people in 2016. Ram et al. (2020) project jobs from PV, battery storage, wind, hydropower and bioenergy; the abstract cites 504,000 jobs in 2030 and 4.18 million in 2050, but the body text lists five figures for different years 'respectively', so the pairing is unclear (p. 1385). Less firewood use benefits women's health.


### 4.2 Costs and emissions

Table A. CO₂ of hybrid designs vs a diesel-only system (Table 3, p. 1392; Ajlan et al. 2017) System Renewable share CO₂ (kg/yr) Reduction Diesel only 0% 271,206 – Wind/diesel 38% 152,212 44% PV/diesel 54% 108,161 60% PV/wind/diesel 64% 84,007 70% PV/wind 100% 0 100% In  rural  India,  a  PV/biogas  generator  microgrid  was  the  most  cost-effective  option  for  Punjab ($0.0735/kWh), and a PV/biomass gasifier/battery system in the western Himalaya cost $0.185/kWh (about 92% less than diesel) with 90.1% lower GHG emissions (p. 1386).


### 4.3 Environmental trade-offs

Wind turbines embody 1,664–2,074 t CO₂e per MW. PV panels carry life cycle impacts such as toxicity and acidification. Hydropower is the most harmful to the environment and aquatic ecosystems; biomass and wind have minor impacts (pp. 1385–1387).


### 4.4 Desalination and climate resilience

A PV/wind/battery system backed by a diesel generator cut water cost by 69% and environmental impacts by 90% vs fossil-based units; for coastal Tamil Nadu villages, water cost $4.57/m³ (p. 1387). Under climate change, PV/wind/hydro systems raised power generation by 2.11–5.46% and guarantee rates by 3.74–71.61% (p. 1381; table p. 1396).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Hybrid systems are more reliable and better at withstanding climate impacts than single-source systems. 2. Raising the renewable share lowers net present costs, fuel use and pollution, in line with energy policies.

3. Large or poorly designed systems raise installation costs, so technical and financial evaluation is needed first. 4. A standard method to evaluate energy complementarity is lacking (pp. 1410–1411).


## 6. Limitations

- Numbers come from individual case studies with different sites, models and assumptions; they are not pooled.
- Some figures in the text are garbled (e.g. the jobs list; investment given as 'million' dollars), so check original sources.
- No emission-saving formula is provided.
- Only a few rural Indian cases; none for the Varuna basin.

title: Recovering wetland biogeomorphic feedbacks to restore the world’s biotic carbon hotspots
authors: Ralph J. M. Temmink (Utrecht University; NIOZ; Radboud University), Leon P. M. Lamers, Christine Angelini, Tjeerd J. Bouma, Christian Fritz, Johan van de Koppel, Robin Lexmond, Max Rietkerk, Brian R. Silliman, Hans Joosten, Tjisse van der Heide (NIOZ)
description: Peatlands, mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass meadows cover about 1% of Earth's surface but store 20% of ecosystem organic carbon, because vegetation and landforms reinforce each other (biogeomorphic feedbacks). These wetlands are lost at about 1% a year, releasing 0.5 Pg C a year, 5% of human carbon emissions, and degraded wetlands keep emitting for centuries. Conservation comes first; restoration works best when it restarts the feedbacks, for example by planting in clumps or rewetting peat at landscape scale.

# Recovering wetland biogeomorphic feedbacks to restore the world’s biotic carbon hotspots


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Recovering wetland biogeomorphic feedbacks to restore the world’s biotic carbon hotspots Ralph J. M. Temmink, Leon P. M. Lamers, Christine Angelini, Tjeerd J. Bouma, Christian Fritz and 6 co- authors

**Authors:**
Ralph J. M. Temmink (Utrecht University; NIOZ; Radboud University), Leon P. M. Lamers, Christine Angelini, Tjeerd J. Bouma, Christian Fritz, Johan van de Koppel, Robin Lexmond, Max Rietkerk, Brian R. Silliman, Hans Joosten, Tjisse van der Heide (NIOZ)

**Journal:**
Science, vol. 376, issue 6593, article eabn1479 (2022)

**Paper type:**
Review

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abn1479 Source used Accepted author manuscript (NIOZ repository); pages are manuscript pages

**Cite as:**
Temmink, R. J. M., Lamers, L. P. M., Angelini, C., Bouma, T. J., Fritz, C., van de Koppel, J., Lexmond, R., Rietkerk, M., Silliman, B. R., Joosten, H., & van der Heide, T. (2022). Recovering wetland biogeomorphic feedbacks to restore the world’s biotic carbon hotspots. Science, 376(6593), eabn1479. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abn1479 Source PDF is the accepted author manuscript (NIOZ repository); page cites are manuscript PDF pages.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Peatlands, mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass meadows cover about 1% of Earth's surface but store 20% of ecosystem organic carbon, because vegetation and landforms reinforce each other (biogeomorphic feedbacks). These wetlands are lost at about 1% a year, releasing 0.5 Pg C a year, 5% of human carbon emissions, and degraded wetlands keep emitting for centuries. Conservation comes first; restoration works best when it restarts the feedbacks, for example by planting in clumps or rewetting peat at landscape scale.


## 1. Background

Burial of organic matter is the largest carbon-sequestering process on the planet. Wetlands cover just 2% of Earth's surface but store more than 20% of global organic ecosystem carbon, and their sequestration rates can be orders of magnitude higher than those of land and ocean ecosystems (p. 8). Restoring this function requires understanding why.


## 2. Aim of the study

To compare carbon stocks and sequestration in oceans, forests and wetlands; explain how vegetation– landform feedbacks make wetlands carbon hotspots; show how human disruption turns them into sources; and show how restoration can restart the feedbacks.


## 3. What the authors did

They compiled published estimates of carbon stocks, densities and recent sequestration rates (Fig. 1, Table S1), global extent and loss rates (Table 1) and carbon released after land-use change (Fig. 3, Table

S2), focusing on 'biogeomorphic wetlands': peatlands, where vegetation retains water and builds peat, and coastal wetlands, where vegetation traps sediment (p. 8).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Stocks and sequestration

Table A. Carbon density and recent sequestration rates (pp. 9–11; Fig. 1) Ecosystem Carbon density (Mg C/ha) Sequestration (g C/m²/yr) Peatlands 1000–2000 100 (boreal), 120 (temperate), 200 (tropical) Mangroves 900 200 Salt marshes 400 250 Seagrass meadows 330 150 Terrestrial forests 150–230 < 50 Oceans 2.4 < 50 Intact coastal wetlands and peatlands sequester 0.7 Pg C a year, 6% of human carbon emissions (11.5 Pg C in 2019). About half of carbon buried in coastal wetlands comes from outside sources. Long-term peat accumulation averages 18 g C/m²/yr (pp. 9–11).


### 4.2 Biogeomorphic feedbacks

In 45% of all wetlands, biogeomorphic feedbacks shape landscapes (p. 9). They are either productivity- stimulating (fens and coastal wetlands: more resources, more growth) or decomposition-limiting (bogs: waterlogged, acidic, nutrient-poor conditions slow decay). Salt marsh sediment can accrete up to 25 mm/yr, mangroves 21 mm/yr and seagrass 10 mm/yr (p. 12).


### 4.3 Losses: from sink to source

Wetlands decline at 0.4–3.3% a year (boreal peatlands stable). Salt marshes have lost 42%, mangroves 35% and seagrass 29% of their area; temperate and tropical peatlands are 57% and 41% degraded. Average loss of about 1% a year releases 0.5 Pg C a year, 5% of human emissions. Drained peat loses soil carbon for a century; coastal soils erode and oxidise quickly (pp. 12–13, Table 1).


### 4.4 Restoration

Restoration often fails (< 50% success) and costs US$750–1,000,000 per ha, because feedbacks only work above a minimum patch size and density. Clumped planting doubled yields; biodegradable structures can mimic large patches; landscape-scale rewetting and paludiculture restore peatlands; water tables can be set to balance CO₂ and CH₄ (pp. 14–15).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Biogeomorphic wetlands are the world's biotic carbon hotspots. 2. Stopping their loss through conservation is of utmost importance. 3. Restoration that recovers landscape-forming feedbacks can turn them from sources back into sinks, supporting the Paris Agreement and the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (p. 15).


## 6. Limitations

- Global literature compilation; loss and emission estimates rest on assumed emission factors (Fig. 3).
- Covers peatlands and coastal wetlands only; inland river floodplains and ponds are not assessed.
- The net climate effect of permafrost thaw is unknown, and rewetting can release CH₄ (pp. 13, 15).

# Low-carbon ammonia production is essential for resilient and sustainable agriculture


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Low-carbon ammonia production is essential for resilient and sustainable agriculture Stefano Mingolla, Lorenzo Rosa

**Authors:**
Stefano Mingolla, Lorenzo Rosa (Carnegie Institution for Science, Stanford, CA, USA)

**Journal:**
Nature Food, vol. 6, pp. 610–621 (June 2025)

**Dates:**
Received 21 May 2024 · Accepted 21 January 2025 · Online 17 February 2025

**Paper type:**
Analysis

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-025-01125-y

**Cite as:**
Mingolla, S., & Rosa, L. (2025). Low-carbon ammonia production is essential for resilient and sustainable agriculture. Nature Food, 6, 610–621. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-025-01125-y The all_orig PDF is truncated; checked against the full publisher copy (Nature Food 6:610–621).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Synthetic nitrogen fertiliser feeds about half the world but is made from fossil fuels. Ammonia production emitted 450–500 Mt CO₂e in 2020 and, with field N₂O and transport, the fertiliser chain emits 1.1–1.3 Gt CO₂e a year. Supply is concentrated (China 28%, USA 9%, India 8% of capacity), and 1.8 billion people depend on imported fertiliser or imported gas. Carbon capture can cut production emissions by about 70% but keeps gas dependence; electrolytic and biomass routes cut more but cost 2–3 times as much and need 100–300 times more land and water. Small decentralised plants could help the global south, with policy support.


## 1. Background

Nitrogen comes from manure (33%) and synthetic fertiliser (67%). From 2000 to 2021 the world population grew 25% and N-fertiliser use 30%, and demand is forecast to rise 2.8–3.7% a year. In 2020, 183 Mt NH₃ was produced, 70% for agriculture (p. 610). In 2021, 46% of nitrogen used worldwide (49 Mt N, US$39 billion) was traded (p. 611).


## 2. Aim of the study

To map the global N-fertiliser supply chain and its vulnerabilities, and to compare the trade-offs of low- carbon ammonia pathways, centralised and decentralised.


## 3. What the authors did

They built a dataset of demand, 407 ammonia plants in 61 countries and 2021 trade flows; calculated a supply-chain vulnerability index (1 minus domestic capacity over agricultural use, with and without gas imports) and the number of people fed by N fertiliser; and compared five pathways (BAU gas, gas + CCS, renewable electrolysis, biomass + CCS, decentralised electrolysis) on cost, GHG, water, land, electricity, fossil dependence and supply-chain complexity (pp. 611–615).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Emissions and energy

Ammonia production alone emitted 450–500 Mt CO₂e (1.3% of the global total) and used about 2% of final energy (8.6 EJ) in 2020; use-phase emissions (~660 Mt CO₂e) and transport (~30 Mt) bring the total to 1,100–1,300 Mt CO₂e a year. A cradle-to-grave view gives 7,400 Mt CO₂e, 41% of food-system emissions (pp. 610–611). Plants use 7.7–10.1 kWh per kg NH₃; 99% of the hydrogen is fossil-based (70% gas, 26% coal). Direct emissions average 2.6–2.9 t CO₂ per t NH₃ (3.2–4.5 t from coal) (pp. 611–612).


### 4.2 Supply, demand and vulnerability

China holds 28% of capacity, the USA 9% and India 8% (45% together). In 2021 China used 20% of N fertiliser,  India 18% and the USA 11%; India is a net importer. Of 3.9 billion people who rely on N fertiliser, 1.2 billion depend on imports, rising to  1.8 billion with imported gas. European ammonia capacity fell 32% in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine (p. 612).


### 4.3 Pathway trade-offs

Table A. Low-carbon ammonia pathways (pp. 615–616; Fig. 4) Pathway Cost (US$/t NH₃) GHG Land (m²/t) Water (m³/t) Gas + CCS 201–512 0.6–0.7 t CO₂e/t (~70% less) 4.6–27.6 4.2–13.4 Renewable electrolysis 337–1,218 65–81% less 72–3,223 – Biomass + CCS 215–1,086 can be negative 637–2,894 248–4,727 Decentralised electrolysis 532–1,894 low – –


### 4.4 Decentralised production

Small plants near farms can reduce transport costs, emissions, import reliance and price volatility, and need less capital; they may become competitive in remote, import-reliant regions by about 2030. But only 3% of N is applied directly as ammonia, so on-farm handling or conversion adds cost, and the effect on field nitrogen use is uncertain (pp. 616–617).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Decarbonising ammonia production is needed for both climate goals and food security. 2. CCS cuts emissions but keeps gas dependence; electrolytic and biochemical routes cut more but cost more and need more land and water. 3. Decentralised production could raise productivity in the global south but requires policy support. 4. Interdisciplinary research must weigh costs, N₂O, water, energy and land (p. 617).


## 6. Limitations

- Focus is on production; farm-level use and N₂O are not modelled (p. 611).
- Mainly production costs; transport distances and routes are not modelled (Methods, Caveats).
- Global estimates; no farm-level or Indian district values.
