**Authors:**
Zhen Yu, Philippe Ciais, Shilong Piao, Richard A. Houghton, Chaoqun Lu, Hanqin Tian, Evgenios Agathokleous, Giri Raj Kattel, Stephen Sitch, Daniel Goll, Xu Yue, Anthony Walker, Pierre Friedlingstein, Atul K. Jain, Shirong Liu, Guoyi Zhou (16 authors)

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 13, article 5374 (2022)

**Dates:**
Received 22 December 2021 · Accepted 25 August 2022

**Paper type:**
Research article (land-use reconstruction and process-model simulation)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32961-2

**Cite as:**
Yu, Z., Ciais, P., Piao, S., Houghton, R. A., Lu, C., Tian, H., Agathokleous, E., Kattel, G. R., Sitch, S., Goll, D., Yue, X., Walker, A., Friedlingstein, P., Jain, A. K., Liu, S., & Zhou, G. (2022). Forest expansion dominates China’s land carbon sink since 1980. Nature Communications, 13, 5374. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32961-2 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Global carbon budgets use FAO land-use data, but China's reported cropland jumped whenever its survey method changed. The authors rebuilt China's land-use history and ran the DLEM model for 1900–


## 2019. China's land ecosystems gained 8.9 ± 0.8 Pg C from 1980 to 2019, a sink missed by FAO-based

models, which instead show land-use losses. Land-use change, mainly forest expansion (58 Mha net since 1900), was the largest driver: about 44% of the sink in the abstract, 50.3% in the factorial results. Climate, nitrogen and CO₂ mattered less.


## 1. Background

Land-use and cover-change (LUCC) emissions are among the most uncertain terms in the global carbon budget and caused about 25% of the historical rise in CO₂. Models use the LUH2 data set, built from FAO country reports of agricultural area and not constrained by forest area (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To build an improved LUCC database for China, use it to simulate carbon stock changes from 1900 to 2019 (focusing on 1980–2019), compare with MsTMIP and TRENDY, and attribute the sink to land use, climate, forest management, nitrogen deposition and CO₂ (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

They showed that FAO data inherited spurious cropland jumps from switching between three Chinese sources  (Agricultural  Yearbook  before  1996,  Land  and  Resources  Statistical  Yearbook  1996–2007, National Land and Resources Bulletin after 2007) with different survey methods and under-reporting incentives. They rebuilt yearly provincial cropland and forest areas benchmarked to the latest surveys

and national forest inventories, mapped them on grids, and ran DLEM at 0.5° with factorial experiments (pp. 2–5).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Land-use data

Cropland grew 56 Mha since 1900 in the new data (LUH2-GCB: 60 Mha), but since 1980 it fell 14 Mha instead  of  rising  41  Mha.  Forest  area  rose  58  Mha  from  1900  to  2019,  while  other  databases underestimated forest expansion after 1980 by 38–102 Mha. FAO's 'land use' definition gave about 30 Mha too much forest in 1990 and 30 Mha too little expansion from 1990 to 2019 (pp. 2–3).


### 4.2 Carbon stocks

Total carbon fell 6.9 ± 0.6 Pg from 1900 to 1980 and rose 8.9 ± 0.8 Pg C from 1980 to 2019, mostly in biomass (p. 4). Forest expansion gave a sink of 0.21 Pg C/yr, while TRENDY shows almost none and MsTMIP a source. The total simulated sink, about −0.28 Pg C/yr, lies within the range of earlier studies (Table 1, p. 6). Table A. LUCC effect on China's carbon stock (p. 5) Source 1900–2010s 1980–2010s This study −5.1 ± 0.7 Pg C +4.3 ± 0.7 Pg C MsTMIP −13.8 ± 7.7 Pg C −7.5 ± 1.6 Pg C TRENDY −9.4 ± 3.3 Pg C −5.3 ± 2.3 Pg C DLEM with LUH2-GCB −11.4 ± 0.6 Pg C −6.5 ± 0.4 Pg C


### 4.3 Attribution

The abstract gives land-use change about 44% of the sink, climate 22.3%, nitrogen deposition 12.9% and CO₂ 8.1%. The factorial results give land-use change 50.3% (3.96 Pg C), climate 18.0% (1.41 Pg C), other factors 0.1–9.54%, and interactions 18.1% (pp. 4–5). Biomass carried 76.3% of the gain, natural forests


### 2.9 Pg C and planted forests 1.6 Pg C; soil gained only 0.7 Pg C (p. 6).

NOTE The abstract and results report different attribution shares; both make land-use change the largest driver.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Biased LUCC data made earlier studies strongly underestimate China's land carbon sink. 2. Land-use change, mainly forest expansion, dominated the sink since 1980; CO₂, N deposition and climate contributed much less. 3. Reforestation can be an important mitigation pathway with biodiversity co-benefits, and policy for carbon neutrality should improve land and forest management (p. 6).


## 6. Limitations

- One process model (DLEM), though checked against MsTMIP and TRENDY and re-run with LUH2 data.
- Historical land-use reconstruction depends on survey records with known biases.
- China only, at national and provincial scale; attribution shares differ between abstract and results.

#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Carbon models usually ignore biodiversity. The authors projected plant species loss in 818 ecoregions under two scenarios, converted it to biomass loss with experimental biodiversity-biomass relationships, and applied this to projected carbon maps. Long-term loss of plant diversity could release 7.44–103.14 Pg C under global sustainability and 10.87–145.95 Pg C under fossil-fuelled development (abstract), on top of direct land-use emissions. Losses concentrate in the Amazon, central Africa and Southeast Asia. Protecting and restoring plant diversity, not just forest area, helps climate mitigation.


## 1. Background

Hundreds of experiments show that more diverse plant communities hold more biomass and carbon, through fuller resource use and the presence of highly productive species. Yet Earth System Models use a few plant functional types and nature-based initiatives focus on forest extent, not diversity (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate the carbon storage lost because of plant biodiversity loss under climate and land-use change scenarios, building on Isbell et al. by accounting for species compositional turnover (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

BILBI, fitted with more than 52 million records of over 254,000 plant species at ~1 km², projected species persistence under SSP1/RCP2.6 (global sustainability) and SSP5/RCP8.5 (fossil-fuelled development). Species-area  relationships  gave  species  loss  per  ecoregion;  biodiversity-biomass  slopes  from  the O'Connor et al. meta-analysis gave proportional biomass loss; this was applied to CMIP5 IPSL-CM5A-MR carbon maps (p. 2).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Projected long-term losses (pp. 2–4) Measure Global sustainability Fossil-fuelled Mean plant species loss (z = 0.25) 16.0% 20.8% Mean biomass loss (b = 0.26) 4.4% 5.9% Vegetation carbon loss, full range 7.40–102.68 Pg C 10.83–145.32 Pg C Central estimate


### 29.55 Pg C


### 42.89 Pg C

Share of land-use emissions to 2100 12–169% 20–271% Losses were highest in the tropics (Amazon, central Africa, Southeast Asia) and moderately high in boreal forests. Southern Australia lost many species but little carbon. Ecoregions losing 10–20% of species lost more carbon in total than those losing more than 20%, because they are larger (pp. 3–5). If soil carbon responded on a similar scale, losses could reach 18.71–259.72 and 26.25–353.47 Pg C. The high-end estimates are large compared with IPCC remaining budgets of 140 Pg C (1.5 °C) and 310 Pg C (2 °C) (pp. 5–6). NOTE The abstract ranges (7.44–103.14 and 10.87–145.95 Pg C) differ slightly from the results-section vegetation-carbon ranges; the paper does not explain the difference.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Biodiversity loss can be a strong driver of carbon emissions, creating a self-reinforcing feedback with climate change. 2. Even a Paris-compliant scenario carries large losses, so extra mitigation may be needed and carbon budgets may be overestimated. 3. Restoration should target plant diversity, with the right native species, not just forest extent; non- native monocultures can harm both biodiversity and carbon (pp. 5–7).


## 6. Limitations

- Biodiversity-biomass slopes come from small-scale, short experiments.
- BILBI allows no adaptation or species gains, so losses are pessimistic.
- Losses are long-term equilibria with no exact date.
- Single climate model (IPSL-CM5A-MR), which overestimates circumpolar carbon; only plant diversity considered.

# The carbon costs of global wood harvests


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

The carbon costs of global wood harvests Liqing Peng, Timothy D. Searchinger, Jessica Zionts and Richard Waite

**Authors:**
Liqing Peng, Timothy D. Searchinger, Jessica Zionts, Richard Waite

**Journal:**
Nature, vol. 620, pp. 110–115 (3 August 2023)

**Dates:**
Received 15 September 2022 · Accepted 10 May 2023 · Published online 5 July 2023

**Paper type:**
Research article (global modelling)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06187-1

**Cite as:**
Peng, L., Searchinger, T. D., Zionts, J., & Waite, R. (2023). The carbon costs of global wood harvests. Nature, 620, 110–115. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06187-1 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Many accounting methods make wood harvests look carbon neutral by offsetting them with forest growth that would happen anyway. The authors built a carbon harvest model (CHARM) that tracks carbon after each harvest against unharvested forest and discounts the flows at 4% for 40 years. Wood harvests from 2010 to 2050 cost 3.5–4.2 Gt CO₂e per year, close to emissions from agricultural expansion. Harvests rise 54% by 2050. The result is robust to the discount rate, and cutting harvests is an underappreciated climate option.


## 1. Background

After agriculture, wood harvest has most reduced carbon in vegetation and soils. Life-cycle studies treat 'sustainable' wood as carbon neutral, national reports net all changes in managed forests (3 billion ha, three-quarters of the world's forests), and land-use papers report harvests net of regrowth. Gross- emission estimates ignore regrowth (pp. 110–111).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate the present and future carbon costs of global wood harvests from 2010 to 2050 under different supply scenarios, using time discounting (p. 110).


## 3. What the authors did

A country fixed-effects model projected demand for four product classes from population, GDP and time. Demand was traced back to roundwood harvest (3,586 million m³ in 2010, 52% wood fuel). CHARM compared carbon in all pools after harvest with an unharvested forest and discounted emissions and removals at 4% for 40 years. Seven supply scenarios were tested (Table 1), and discount rates of 0–6% over 40 or 100 years (pp. 111–113).


## 4. Main findings

Harvests rise 54%, from 3.7 to 5.7 billion m³ (long-lived products +69%, paper +128%, wood fuel +22%, industrial waste fuel +91%). Annual carbon costs are  3.5–4.2 Gt CO₂e across scenarios; 2010 harvest levels alone cost 3.2 Gt CO₂e/yr, and existing demand gives 78% of costs. Industrial wood and wood fuel each give about half (p. 112). Table A. Carbon cost by scenario (Fig. 3, p. 114) Scenario Total (Gt CO₂e/yr) Substitution benefit 1 Secondary forest harvest and regrowth 4.1 −0.9 2 Conversion to plantations 3.7 −0.9 3 Mixed harvest (half mature) 4.2 −0.9 4 New tropical plantations 3.6 −0.8 5 25% higher plantation productivity 3.5 −0.9 6 Higher harvest efficiency 3.9 −0.9 7 Wood fuel cut 50% by 2050 3.6 −0.8 Harvests need 756–855 Mha in clear-cut equivalents; a 50% cut in wood fuel saves 70 Mha. Sensitivity runs give about 3–5 Gt CO₂e/yr. A 100-year horizon lowers costs only 3%, and 2–6% discounting changes them −12% to +1%. Only 0% discounting over 100 years cuts costs by 40% (pp. 112–113). NOTE The paper gives 3.5–4.2 Gt CO₂e/yr in the text but 3.6–4.2 in the Fig. 3 caption, and 756–855 Mha in the text but 761–855 Mha in Extended Data Fig. 2.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Ongoing and rising wood harvests have major carbon costs that common accounting hides. 2. Forest growth that would occur anyway should not be credited to new harvests. 3. Reducing harvests is a rarely identified mitigation 'wedge' that can buy time, if it does not shift emissions elsewhere (p. 114).


## 6. Limitations

- Soil carbon losses and indirect effects (such as road building) are omitted, so results are probably conservative.
- Wood fuel demand projections are the most uncertain.
- No economic counterfactual of how markets would respond; global, not local.

#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

**Authors:**
Stephen Sitch, Michael O’Sullivan, Eddy Robertson, Pierre Friedlingstein, Clément Albergel, Peter Anthoni, Almut Arneth, Vivek K. Arora, Ana Bastos, Vladislav Bastrikov, Nicolas Bellouin, Josep G. Canadell, Louise Chini, Philippe Ciais, Stefanie Falk, Ian Harris, George Hurtt, Akihiko Ito, Atul K. Jain, Matthew W. Jones, Fortunat Joos, Etsushi Kato, Daniel Kennedy, Kees Klein Goldewijk, Erik Kluzek, Jürgen Knauer, Peter J. Lawrence, Danica Lombardozzi, Joe R. Melton, Julia E. M. S. Nabel, Naiqing Pan, Philippe Peylin, Julia Pongratz, Benjamin Poulter, Thais M. Rosan, Qing Sun, Hanqin Tian, Anthony P. Walker, Ulrich Weber, Wenping Yuan, Xu Yue, Sönke Zaehle (42 authors)

**Journal:**
Global Biogeochemical Cycles, vol. 38, issue 7, e2024GB008102 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 10 January 2024 · Accepted 10 June 2024

**Paper type:**
Research article (model ensemble overview)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GB008102

**Cite as:**
Sitch, S., O’Sullivan, M., Robertson, E., Friedlingstein, P., Albergel, C., Anthoni, P., Arneth, A., Arora, V. K., Bastos, A., Bastrikov, V., Bellouin, N., Canadell, J. G., Chini, L., Ciais, P., Falk, S., Harris, I., Hurtt, G., Ito, A., Jain, A. K., . . . Zaehle, S. (2024). Trends and drivers of terrestrial sources and sinks of carbon dioxide: An overview of the TRENDY project. Global Biogeochemical Cycles, 38(7), e2024GB008102. https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GB008102 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

TRENDY is an annual ensemble of Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (17 in TRENDY-v11) run with a common protocol to supply land fluxes to the Global Carbon Budget. Factorial runs split land carbon change into effects of CO₂, climate and land use. Over 2012–2021, rising CO₂ gave a sink of 3.8 ± 0.8 Pg C/yr and climate reduced it by 0.58. Land-use change emitted 1.6 ± 0.5 Pg C/yr, leaving a net land sink of 1.7 ± 0.6 Pg C/yr. Forests and semi-arid lands contribute about equally to the natural sink. The largest net uptake is outside the tropics.


## 1. Background

Land ecosystems absorb almost one third of human CO₂ emissions, and land-use change adds emissions. Regular regional and global estimates are needed for Paris Agreement stocktakes. TRENDY has run annually since 2013 and supports the Global Carbon Budget and RECCAP-2 (pp. 2–3).


## 2. Aim of the study

To document the TRENDY-v11 protocol and forcing data, benchmark the models against observations, and present land carbon sources and sinks for 2012–2021 (p. 3).


## 3. What the authors did

Seventeen DGVMs ran at about 0.5° from 1700 to 2021 with CRUJRA climate and LUH2-GCB land use. Four factorial simulations (S0 control, S1 CO₂, S2 CO₂ + climate, S3 all forcings) attribute changes to drivers. Models enter the budget only if they reach steady state, show a net land sink in the 1990s and 2000s, and a land-use source in the 1990s. Performance was benchmarked in ILAMB (pp. 9–12).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Benchmarking

The ensemble matches spatial biomass patterns reasonably but overestimates tropical and boreal biomass and underestimates mid-latitude biomass. It performs well for soil carbon (overestimating high latitudes), GPP, runoff and evapotranspiration (pp. 12–13).


### 4.2 Global and regional fluxes

Table A. Decadal net land flux and attribution, Pg C/yr (Table 3, p. 19) Region CO₂ Climate Land use Net North America 0.55 0.08 −0.16 0.47 Russia 0.35 0.12 −0.06 0.41 Africa 0.74 −0.06 −0.41 0.28 East Asia 0.29 0.02 −0.11 0.20 South America 1.00 −0.50 −0.37 0.13 Europe 0.16 −0.05 0.01 0.13 South Asia 0.13 0.01 −0.09 0.06 Southeast Asia 0.43 −0.08 −0.36 −0.02 Global, 2012–2021 3.83 −0.58 −1.55 1.70 Global, 2000–2009 3.33 −0.47 −1.54 1.33 Russia and North America have the largest net sinks. Tropical regions have the largest gross effects, which cancel to a moderate net. Climate is the most important driver of regional trends this century (p. 17).


### 4.3 Ecosystems

Forests and semi-arid ecosystems contribute about equally to the mean and trend of the natural sink; semi-arid ecosystems dominate interannual variability, which follows ENSO. The tropical forest share of the trend declined from 1982–2001 to 2002–2021 (pp. 1, 15). NOTE DGVM land-use emissions include the 'loss of additional sink capacity', about 40% of present-day DGVM land-use emissions, so they are not directly comparable with bookkeeping or national inventory numbers (p. 10).


## 5. Conclusions

1. TRENDY gives regularly updated, process-based estimates of land sources and sinks for the Global Carbon Budget and regional assessments. 2. The net land sink results from large opposing effects of CO₂ fertilisation and land-use change. 3. Future work: weight models by benchmark skill, use multiple climate and national land-use data sets, and add near-real-time assessments (pp. 17–19).


## 6. Limitations

- One climate data set and one land-use reconstruction drive all models.
- The CO₂ fertilisation effect is highly uncertain across models; few models represent demography, drought mortality or land management.
- Coarse (0.5°) resolution; known problems with China's land-use data.

# The Unseen Effects of Deforestation: Biophysical Effects on Climate


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

The Unseen Effects of Deforestation: Biophysical Effects on Climate Deborah Lawrence, Michael Coe, Wayne Walker, Louis Verchot and Karen Vandecar

**Authors:**
Deborah Lawrence, Michael Coe, Wayne Walker, Louis Verchot, Karen Vandecar

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Forests and Global Change, vol. 5, article 756115 (2022)

**Dates:**
Received 10 August 2021 · Accepted 2 March 2022 · Published 24 March 2022

**Paper type:**
Original research (review, synthesis and new CO₂ analysis)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/ffgc.2022.756115

**Cite as:**
Lawrence, D., Coe, M., Walker, W., Verchot, L., & Vandecar, K. (2022). The unseen effects of deforestation: Biophysical effects on climate. Frontiers in Forests and Global Change, 5, 756115. https://doi.org/10.3389/ffgc.2022.756115 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Forest policy values only carbon, but forests also change climate through albedo, evapotranspiration and canopy roughness. The authors combined modelled biophysical effects of deforestation with a new latitude-by-latitude estimate of the CO₂ in aboveground biomass. Tropical deforestation causes strong net global warming from both routes. Up to 50°N, deforestation still warms the planet overall; beyond 50°N, brighter snowy land makes it cool. Locally, at all latitudes, biophysical effects far outweigh CO₂: forests cut heat extremes. Carbon-only metrics undervalue forests.


## 1. Background

Forests hold over 360 Pg C in vegetation and over 800 Pg C with soils, and land ecosystems remove 29% of annual CO₂ emissions. Forests also affect climate directly through albedo, evapotranspiration and roughness, which moderate local temperature (p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To review biophysical mechanisms, synthesise their forcing across latitudes, and combine them with a new analysis of the CO₂ effect of forest biomass to assess the net local and global effect of deforestation (p. 1).


## 3. What the authors did

Local effects were synthesised from satellite, flux-tower and in situ studies. Global biophysical effects per 10° band came from the Davin and de Noblet-Ducoudré (2010) total-deforestation experiment (land only), with BVOC effects scaled from Scott et al. (2018). The CO₂ effect used a 2016 global 500 m aboveground carbon map, 2.12 Gt C per ppm, 23% ocean uptake, and a sensitivity of 0.107 °C per 10 ppm (pp. 4–6).


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Local temperature

Tropical forests are cooler than nearby cleared land by 0.2–2.4 °C (mean 0.96 °C); temperate effects are 0.02–1.0 °C (mean 0.4 °C); boreal clearing usually cools by under 1 °C a year. Warming from clearing is larger by day and in the hot season. Past deforestation explains about one third of the increase in hottest-day intensity (pp. 6–7).


### 4.2 Global temperature by latitude

Table A. Biophysical versus CO₂ effect of deforesting each band (p. 6) Band Biophysical effect Relative to CO₂ warming 10°S–10°N Warming About 35% as large, adds to it 10–20°S and 10–20°N Warming About 60% as large, adds to it 20–30°N Near zero Albedo balances roughness, ET and BVOC 30–40°N Cooling Offsets about 40% 40–50°N Cooling Offsets about 85% Above 50°N Cooling 3–6 times larger: net cooling Net deforestation causes warming at all latitudes up to 50°N, an area holding about 65% of global forests (p. 6). NOTE Near the Varuna basin's latitude (20–30°N) the paper finds annual biophysical effects close to zero, both locally and globally. Trees there still cool the planet through carbon, and cool hot seasons and daytime locally (pp. 6–7).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Carbon-centric metrics do not capture the value of forests for mitigation and adaptation. 2. In the tropics, biophysical effects amplify carbon benefits; reforestation there cuts warming about three times more per area than in boreal zones. 3. Forests provide local climate stability at all latitudes, so policy should treat mitigation and adaptation together (pp. 8, 10).


## 6. Limitations

- Global biophysical estimates come from one model of complete, idealised deforestation.
- Aboveground carbon only; synthesis of studies with different methods.
- Future warming, drier conditions, less snow and disturbance will change these effects.

L. Duncanson, M. Liang, V. Leitold, J. Armston, S. M. Krishna Moorthy, R. Dubayah, S. Costedoat, B. J. Enquist, L. Fatoyinbo, S. J. Goetz, M. Gonzalez-Roglich, C. Merow, P. R. Roehrdanz, K. Tabor, A. Zvoleff (15 authors)

**Journal:**
Nature Communications, vol. 14, article 2908 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 6 December 2022 · Accepted 14 April 2023

**Paper type:**
Research article (satellite lidar analysis)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38073-9

**Cite as:**
Duncanson, L., Liang, M., Leitold, V., Armston, J., Krishna Moorthy, S. M., Dubayah, R., Costedoat, S., Enquist, B. J., Fatoyinbo, L., Goetz, S. J., Gonzalez-Roglich, M., Merow, C., Roehrdanz, P. R., Tabor, K., & Zvoleff, A. (2023). The effectiveness of global protected areas for climate change mitigation. Nature Communications, 14, 2908. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38073-9 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Protected areas were rarely set up for climate, and their carbon impact had not been measured globally. Using about 412 million lidar samples from NASA's GEDI mission, the authors estimate that protected areas hold 61.4 Gt of aboveground carbon, 26% of mapped woody carbon on about 11% of forest area. Compared with matched unprotected land, protection preserved an extra 9.65 Gt C, roughly one year of fossil emissions, mainly through avoided deforestation. Brazil's Amazon gives 36.6% of the signal.


## 1. Background

Global terrestrial aboveground carbon was about 308 Gt in 2010, with uptake of about 8 Gt CO₂ a year. Protected forests are thought to give about 27% of the net global sink, but past satellite biomass maps saturate in dense forests, so the carbon effect of protection was uncertain (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate aboveground carbon in protected areas and the additional carbon attributable to protected status (carbon effectiveness) within the GEDI domain (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

GEDI lidar (25 m footprints, 52°N–52°S) was aggregated to 1 km carbon density. Each protected pixel was matched to unprotected pixels similar in 2000 in climate, human pressure, land type and country; 2020 differences represent about 20 years of protection. Landsat forest loss and a year-2000 carbon map were used to test whether the gap came from avoided loss, faster growth, or siting (pp. 2, 7).


## 4. Main findings

Protected areas store 61.4 ± 0.31 Gt C, 26% of the 235 Gt mapped, on about 11% of the 16.2 Mkm² forested area. They hold on average 28% more carbon than matches, a total of 9.65 ± 0.9 Gt; 62.7% of forested PAs had significantly more carbon (p. 2). Table A. Additional carbon by continent (Table 1, p. 5) Continent Extra C (Gt) Total C in PAs (Gt) PA area (Mkm²) South America 4.94 ± 0.47 29.12 4.49 Asia 1.38 ± 0.59 9.08 2.05 Africa 1.20 ± 0.17 9.58 4.33 North America 0.86 ± 0.33 5.99 2.32 Oceania 0.65 ± 0.32 2.26 1.65 Europe 0.61 ± 0.13 5.37 1.32 Globe 9.64 ± 0.9 61.41 16.15 The gap is mainly avoided deforestation; in about 18% of PAs, higher carbon without detected loss suggests avoided degradation or faster regrowth. PAs created after 2000 began with similar carbon to their matches, so siting does not explain the result. Brazil contributes 3.54 Gt (36.6%). African PAs are smaller (median 85 km² vs 127 km² in South America) and under rising pressure, and are most effective in savannas and shrublands. Mangrove PAs show almost no effect (pp. 2–5). NOTE Table 1 gives 9.64 ± 0.9 Gt and 61.41 Gt, while the abstract gives 9.65 ± 0.88 and 61.43 ± 0.31 Gt: rounding differences.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Protected areas effectively prevent carbon emissions from deforestation and degradation and are an essential natural climate solution. 2. Maintaining and expanding PAs in high-carbon, high-loss forests is essential for carbon goals. 3. PAs also keep taller, denser canopies, giving biodiversity co-benefits; CBD targets support UNFCCC goals (pp. 5–7).


## 6. Limitations

- No data north of ~52°N; North America and Europe underestimated.
- Aboveground woody carbon only; no belowground carbon or future sequestration.
- No leakage analysis and no comparison of PA types or governance.

# Emerging climate impact on carbon sinks in a consolidated carbon budget


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Emerging climate impact on carbon sinks in a consolidated carbon budget Pierre Friedlingstein, Corinne Le Quéré, Michael O’Sullivan, Judith Hauck and 20 co-authors

**Authors:**
Pierre Friedlingstein, Corinne Le Quéré, Michael O’Sullivan, Judith Hauck, Peter Landschützer, Ingrid T. Luijkx, Hongmei Li, Auke van der Woude, Clemens Schwingshackl, Julia Pongratz, Pierre Regnier, Robbie M. Andrew, Dorothee C. E. Bakker, Josep G. Canadell, Philippe Ciais, Thomas Gasser, Matthew W. Jones, Xin Lan, Eric Morgan, Are Olsen, Glen P. Peters, Wouter Peters, Stephen Sitch, Hanqin Tian (24 authors)

**Journal:**
Nature, vol. 649, pp. 98–103 (issue 1 January 2026)

**Dates:**
Received 23 July 2025 · Accepted 23 October 2025 · Published online 12 November 2025

**Paper type:**
Research article

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09802-5

**Cite as:**
Friedlingstein, P., Le Quéré, C., O’Sullivan, M., Hauck, J., Landschützer, P., Luijkx, I. T., Li, H., van der Woude, A., Schwingshackl, C., Pongratz, J., Regnier, P., Andrew, R. M., Bakker, D. C. E., Canadell, J. G., Ciais, P., Gasser, T., Jones, M. W., Lan, X., Morgan, E., . . . Tian, H. (2026). Emerging climate impact on carbon sinks in a consolidated carbon budget. Nature, 649, 98–103. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09802-5 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The Global Carbon Budget has never balanced, and its imbalance had a significant trend. The authors correct four known biases: land-use emissions now include CO₂-driven carbon-density changes, the land sink accounts for real land cover and river export, and the ocean sink accounts for skin temperature and model bias. The land sink falls to 2.7 GtC/yr, the ocean sink rises to 3.1 GtC/yr, and the imbalance drops to −0.1. Climate change has cut the land sink by 23% and added 8.3 ppm to atmospheric CO₂ since 1960.


## 1. Background

Fossil CO₂ emissions keep rising: CO₂ reached 423 ppm in 2024 and human-induced warming 1.36 °C. The 2024 Global Carbon Budget had an imbalance of −0.4 GtC/yr over the last decade and a significant trend of −0.14 GtC/yr per decade, which prevented robust interpretation of sink trends (pp. 3–4).


## 2. Aim of the study

To integrate recent advances in observations and process understanding to resolve long-standing issues in the budget, and then quantify how climate change is affecting the sinks (pp. 3–5).


## 3. What the authors did

Static carbon densities in bookkeeping models were replaced with transient densities from DGVMs; the land sink was corrected for replaced sinks and sources (real land cover) and for the anthropogenic increase in lateral carbon export; the ocean sink was corrected for the cool skin and warm layer in fCO₂ products and a ~10% low bias in ocean models. Extra model runs under constant climate isolated the climate effect (pp. 5–9, Methods).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Consolidated budget, 2014–2023 (pp. 6–9) Component Value (GtC/yr) Change Fossil emissions 9.7 ± 0.5 No correction needed Land-use emissions 1.2 ± 0.7 +0.11 (transient densities) Land sink 2.7 ± 0.9 −0.5 (RSS), −0.07 (lateral export) Ocean sink 3.1 ± 0.5 +0.2 (+8%) Net land flux 1.4 Down 31% from 2.1 Budget imbalance −0.1 ± 1.3 From −0.4 The ocean sink is now about 15% larger than the land sink (it was 10% lower). The revised budget agrees with atmospheric inversions and O₂-based estimates. Climate change reduced the land sink by 0.8 ± 0.9 GtC/yr (−23%) and the ocean sink by 0.18 GtC/yr (−6%); the cumulative loss of 30 ± 6 GtC since 1960 added 8.3 ± 1.4 ppm (8%) to atmospheric CO₂ (pp. 8–9). On land, CO₂ fertilisation gives a 3.6 GtC/yr sink, while climate (0.9) and land use (1.2) are sources, leaving 1.4 GtC/yr. Deforestation drives losses in Africa and Southeast Asia; climate dominates in South America. North America, Europe and China are net sinks from land-use change (pp. 8–10). NOTE The paper gives the revised net land flux as 1.4 ± 1.1 and 1.4 ± 1.2 GtC/yr in different places, and the GCB2024 imbalance as ± 1.4 and ± 1.3.


## 5. Conclusions

1. The consolidated budget has virtually no imbalance and no significant imbalance trend (−0.06 GtC/decade, p = 0.14). 2. Climate change is already reducing the efficiency of the sinks, especially on land. 3. Halting deforestation and limiting warming are needed to stop more of the land biosphere becoming a CO₂ source (pp. 9–10).


## 6. Limitations

- Large interannual variability remains in the imbalance; agreement may reflect compensating errors.
- Degradation, long-term fire effects, ocean small-scale processes and Southern Ocean coverage need work.
- Corrections are within the old uncertainty ranges; global and regional scale only.

# Crop residue burning practices across north India inferred from household survey data: Bridging gaps in satellite observations


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Crop residue burning practices across north India inferred from household survey data: Bridging gaps in satellite observations Tianjia Liu, Loretta J. Mickley, Sukhwinder Singh, Meha Jain, Ruth S. DeFries and Miriam E. Marlier

**Authors:**
Tianjia Liu, Loretta J. Mickley, Sukhwinder Singh, Meha Jain, Ruth S. DeFries, Miriam E. Marlier

**Journal:**
Atmospheric Environment: X, vol. 8, article 100091 (2020) Version used EarthArXiv postprint (peer-reviewed); pages refer to the postprint

**Paper type:**
Research article (satellite + household survey study)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aeaoa.2020.100091

**Cite as:**
Liu, T., Mickley, L. J., Singh, S., Jain, M., DeFries, R. S., & Marlier, M. E. (2020). Crop residue burning practices across north India inferred from household survey data: Bridging gaps in satellite observations. Atmospheric Environment: X, 8, 100091. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aeaoa.2020.100091 Postprint (EarthArXiv); page numbers refer to the postprint.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

MODIS misses many small, short crop fires in north India, and global inventories differ ten-fold there. The authors surveyed over 2,000 farmers in Punjab, Haryana, UP and Bihar and used the answers to correct satellite fire power for small fires, haze, partial burning and the daily fire cycle. Post-monsoon burning averaged 10.4 Tg dry matter and 14.9 Tg CO₂ a year (2003–2018), 3.4 times global inventories for OC+BC. Punjab dominates, but UP and Bihar still harvest mostly by hand, so burning could rise 67–207% as combines spread.


## 1. Background

Post-monsoon (October–November) crop burning worsens air quality across north India. MODIS has 500 m–1 km pixels and two overpasses a day per satellite, so it misses small, short fires and fires under haze; inventories based on it differ by up to an order of magnitude (p. 1). Burning spread with combine harvesters from the mid-to-late 1980s (p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To use household survey data to bridge gaps in satellite observations and improve post-monsoon fire emission estimates for Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar over 2003–2018, producing a gridded inventory (SAGE-IGP) (pp. 1–2).


## 3. What the authors did

In 2017, over 2,000 farmers were asked about the 2016–17 rice harvest and residue burning; 20 households per village were chosen by stratified purposive sampling to represent landholding sizes and

social classes. In 2018, the survey was repeated with 90% of the same participants for 2017–18, adding questions on burning start year, method, time, wait and reasons (p. 3). MODIS FRP was adjusted for VIIRS small fires, cloud/haze gaps, partial burning and the diurnal cycle, converted to dry matter (0.41 kg/MJ) and emissions, and validated bottom-up for Punjab (pp. 7–8, 12). BOTTOM-UP FORMULA (EQ. 4, P. 7) Emissions = fraction burned × crop production × residue-to-crop ratio (1.4–1.8) × dry-matter fraction (0.82–0.88) × combustion completeness (0.89 whole-field, 0.67 partial) × emission factor.


## 4. Main findings

The corrections raise FRP by 109% (VIIRS), 142% (haze gap-fill), 33% (partial burning) and 361% (diurnal cycle). Average seasonal burning is 10.4 ± 3 Tg dry matter, giving 65 ± 18 Gg OC, 5.6 ± 1.6 Gg BC, 791 ± 225 Gg CO and 14.9 ± 4.2 Tg CO₂. Punjab gives 70% of dry matter and 67% of aerosols. Dry matter burned rose 112% over 2003–2018, while raw MODIS showed an insignificant 16% (p. 12). Table A. Survey results by state, 2016–17 (pp. 10–11, Figs. 1 and 4) State Fully mechanised Partial burning Peak burning Punjab 93% 30% Midday and evening Haryana 62% 43% Midday and evening Uttar Pradesh 21% (71% manual) 50% Evening (2–6 pm) Bihar 26% (61% manual) 57% Evening (2–6 pm) In 2017, 53% of Punjab farmers burned rice residue against 9–30% in the other states. If all households harvested by combine, burned area would rise 2–27% in Punjab and Haryana but 67–207% in UP and Bihar. 56–92% burn because of the short gap before sowing; nearly 90% believe burning affects air quality in nearby cities (p. 11). Modelled Delhi PM2.5 correlates better with SAGE-IGP (r = 0.6) than with global inventories (0.39–0.45) (p. 13).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Household surveys and crop statistics can constrain fire timing and fuel consumption, the main sources of disagreement among inventories. 2. SAGE-IGP gives daily 0.25° emissions for 2003–2018 for air-quality and health studies. 3. Burning is likely to expand among smallholders in the eastern plain, where satellites see fires poorly (pp. 16–17).


## 6. Limitations

- Survey samples for Haryana, UP and Bihar are only 10–29% of Punjab's.
- Burn rates may be under-reported because of fire bans; daily cycle and partial-burn share assumed uniform per state and over time.
- Post-monsoon rice residue only; state budgets disaggregated to a grid with statistical noise.

# Unlocking the unsustainable rice-wheat system of Indian Punjab: Assessing alternatives to crop-residue burning from a systems perspective


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Unlocking the unsustainable rice-wheat system of Indian Punjab: Assessing alternatives to crop- residue burning from a systems perspective Andrea S. Downing, Manish Kumar, August Andersson, Amar Causevic and 5 co-authors

**Authors:**
Andrea S. Downing, Manish Kumar, August Andersson, Amar Causevic, Örjan Gustafsson, Niraj U. Joshi, Chandra Kiran B. Krishnamurthy, Bert Scholtens, Beatrice Crona (9 authors)

**Journal:**
Ecological Economics, vol. 195, article 107364 (2022)

**Dates:**
Received 24 June 2021 · Revised 24 January 2022 · Accepted 26 January 2022

**Paper type:**
Research article (emissions review, causal loop diagrams, value chain analysis)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2022.107364

**Cite as:**
Downing, A. S., Kumar, M., Andersson, A., Causevic, A., Gustafsson, Ö., Joshi, N. U., Krishnamurthy, C. K. B., Scholtens, B., & Crona, B. (2022). Unlocking the unsustainable rice-wheat system of Indian Punjab: Assessing alternatives to crop-residue burning from a systems perspective. Ecological Economics, 195, 107364. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2022.107364 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Crop residue burning in Punjab persists despite bans, machines and supposedly profitable alternatives. The authors review black carbon inventories (27–83 Gg/yr for India; 1.5–47.2 Gg/yr for Punjab), map the feedbacks driving burning in a causal loop diagram, and trace who invests in rice and wheat value chains. Price supports, procurement and a short gap between crops lock the system into burning. The Government of India has the greatest financial leverage and risk. Change needs crop diversification, circular business models and green finance, not more pressure on farmers.


## 1. Background

Black carbon from residue burning harms health and climate and can threaten farming. Punjab covers 1.5% of India's area but supplied about 27% of rice and 37% of wheat to the national stock in 2015–16; rice-wheat covers at least 80% of its gross cropped area. Minimum support prices and Food Corporation of India procurement, which reduced hunger, now sustain an unsustainable system (pp. 1–3).


## 2. Aim of the study

(a) Understand system feedbacks driving farm practices; (b) identify system-wide effects of alternatives to burning; (c) identify companies and financial actors investing in Punjab's agriculture (p. 1).


## 3. What the authors did

They compared BC estimates from five inventories, built a causal loop diagram of 37 elements and 76 interactions, mapped rice, basmati and wheat value chains, and used Prowess and Orbis to identify 166 listed companies and 1,776 shareholders (pp. 4–5, 7).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. BC from crop residue burning by inventory (Table 1, p. 5) Inventory Resolution India (Gg/yr) Punjab (Gg/yr) ECLIPSE (2015) 0.5° 46 1.5 EDGAR (2015) 0.1° 44 2.3 PKU-Fuel (2014) 0.1° 27 3.2 IIT-Bombay (2015) 0.25° 83 47.2 Paliwal et al. (2011) 40 km 64 7.6 Nearly 30% of burning occurs in April–May and 68% in October–November; rice residue contributes most BC (p. 4). Reinforcing loops (agricultural policy; pressure to burn from groundwater rules and short rotation) and only degradation-type stabilising loops show a lock-in (p. 5). Basmati, grown mainly in districts bordering Pakistan, is rarely burned, while non-basmati covers 80% of the rice area (pp. 7, 9). The Government of India holds shares in 15 of the 25 companies owned by the top shareholders and is the single largest investor; Blackrock and Vanguard have blockholding power. Corporate actors have little risk exposure and so little incentive, but enough stake to influence change (pp. 7, 10).


## 5. Conclusions

1. The problem is not farmers but the rules, constraints and needs they respond to; solutions must enable them. 2. Do less harm (address root causes, not quick fixes) and do good (diversification, circular business models, green finance). 3. Banks and the stock exchange can set sustainability conditions and disclosure rules (pp. 10–11).


## 6. Limitations

- Punjab only; more mechanised with larger farms than eastern UP.
- BC inventories vary widely; causal loop diagrams are qualitative and omit adaptation.
- Investor analysis covers listed companies only; millers are mostly private.

title: Evaluating the potential and eligibility of conservation agriculture practices for carbon credits
authors: Adeeth A. G. Cariappa, Noufa C. Konath, Tek B. Sapkota, Vijesh V. Krishna
description: The authors test whether conservation agriculture (CA) in the wheat season can earn carbon credits in Punjab and Bihar under Verra's VM0042. # Evaluating the potential and eligibility of conservation agriculture practices for carbon credits


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Evaluating the potential and eligibility of conservation agriculture practices for carbon credits Adeeth A. G. Cariappa, Noufa C. Konath, Tek B. Sapkota and Vijesh V. Krishna

**Authors:**
Adeeth A. G. Cariappa, Noufa C. Konath, Tek B. Sapkota, Vijesh V. Krishna

**Journal:**
Scientific Reports, vol. 14, article 9193 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 16 November 2023 · Accepted 8 April 2024

**Paper type:**
Research article (farm surveys, remote sensing, carbon methodology test)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-59262-6

**Cite as:**
Cariappa, A. A. G., Konath, N. C., Sapkota, T. B., & Krishna, V. V. (2024). Evaluating the potential and eligibility of conservation agriculture practices for carbon credits. Scientific Reports, 14, 9193. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-59262-6 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The authors test whether conservation agriculture (CA) in the wheat season can earn carbon credits in Punjab and Bihar under Verra's VM0042. CA cuts 1.23–1.97 t CO₂e/ha, worth USD 18–30/ha to farmers at USD 25 a credit, with no significant yield penalty. Punjab's burning ban and the fact that most farmers already do not burn make 'no burning' ineligible there, dropping farmer income to USD 16/ha; credit prices need to rise ~60%. Zero tillage of wheat (both states) and less N overuse (Punjab) pass all tests.


## 1. Background

Agrifood systems cause nearly a third of global GHG emissions. Carbon credits (1 credit = 1 t CO₂e) can reward farmers, but Verra's VM0042 v2.0 (active since 30 May 2023) sets strict eligibility rules. Emissions from residue burning in India rose 75% from 2011 to 2020 (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To evaluate the potential and eligibility of wheat-season CA practices for carbon credits in Punjab and Bihar under VM0042 (p. 1).


## 3. What the authors did

CIMMYT  household  surveys  (Punjab:  1,021  households  in  52  villages;  Bihar:  1,003  households, interviewed 2021) gave 1,021 and 1,002 plots. Emissions were estimated with an R version of CCAFS- MOT, and adopters were compared with non-adopters by propensity score matching. Sentinel-2 mapped burned area (2022) and zero tillage (pp. 9–10).

- Additionality: not required by law, and baseline adoption below 20% of area.
- Yield penalty: no more than 5% yield loss.
- Quantitative adjustment: fertiliser cut above 5% (p. 1).

## 4. Main findings

Table A. Wheat-season emission cuts by practice, kg CO₂e/ha (Fig. 1, p. 3) Practice Bihar Punjab Zero tillage 265 (assumed) 265 Reduced tillage 219 61 Not burning crop residue 618 903 Not overusing N fertiliser 249 258 Not irrigating > 3 times 100 544 Total with zero tillage 1,233 1,971 At USD 25 a credit, credits are worth INR 2,423 (~USD 31)/ha in Bihar and INR 3,873 (~USD 49)/ha in Punjab; 60% reaches farmers (USD 18 and 30/ha). A typical farmer gains ~USD 11 (1.9% of season income) in Bihar and ~USD 145 (7.1%) in Punjab (Table 1, p. 4). CORRECTION TO THE OLD NOTES The 265 kg CO₂e/ha figure is the cut from zero tillage (measured in Punjab, assumed for Bihar), not from not burning residue. Not burning saves 618 (Bihar) and 903 (Punjab) kg CO₂e/ha (Fig. 1, p. 3). In Punjab ~30% of farmers use zero or reduced tillage, 73% do not burn and 81% irrigate at most three times, so these are common practice; 86% overuse N, so cutting N is eligible. Without 'no burning' Punjab credits fall to 1.1 t/ha and farmer income to USD 16/ha. Bihar: 34 of 38 districts have zero tillage below 20%. No CA practice showed a significant yield penalty (pp. 3–6, Table 2).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Zero tillage of wheat (Punjab and Bihar) and reduced N overuse (Punjab) meet all conditions. 2. Credit prices must rise at least 60% (USD 16 vs USD 26/ha needed) for lasting adoption. 3. Government could fund a price floor from fertiliser or electricity subsidies; projects need strong MRV and extension (pp. 8–9).


## 6. Limitations

- Wheat season and two states only; not UP.
- Emissions modelled with CCAFS-MOT, not measured.
- Adoption measured as share of farmers, not area (the paper shows these are close).
- Eligibility depends on current laws and adoption; project costs only roughly deducted (10%).

#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Assessing the carbon footprint of marginal and smallholders farming systems: A typology driven approach N. Arivukkumar, P. M. Shanmugam, Balaji Kannan, C. S. Sumathi, M. Prahadeeshwaran, S. P. Sangeetha and G. Raghavi

**Authors:**
N. Arivukkumar, P. M. Shanmugam, Balaji Kannan, C. S. Sumathi, M. Prahadeeshwaran, S. P. Sangeetha, G. Raghavi (7 authors)

**Journal:**
Plant Science Today, vol. 11 (sp4), pp. 01–07 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 25 September 2024 · Accepted 15 October 2024 · Online 28 December 2024

**Paper type:**
Research article (household survey, farm typology, Cool Farm Tool)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.14719/pst.5213

**Cite as:**
Arivukkumar, N., Shanmugam, P. M., Kannan, B., Sumathi, C. S., Prahadeeshwaran, M., Sangeetha, S. P., & Raghavi, G. (2024). Assessing the carbon footprint of marginal and smallholders farming systems: A typology driven approach. Plant Science Today, 11(sp4), 01–07. https://doi.org/10.14719/pst.5213 Open access under CC BY 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The authors surveyed 250 marginal and small farm households in western Tamil Nadu, grouped them into four farm types by PCA and cluster analysis, and used the Cool Farm Tool on one representative farm per type. Cash crop and plantation farms had the highest crop-side emissions (residue burning, fertiliser production and application), cereal farms the lowest, and the livestock farm the highest enteric (10,500 kg CO₂e/yr) and manure emissions. CFT also estimated soil carbon sequestration (6,071–15,905 kg CO₂e/yr). Mitigation must fit each farm type.


## 1. Background

Agriculture contributes 14–17% of GHG emissions. Direct measurement is too costly for countries dominated by marginal and small farms, which are very diverse; farm typologies with calculators such as CFT are a practical alternative (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To identify farm types and quantify the GHG balance of each among marginal and small households in western Tamil Nadu using the Cool Farm Tool (p. 2).


## 3. What the authors did

A 2022–23 questionnaire (baseline 2020–21) covered 250 households in Coimbatore, Tiruppur and Erode. PCA gave three components (56.7%, 22.3%, 12.5% of variation) and Ward clustering four types. One representative farm per type was surveyed in depth in February–April 2024 and run through CFT,

which uses IPCC Tier 1–2 equations and counts soil carbon sequestration as a sink. Trees, electricity, irrigation and post-harvest processing were not counted (pp. 2–3).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. GHG by operation, kg CO₂e/yr per representative farm (Table 2, p. 5) Operation Type 1 Type 2 Type 3 Type 4 Residue management 128.66 98.06 1,475.20 1,087.73 Fertiliser production 545.76 1,440.66 1,850.56 2,153.33 Soil application 414.26 1,094.36 1,565.36 1,689.93 Crop protection 5.13 8.90 16.83 21.56 Energy usage 388.42 570.54 927.83 1,084.64 Enteric fermentation 5,813.00 10,500.00 7,823.33 5,888.23 Manure management 477.30 1,221.83 949.40 618.03 Carbon sequestration (sink) 6,071.38 9,121.23 10,664.06 15,905.11 Types 3 and 4 emit most from residue management because they burn sugarcane and banana residues; types 1 and 2 feed cereal residues to livestock. Fertiliser emissions track area under fertiliser-hungry crops. Type 2's larger herd, especially improved cows, drives its enteric and manure emissions. Type 4's sink reflects rotation, residue incorporation, minimal disturbance and perennials (pp. 4–5). CORRECTION TO THE OLD NOTES The old limitations said the study has no sequestration accounting. In fact CFT estimated soil carbon sequestration for every farm type, from 6,071 (type 1) to 15,905 (type 4) kg CO₂e/yr (Table 2, p. 5).


## 5. Conclusions

1. GHG emissions differ significantly across the four farm types. 2. Plantation and cash crop farms have higher crop emissions; the livestock farm has higher livestock emissions. 3. Mitigation should be tailored to farm type, and CFT gives a whole-farm picture (p. 5).


## 6. Limitations

- One representative farm per type; totals per farm, not per hectare.
- Generic CFT factors; trees, electricity and irrigation excluded.
- Some text values differ from Tables 1–2 (type 4 n = 24 vs 26; type 1 fertiliser 414 vs 546).
- Western Tamil Nadu crops differ from the Varuna basin's rice-wheat.

# Nutritional strategies to mitigate methane emission from livestock in India– A review


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Nutritional strategies to mitigate methane emission from livestock in India– A review M. R. Kumar, K. Mounica, K. S. Rani, A. Teja and K. A. Rao

**Authors:**
M. R. Kumar, K. Mounica, K. S. Rani, A. Teja, K. A. Rao (Sri Venkateswara Veterinary University)

**Journal:**
Indian Journal of Animal Health, vol. 62(2), Special Issue, pp. 157–166 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 8 September 2023 · Accepted 5 November 2023 · Online 24 November 2023

**Paper type:**
Review article (narrative)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.36062/ijah.2023.spl.01423

**Cite as:**
Kumar, M. R., Mounica, K., Rani, K. S., Teja, A., & Rao, K. A. (2023). Nutritional strategies to mitigate methane emission from livestock in India– A review. Indian Journal of Animal Health, 62(2) Special Issue, 157–166. https://doi.org/10.36062/ijah.2023.spl.01423 Page numbers are the journal's printed pages (157–166).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This review gathers feeding strategies to cut enteric methane, the main livestock GHG in India (10.09 Mt CH₄, 73.3% of agricultural methane; INCCA 2010). Tender grasses, more concentrate and balanced rations reduce methane; ration balancing cut it by about 10–11% in Indian field trials and is the most practical large-scale option. Fats, oils, nitrate, probiotics and many herbal additives (Harit Dhara up to 17–20%) also work, but antibiotics and ionophores are not recommended, and herbal products need formulation and commercialisation.


## 1. Background

India has the world's largest cattle and buffalo population. Methane has 27–28 times the warming potential of CO₂. Buffaloes (50 kg CH₄/animal/yr) made up 42% of India's livestock methane in 2003, and methanogenesis wastes about 7% of gross energy intake (pp. 157–158).


## 2. Aim of the study

To review laboratory and field-tested nutritional strategies for mitigating livestock methane in India, to guide future research (p. 157).


## 3. What the authors did

A narrative review grouped by approach: nutrient supplementation, greens and legumes, fats and fatty acids, microbial interventions, plant bioactive compounds and essential oils. Table 1 lists 22 plants with anti-methane metabolites (pp. 159–161).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Reported methane reductions (pp. 159–163) Strategy Reported effect Source in review Balanced ration, crossbred cows −10.1% g/d; −13.5% g/kg milk Garg et al. (2013) Balanced ration, buffalo and cattle −10 to −11% Kannan et al. (2010) UMMB supplementation −10% Mohini and Singh (2010) Harit Dhara (150–200 g/d) up to −17 to −20% ICAR-NIANP Condensed tannins −13 to −16% per kg DMI Carulla; Grainger Fat, per +1% of DM −3.5 to −5.6% Three meta-estimates Monensin 50–100 mg/d −14 to −35% Singh (2010) Canola oil, beef cattle up to −32% Beauchemin and McGinn (2006) Grass maturity raised methane from 4.5–5.3% to 6–7% of gross energy intake. Concentrates cut enteric methane but raise manure methane, with a net reduction. Antibiotics leave residues in milk and ionophores' effects fade, so plant extracts are preferred (pp. 159–160). CHECK BEFORE REUSING The review states that India's 417.85 million cattle and buffalo contribute 29.56 billion t CO₂e (p. 158). That is implausible (larger than half of global GHG emissions) and should not be cited.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Ruminants are the main methane producers; farmers adopt measures only if they pay. 2. Ration balancing, green fodder and fewer high-producing animals are practical levers. 3. Herbal products need dosing, formulation and commercialisation, with government support for industry (pp. 157, 162–163).


## 6. Limitations

- Narrative review; study quality and methods vary.
- Many results are in vitro or from non-Indian animals and diets.
- Costs and adoption barriers are not analysed in detail.
- Some figures need checking against the original sources.

**Authors:**
Jeetendra Prakash Aryal, Tek Bahadur Sapkota, Timothy J. Krupnik, Dil Bahadur Rahut, Mangi Lal Jat, Clare M. Stirling (6 authors)

**Journal:**
Environmental Science and Pollution Research, vol. 28, pp. 51480–51496 (2021)

**Dates:**
Received 16 January 2021 · Accepted 13 April 2021

**Paper type:**
Research article (household survey and econometrics)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-021-13975-7

**Cite as:**
Aryal, J. P., Sapkota, T. B., Krupnik, T. J., Rahut, D. B., Jat, M. L., & Stirling, C. M. (2021). Factors affecting farmers' use of organic and inorganic fertilizers in South Asia. Environmental Science and Pollution Research, 28, 51480–51496. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-021-13975-7 Open access under CC BY 4.0. Page numbers are the journal's printed pages.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using a 2013 survey of 2,528 households in Haryana, Bihar, the Nepal Terai and Bangladesh, the authors model what drives urea, DAP and manure use on rice and wheat and who overuses nitrogen. 33.6% of rice fields got more than 120 kg N/ha and 18.5% of wheat fields more than 140 kg N/ha. Overuse is highest in Haryana and lowest in Nepal; larger, wealthier, irrigated and more educated households overuse more, while training reduces overuse. Manure use is declining everywhere. The authors call for training, extension and nudges on nutrient-use efficiency.


## 1. Background

Fertiliser N is a leading cause of agricultural N₂O. In Punjab and Haryana N use rose from 2–8 kg N/ha in the 1960s to more than 160–180 kg N/ha in 2017, and many farmers do not know recommended rates. Earlier work found a wheat yield penalty above 140 kg N/ha and a rice plateau above 100 kg N/ha (pp. 51481, 51483).


## 2. Aim of the study

To examine socio-economic and geographic factors affecting inorganic and organic fertiliser use on rice and wheat in South Asia, and the factors behind N overuse (p. 51480).


## 3. What the authors did

Multistage sampling chose 38 villages (14 Bangladesh, 12 Bihar, 13 Haryana, 12 Nepal) in 2013. Total N = urea × 46% + DAP × 18% + manure × 0.5%. Multiple regression explained urea and DAP rates, Heckman two-step models manure adoption and amount, and a probit model N overuse (rice > 120, wheat > 140 kg N/ha; results similar at 100 and 120) (pp. 51482–51483, 51491).

Table A. Sample by site (Table 1, p. 51483) Site Households Rice plots Wheat plots Bangladesh (3 districts) 630 1,182 0 Bihar (Vaishali) 641 1,299 1,544 Haryana (Karnal) 626 665 667 Nepal (Rupandehi) 631 1,576 977


## 4. Main findings

Table B. Average N applied, kg N/ha, manure at 0.5% N (Appendix Tables 8–9) Site Rice Wheat Haryana 177.4 178.1 Bangladesh 148.4 na Bihar 118.3 129.6 Nepal 112.3 115.9 Male-headed households, those with secondary or higher education, larger land, off-farm income, wealth, irrigation and owned land were more likely to overuse N; training, distance to market and fertile or deep soils lowered it (Table 7). Manure reached 47% of rice plots in Bihar and Nepal and 26% in Bangladesh; focus groups everywhere reported declining manure use (pp. 51484, 51491). DATA NOTE The text gives 1,604 wheat fields in Bihar (p. 51482) but Table 1 and the models use 1,544. The 2% N manure variant in the appendix raises totals by 14–28 kg N/ha.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Wealth, gender, education, migration, market access, training and off-farm income shape fertiliser use. 2. Where overuse is routine, training, education and behavioural nudges are needed; few farmers know the harms of overuse. 3. Declining manure use needs extension and scale-appropriate machinery to cut labour and cost (pp. 51492–51493).


## 6. Limitations

- Cross-sectional data from 2013; fertiliser amounts farmer-reported.
- Manure N assumed (0.5%); overuse thresholds are single cut-offs.
- One district per Indian state; no Uttar Pradesh site.
- N₂O is not estimated directly.

title: India’s fertilizer policies: implications for food security, environmental sustainability, and climate change
authors: Tek B. Sapkota (CIMMYT), Bijay-Singh
description: The authors trace India's fertiliser policies from the 1950s and their effects. Subsidies made urea very cheap (farmers pay 22% of the world price), and food grain output kept pace with a tripling population, with gains linked to lower rural poverty. But unequal subsidies caused urea overuse and P and K underuse, lowering efficiency and raising N₂O and nitrate losses; soil N surplus rose to 100.8 kg N/ha by 2021. # India’s fertilizer policies: implications for food security, environmental sustainability, and climate change


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

India's fertilizer policies: implications for food security, environmental sustainability, and climate change Tek B. Sapkota and Bijay-Singh

**Authors:**
Tek B. Sapkota (CIMMYT), Bijay-Singh

**Journal:**
Regional Environmental Change, vol. 25, article 63 (2025)

**Dates:**
Received 17 June 2024 · Accepted 7 April 2025 · Published 6 May 2025

**Paper type:**
Review (policy analysis with secondary quantitative data)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10113-025-02395-9

**Cite as:**
Sapkota, T. B., & Bijay-Singh. (2025). India's fertilizer policies: implications for food security, environmental sustainability, and climate change. Regional Environmental Change, 25, 63. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10113-025-02395-9 Open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The authors trace India's fertiliser policies from the 1950s and their effects. Subsidies made urea very cheap (farmers pay 22% of the world price), and food grain output kept pace with a tripling population, with gains linked to lower rural poverty. But unequal subsidies caused urea overuse and P and K underuse, lowering efficiency and raising N₂O and nitrate losses; soil N surplus rose to 100.8 kg N/ha by


## 2021. They recommend recalibrating subsidies, soil-test-based advice and gradual urea price

liberalisation while keeping P and K affordable for smallholders.


## 1. Background

India is self-sufficient in food grains, but production is resource-intensive, cereal-centric and regionally imbalanced. From 1971–72 to 2021–22 food grains rose 3× while N use rose 11.3×, P₂O₅ 14.2× and K₂O 5.71× (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To  analyse,  with  quantitative  data,  how  fertiliser  policies  shaped  consumption  and  nutrient management, and their effects on rural producers, the environment and climate (p. 1).


## 3. What the authors did

They combined policy history (FAI, Katyal 2023) with consumption, production and poverty data (FAI, Government of India) and FAOSTAT soil N budgets and Tier 1 N₂O, using growth rates, regressions and an interrupted time series of policy effects adapted from Praveen et al. (2020) (pp. 2–3, 5).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Key numbers (pp. 3, 5–8) Indicator Value Average subsidy 2010–2022 (urea / DAP / MOP) USD 228.5 / 110.4 / 70.5 per t Share of world price paid by farmers 22% urea, 71% DAP, 73% MOP Wheat per capita, 1951 → 2022 24 → 68.8 kg/yr Nutrient use, 2021 137.9 kg/ha (63× 1961) N:P ratio after P and K decontrol 2.42 (1991) → 3.29 (1993) Soil N surplus, 1961 → 2021 17.5 → 100.8 kg N/ha Districts > 200 kg/ha nutrients (2022–23) 28% Per capita rice stayed stable and wheat rose 2.4×. A 46 kg/ha rise in fertiliser use is associated with 0.5 t/ha more grain and a 6% fall in rural poverty. Unequal subsidies left N overused and P and K underused; neem-coated urea showed no clear yield or urea-rate effect, and Soil Health Cards have yet to show socio-economic impact (pp. 6–9). CORRECTION TO THE OLD NOTES The old notes said India's N balance became surplus only after 1984. That holds only when mineral fertiliser is the sole N input (Katyal 2023). With all N inputs counted, India already had a surplus of 17.5 kg N/ha in 1961, rising to 100.8 kg N/ha in 2021 (p. 8, Fig. 5).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Fertiliser policies were crucial for food security and socio-economic progress. 2. Unequal subsidies caused imbalanced use, lower efficiency, N₂O emissions and nitrate pollution. 3. Recalibrate subsidies, promote soil-based recommendations, and liberalise urea gradually while keeping P and K affordable (pp. 10–11).


## 6. Limitations

- National secondary data may miss regional variation (the authors say so).
- N₂O from FAOSTAT Tier 1; policy effects from trends and time series, not causal designs.
- Reform may meet political resistance; organic inputs get little attention (p. 10).

# Influence of 36 years of integrated nutrient management on soil carbon sequestration, environmental footprint and agronomic productivity of wheat under rice-wheat cropping system


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Influence of 36 years of integrated nutrient management on soil carbon sequestration, environmental footprint and agronomic productivity of wheat under rice-wheat cropping system Shivani Ranjan, Sanjay Kumar, Swaraj Kumar Dutta, Smruti Ranjan Padhan, Parmeswar Dayal, Sumit Sow, Dhirendra Kumar Roy, Dibyajyoti Nath, Kirttiranjan Baral, Vikram Bharati

**Authors:**
Shivani Ranjan, Sanjay Kumar, Swaraj Kumar Dutta, Smruti Ranjan Padhan, Parmeswar Dayal, Sumit Sow, Dhirendra Kumar Roy, Dibyajyoti Nath, Kirttiranjan Baral, Vikram Bharati

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Environmental Science, vol. 11, article 1222909 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 15 May 2023 · Accepted 30 August 2023 · Published 14 September 2023

**Paper type:**
Original research: 36-year long-term field experiment (open access, CC BY)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2023.1222909

**Cite as:**
Ranjan, S., Kumar, S., Dutta, S. K., Padhan, S. R., Dayal, P., Sow, S., Roy, D. K., Nath, D., Baral, K., & Bharati, V. (2023). Influence of 36 years of integrated nutrient management on soil carbon sequestration, environmental footprint and agronomic productivity of wheat under rice-wheat cropping system. Frontiers in Environmental Science, 11, 1222909. https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2023.1222909 Open access article under a Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

In a rice-wheat experiment running since 1984 at Sabour, Bihar, replacing half the rice nitrogen with farmyard manure (and giving full fertiliser to wheat, T6) gave the highest soil carbon stock (16.85 Mg/ha), a sequestration rate of 0.22 Mg C/ha/yr and the highest wheat yield (4.29 Mg/ha, +24.7% over fertiliser alone). Replacing a quarter of the N with FYM (T7) gave the lowest modelled emission intensity, 206.6 kg CO₂-eq per tonne of grain. Plots with no inputs lost soil carbon.


## 1. Background

Wheat is grown on about 32 Mha in India. Years of intensive farming and unbalanced fertiliser use have left soils short of nutrients and low in organic matter; the paper cites an annual NPK requirement of 28 Mt against 18 Mt supplied, a negative balance of 10 Mt (p. 2). Integrated nutrient management (INM) combines chemical fertilisers with organic sources such as farmyard manure (FYM), crop straw and green manure. Long-term fertiliser experiments are the best way to see how such practices change soil organic carbon (SOC) and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, since these change slowly.


## 2. Aim of the study

To test how 36 years of different INM combinations affect SOC sequestration, the environmental footprint (GHG emission intensity) and wheat productivity in a rice-wheat system of the eastern Indo- Gangetic Plains (EIGP).


## 3. What the authors did

The experiment began in  1984 at the Bihar Agricultural University research farm, Sabour (humid subtropical; average rainfall 1280 mm, 75–80% from mid-June to mid-October). It has 11 treatments in a randomised block design with three replications (plots 8.10 × 4.20 m). Organic sources were FYM, wheat straw and green manure (Sesbania aculeata), replacing 25% or 50% of the nitrogen in rice. Table A. Treatments (Table 2 of the paper) Code Rice Wheat T1 Control (no fertiliser, no manure) Control T2 50% RDF 50% RDF T3 50% RDF 100% RDF T4 75% RDF 75% RDF T5 100% RDF 100% RDF T6 50% RDF + 50% N through FYM 100% RDF T7 75% RDF + 25% N through FYM 75% RDF T8 50% RDF + 50% N through wheat straw 100% RDF T9 75% RDF + 25% N through wheat straw 75% RDF T10 50% RDF + 50% N through green manure 100% RDF T11 75% RDF + 25% N through green manure 75% RDF RDF for wheat was 120-60-40 kg/ha N-P₂O₅-K₂O; for rice 80-40-20 kg/ha. Measurements were made on wheat (cv. HD-2967) in the 2020–21 winter season. Soil (0–15 cm) was sampled after harvest on 5 April


## 2021. SOC stock = SOC × bulk density × depth × 10; sequestration rate = (SOC stock − initial stock) / years.

GHG emissions were estimated with the CCAFS Mitigation Options Tool (GWP of 34 for CH₄ and 298 for N₂O) and divided by grain yield to give emission intensity.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Soil carbon

SOC stocks after 36 rice-wheat cycles ranged from 8.05 Mg/ha (control) to 16.85 Mg/ha (T6), against an initial stock of 10.28 Mg/ha. T6 and T8 raised the SOC stock by 36.4% and 29.9% over full fertiliser (T5). Carbon sequestered ranged from −2.24 to 8.07 Mg/ha, and the sequestration rate from −0.06 to 0.22 Mg C/ha/yr. Plots with no inputs (T1) or only 50% RDF to rice (T2, T3) lost organic carbon. FYM was the most effective organic source. The carbon pool index ranged from 1.06 to 2.40 (highest in T6), and bulk density fell from 1.49 to 1.37 Mg/m³ under T6.

NOTE ON THE 46.4% FIGURE The abstract says SOC rose by 46.4% (18.29 Mg/ha) over full fertiliser; the Results text (p. 5) gives 44.9%, which matches Table 3 (18.29 vs 12.62 Mg/ha organic carbon). For SOC stock the gain is 36.4% (16.85 Mg/ha). Quote the Table 3 values.


### 4.2 Yield and nutrient-use efficiency

Table B. Wheat yield, organic carbon and carbon pool index (Table 3 of the paper) Treatment Grain yield (Mg/ha) Organic C (Mg/ha) CPI T1 Control 0.96 8.06 1.06 T2 2.33 9.26 1.22 T3 3.58 10.15 1.33 T4 2.90 10.83 1.42 T5 100% RDF 3.44 12.62 1.66 T6 4.29 18.29 2.40 T7 3.76 17.02 2.24 T8 3.80 17.25 2.26 T9 3.29 16.20 2.13 T10 3.92 17.02 2.24 T11 3.66 16.28 2.14 LSD (p ≤ 0.05) 0.49 0.62 0.08 T6 gave the highest wheat yield, 4.29 Mg/ha (+24.7% over T5). Note that T6 received the FYM in the rice season  and  full  RDF  in  wheat;  the  abstract's  wording  ('during  wheat  cultivation')  is  misleading. Agronomic efficiency ranged from 20.65–31.06 kg/kg for N, 94.58–142.23 for P and 74.96–112.73 for K, highest in T7 and lowest in T5. Partial factor productivity of N ranged from 28.68 to 41.76 kg/kg. SOC stock correlated strongly with yield (r = 0.82).


### 4.3 Emission intensity

Combined organic-inorganic treatments had lower emission intensity than fertiliser alone. The lowest was 206.6 kg CO₂-eq/Mg grain (T7); the highest were the control (328.1, because of its low yield) and full RDF (286.9). Emission intensity was negatively correlated with yield (r = −0.667).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Organic manure with balanced chemical fertiliser significantly increased SOC sequestration and yield and reduced emission intensity. 2. FYM was more effective than wheat straw or green manure. 3. Carbon management in this system is only just above the threshold level and must be increased to restore soil health and productivity.


## 6. Limitations

- One research station and one measured wheat season (2020–21, an unusually dry season with 0.4 mm rain).
- GHG emissions were estimated with a model (CCAFS-MOT), not measured in the field.
- SOC was measured only in the top 15 cm; FYM availability on farms may limit adoption at these rates.
- The paper has small internal inconsistencies (46.4% vs 44.9% SOC gain; initial SOC 10.30 vs 10.28 Mg/ha; site longitude printed as 78°E).

#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Enhancing productivity, soil health, and reducing global warming potential through diverse conservation agriculture cropping systems in India's Western Indo-Gangetic Plains M.K. Gora, H.S. Jat, J.K. Ladha, Madhu Choudhary, P.C. Sharma, A.K. Yadav, L.K. Singh, Tek B. Sapkota, Yadvinder Singh, Kailash Prajapat, R.K. Yadav, M.L. Jat, T.J. Krupnik, M.K. Gathala

**Authors:**
M.K. Gora, H.S. Jat, J.K. Ladha, Madhu Choudhary, P.C. Sharma, A.K. Yadav, L.K. Singh, Tek B. Sapkota, Yadvinder Singh, Kailash Prajapat, R.K. Yadav, M.L. Jat, T.J. Krupnik, M.K. Gathala

**Journal:**
Field Crops Research, vol. 315, article 109476 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 4 February 2024 · Revised 2 June 2024 · Accepted 15 June 2024 · Online 24 June 2024

**Paper type:**
Research article: 8-year field experiment

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fcr.2024.109476

**Cite as:**
Gora, M. K., Jat, H. S., Ladha, J. K., Choudhary, M., Sharma, P. C., Yadav, A. K., Singh, L. K., Sapkota, T. B., Singh, Y., Prajapat, K., Yadav, R. K., Jat, M. L., Krupnik, T. J., & Gathala, M. K. (2024). Enhancing productivity, soil health, and reducing global warming potential through diverse conservation agriculture cropping systems in India's Western Indo- Gangetic Plains. Field Crops Research, 315, 109476. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fcr.2024.109476 Journal version © 2024 Elsevier B.V.; the eScholarship (UC Davis) copy used here is made available under CC BY 4.0. Page numbers refer to the journal pagination.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

An eight-year trial (2014–2022) at ICAR-CSSRI Karnal compared farmers' rice-wheat practice with six conservation agriculture (CA) scenarios using zero tillage, residue retention and diversified rotations. On average CA cut net global warming potential by 47.2%, raised surface soil C stock by 49.6%, system yield by 8.5% and profit by 23.0%. Maize-based rotations gave the best all-round result (+20.7% yield, +40.3% profit, −55.6% GWP).


## 1. Background

The rice-wheat system covers  13.5 million ha in South Asia and underpins food security and rural livelihoods. Intensive tillage, flooding and residue burning have depleted soil organic matter, slowed yield growth and raised greenhouse gas emissions (pp. 1–2). Conservation agriculture combines (a) reduced or zero tillage with residue cover, (b) crop diversification such as replacing rice with an upland crop, and (c) legumes in cereal rotations. The authors note a lack of medium- to long-term studies that look at soil quality, GHG mitigation and carbon balance together.


## 2. Aim of the study

To develop resilient, climate-smart cropping systems within the rice-wheat system and test their effect on crop productivity, economic returns, soil quality, nutrient balances and GHG emissions over eight years.


## 3. What the authors did

The trial ran from 2014 to 2022 at the ICAR-Central Soil Salinity Research Institute farm, Karnal, Haryana (semi-arid subtropical; average rainfall 670 mm, 70–80% in June–September; silty loam, OC 0.56%, pH 8.02). Seven scenarios were laid out in a randomised block design with three replications on 600 m² plots. Scenarios were adjusted after four years to raise cropping intensity (Table 1, p. 3). Table A. Scenarios in 2019–2022 (from Table 1 of the paper) Scenario Rotation Management Sc1 Rice – wheat – fallow Farmers' practice: tilled, transplanted rice, residue removed Sc2 DSR rice – wheat – fallow Tilled rice, zero-till wheat, rice residue retained Sc3 Rice – wheat – mung bean Zero tillage, residue retained Sc4 Maize – mustard – mung bean Permanent beds, zero till, partial residue Sc5 Maize – wheat – mung bean Permanent beds, zero till, partial residue Sc6 Soybean – wheat – mung bean Permanent beds, zero till, partial residue Sc7 Pigeon pea – wheat – mung bean Permanent beds, zero till, partial residue In Sc4 and Sc5 about 60–65% of maize stover and 25–30% of anchored wheat stubble were kept on the surface. Soil was sampled every June at 0–15 and 15–30 cm. GHG emissions covered methane and nitrous oxide from soil, residue burning, and emissions from fertiliser manufacture, fuel and irrigation energy, with CH₄ and N₂O converted at GWPs of 34 and 298 (IPCC 2013); net GWP also accounted for soil carbon change.


## 4. Main findings

Table B. Percent change over farmers' practice Sc1 (Table 6 of the paper) Indicator All CA Rice-based Maize-based Legume-based System yield +8.5 +3.5 +20.7 +1.2 Economic profit +23.0 +11.1 +40.3 +17.6 Soil quality index +111.4 +74.2 +138.4 +121.7 Carbon stock +49.6 +59.7 +43.3 +45.9 Apparent N balance −64.4 +10.4 −78.9 −124.6 GWP −47.2 −28.0 −55.6 −58.1


### 4.1 Soil quality

CA scenarios had lower bulk density (range 1.34–1.52 Mg/m³ at 0–15 cm, highest in Sc1 and lowest in Sc5), better aggregation (water-stable aggregates +24.5% and mean weight diameter +118.7% at the surface) and faster infiltration. Surface organic C was 63.7% higher and C stock 49.9% higher (the

abstract and Table 6 give 49.6%). Available N, P and K rose by 10.2%, 28.6% and 21.8%. Earthworm density rose several-fold, reaching 333 per m² in Sc5.


### 4.2 Greenhouse gases

Flooded rice with residue burning (Sc1) emitted the most methane, 1972 kg CO₂-eq/ha in the rice season and 2299 kg CO₂-eq/ha for the system. CA scenarios had higher N₂O (1428–2211 vs 1041 kg CO₂-eq/ha), but lower methane and energy emissions: wet-season emissions from energy and inputs fell from 2853 kg CO₂-eq/ha in Sc1 by up to 72% in Sc5–Sc7. Net GWP fell by 47.2% on average.


### 4.3 Yield and economics

System yield ranged from 11.93 to 14.57 Mg/ha (rice equivalent) and returns from US$6616 to 9595/ha; both were highest in Sc5 and lowest in Sc1. Note that the Results text says yield and returns of CA rose 'approximately 9%', while Table 6 gives +8.5% for yield and +23.0% for profit.


## 5. Conclusions

1. CA practices and diversified rotations can reverse falling productivity, lower returns, soil degradation and rising environmental impacts in north-west India's rice-wheat system. 2. Maize-based rotations gave the highest overall benefits; rice-based CA gave the largest carbon-stock gain; legume rotations gave the largest GWP cut and the most negative N balance. 3. Wide adoption needs policy: carbon credit payments and guaranteed markets with supportive prices.


## 6. Limitations

- One research station in the western IGP; the Varuna basin (eastern IGP) has higher rainfall and smaller farms.
- Scenarios were changed after four years, so the eight-year effects mix two designs.
- Results are percent changes against farmers' practice, not annual sequestration rates; soil measured only to 30 cm.
- Shifting from rice to maize depends on procurement and prices.
