# Conservation agriculture enhances crop productivity and soil carbon fractions in Indo-Gangetic Plains of India


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Conservation agriculture enhances crop productivity and soil carbon fractions in Indo- Gangetic Plains of India Ajay Kumar Mishra, Hitoshi Shinjo, Hanuman Sahay Jat, Mangi Lal Jat, Raj Kumar Jat, Shinya Funakawa

**Authors:**
Ajay Kumar Mishra, Hitoshi Shinjo, Hanuman Sahay Jat, Mangi Lal Jat, Raj Kumar Jat, Shinya Funakawa

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, vol. 8, article 1476292 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 5 August 2024 · Accepted 30 September 2024 · Published 28 October 2024

**Paper type:**
Original research: two short-term field trials (open access, CC BY)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2024.1476292

**Cite as:**
Mishra, A. K., Shinjo, H., Jat, H. S., Jat, M. L., Jat, R. K., & Funakawa, S. (2024). Conservation agriculture enhances crop productivity and soil carbon fractions in Indo- Gangetic Plains of India. Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 8, 1476292. https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2024.1476292 Open access article under a Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Two conservation agriculture trials started in 2012 at Karnal (Haryana) and Samastipur (Bihar) compared conventional puddled rice-wheat with zero-till and raised-bed systems with residue retention and mungbean. CA raised system yield by up to 20.2% (Karnal) and 23.0% (Samastipur). Total organic carbon gains were concentrated in the top 5 cm, while labile fractions (POXC, coarse particulate organic matter) responded more strongly, so the authors propose them as early indicators of carbon sequestration.


## 1. Background

The Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP) face land degradation and stagnant yields from intensive tillage, puddling and residue burning in the rice-wheat system. CA (minimal tillage, residue recycling, diversification) can build soil carbon, but total organic carbon (TOC) changes slowly and is hard to detect in experiments shorter than about five years. Labile fractions, such as permanganate-oxidisable carbon (POXC) and particulate organic matter (POM), may respond sooner (pp. 1–3).


## 2. Aim of the study

To evaluate the effect of resource-conserving practices on crop yield and TOC stocks at Karnal (western IGP) and Samastipur (middle IGP), to track changes in physical carbon fractions after 3 and 5 years, and to relate carbon stocks to labile fractions and crop residue inputs.


## 3. What the authors did

Trials started in 2012 (June at Karnal, November at Samastipur); the sites are about 1,300 km apart. Karnal had six treatments (K1–K6) and Samastipur four (S1–S4). Soil was sampled at 0–5 and 5–15 cm

after 3 and 5 years (2015 and 2017 at Karnal; 2016 and 2018 at Samastipur). TOC was measured by an improved chromic acid (Tyurin) method because the soils contain carbonates; POXC by KMnO₄ oxidation; and soil was wet-sieved into coarse POM (2,000–250 μm), fine POM (250–53 μm) and an organo-mineral fraction (< 53 μm). System yield was expressed as rice-equivalent using minimum support prices. Table A. Treatments (Tables 1–2 of the paper) Code System Residue K1, S1 Conventional-till puddled rice – wheat Removed K2 Conventional-till rice – wheat – mungbean Retained K3 Zero-till direct-seeded rice – wheat Removed K4, S2 Zero-till direct-seeded rice – wheat – mungbean Retained K5 Permanent-bed maize – wheat Removed K6, S3 Permanent-bed maize – wheat – mungbean Retained S4 Permanent-bed maize – mustard – mungbean Retained


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Yields

At Karnal, five-year mean system yield ranged from 11.9 Mg/ha (K1) to  14.3 Mg/ha (K6, +20.2%). Treatments with residue and mungbean (K2, K4, K6) did best. At Samastipur, S2 (15.0 Mg/ha) and S4 (13.7 Mg/ha) gave the highest system yields; S2 was 23.0% above S1. Raised-bed maize at Samastipur yielded less than conventional rice (Table 3, p. 9).


### 4.2 Carbon and nitrogen stocks

At Karnal, TOC stock at 0–5 cm in K4 and K6 was 17% and 11% higher than K1 in 2015, and 17% and 20% higher in 2017; over 0–15 cm the gain was 8–13%. At Samastipur, 0–5 cm TOC was highest in S2 (+24%) and S3 (+26%) in 2016 and in S2 (+20%) in 2018; over 0–15 cm S3 was highest (+11% in 2016, +8% in 2018). Below 5 cm, Samastipur stocks did not change significantly (p. 9). READ WITH CARE The abstract says there were no significant differences in C and N stocks at Karnal after 3 years and that Samastipur's maize-mustard-mungbean (S4) raised C stocks. The Results report significant 0–5 cm TOC differences at Karnal in 2015 and the largest Samastipur gains in S2 and S3. The Discussion's figure of a 72.3% C-stock increase for K6 does not match the 17–20% in the Results; quote the Results values.


### 4.3 Labile carbon and fractions

- POXC stock showed no treatment differences at Karnal in 2015; in 2017 it was 37.0% higher in K4 than K1 (0–5 cm). At Samastipur in 2018, S2 had 93.8% more POXC than S1.
- Residue increased coarse POM mass: +78.8% (K4) and +79.7% (K6) over K1 in 2015; K4 reached 3.90× K1 by 2017. K4's cPOM carbon was 3.42 Mg C/ha at 0–5 cm and 4.94 Mg C/ha at 0–15 cm (3.53× K1).
- At Samastipur, S2 had 3.19× (2016) and 2.41× (2018) the cPOM mass of S1. Carbon stocks correlated with crop residue carbon input (Table 10).

## 5. Conclusions

1. CA practices (no-till, residue management, crop diversification) significantly promote carbon sequestration, but outcomes depend on study duration, site and the fraction measured. 2. Three years was not enough to detect changes in soil carbon and nitrogen fractionation at Karnal; it was at Samastipur. 3. Coarse POM carbon and nitrogen, POXC and POC are useful early indicators of short-term CA effects; practices should be tailored to local soil and climate.


## 6. Limitations

- Short-term (3–5 years) trials at two research-managed sites.
- Soil sampled only to 15 cm; no greenhouse gas measurements.
- Abstract, Results and Discussion give somewhat different accounts of the 3-year carbon results.

Degraded land rehabilitation through agroforestry in India: Achievements, current understanding, and future prospectives Dinesh Jinger, Rajesh Kaushal, Raj Kumar, Venkatesh Paramesh and 18 co-authors (full list in the citation)

**Authors:**
Dinesh Jinger, Rajesh Kaushal, Raj Kumar, Venkatesh Paramesh, Archana Verma, Monika Shukla, Sangram Bhanudas Chavan, Vijaysinha Kakade, Sneha Dobhal, Appanderanda Ramani Uthappa, Trisha Roy, Vibha Singhal, Madhu Madegowda, Dinesh Kumar, Poonam Khatri, Dhakshanamoorthy Dinesh, Gaurav Singh, Ashok Kumar Singh, Arun Jyoti Nath, Neeshu Joshi, Ekta Joshi, Sanju Kumawat

**Paper type:**
Review (open access, CC BY)

**DOI:**

**Cite as:**
Jinger, D., Kaushal, R., Kumar, R., Paramesh, V., Verma, A., Shukla, M., Chavan, S. B., Kakade, V., Dobhal, S., Uthappa, A. R., Roy, T., Singhal, V., Madegowda, M., Kumar, D., Khatri, P., Dinesh, D., Singh, G., Singh, A. K., Nath, A. J., Joshi, N., Joshi, E., & Kumawat, S. (2023). Degraded land rehabilitation through agroforestry in India: Achievements, current understanding, and future prospectives. Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, 11, 1088796. https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2023.1088796 Open access article under a Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). Figures in this summary are quoted from the review; most come from the studies it cites.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

About 120.7 Mha of India's land is degraded, most of it by water and wind erosion. The review compiles agroforestry systems developed by Indian research for eroded, sloping, ravine, mined, waterlogged, saline, sodic and acid lands. Reported carbon sequestration ranges from 1.55 to 20–25 Mg C/ha/yr depending on zone and system (Middle Gangetic Plains: 2.32), and hedgerows cut soil loss by 94% in north-east India. The authors call for agroforestry business models and policy support.


## 1. Background

India has about 120.7 Mha of degraded land and wasteland (NAAS 2010). Water erosion affects 73.3 Mha and wind erosion 12.4 Mha of arable land, together about 71% of the degraded area; chemical degradation (salinity, sodicity, acidity) and physical degradation (waterlogging, mining) make up the rest. A newer estimate (SAC 2021) gives 97.8 Mha (29.7% of the country). Drivers include 2.07 Mha of tree cover loss in 2001–2021, uncontrolled grazing (5.65 Mha), shifting cultivation (7.6 Mha) and heavy fertiliser use (pp. 1–2).

Table A. Degraded land in India (Mha; Table 1 of the review) Type Arable land Open forest Water erosion 73.27 9.30 Wind erosion 12.40 – Chemical degradation (salt-affected, acid) 17.45 7.23 Physical degradation (mining, waterlogging) 1.07 – Total 104.19 16.53 Grand total 120.72


## 2. Aim of the study

To review the achievements of Indian agroforestry research in rehabilitating degraded land, summarise the systems suited to each kind of degradation and agro-climatic zone, and set out future strategies.


## 3. What the authors did

This is a literature review. The authors compiled degraded-area statistics, the drivers of degradation, the prevalent agroforestry systems of each agro-climatic zone with their carbon sequestration and food production potential (Table 4), and systems tested on sloping, gully and shifting-cultivation land, mined and waterlogged land, and salt-affected and acid soils (Tables 5–9). Values are quoted from the cited studies.


## 4. Main findings


### 4.1 Carbon sequestration by zone

Table B. Selected rows of Table 4 (Mg C/ha/yr) Zone System C sequestration Western Himalayan Apricot or peach + tulsi 1.80–2.0 Eastern Himalayan Mulberry + Setaria silvipasture 1.55 Lower Gangetic Eucalyptus + rice-wheat 10.7 Middle Gangetic Teak + sorghum/groundnut 2.32 Upper Gangetic Shisham + mustard 2.83 Trans-Gangetic Poplar + wheat/potato/turmeric 9.12 Southern Plateau Leucaena + Gliricidia + Stylosanthes 23.2 Gujarat Plains Melia dubia + lemon grass 20–25 Island regions Coconut + Calliandra 3.50 CORRECTION TO THE ABSTRACT'S RANGE The abstract describes sequestration as '1.80 Mg C/ha/yr in the Western Himalayan region to 3.50 in the island regions'. These are the first and last rows of Table 4, not its range: the table runs from 1.55 (Eastern Himalaya) to 20–25 (Gujarat). For the Varuna basin, the Middle Gangetic Plains row (2.32) is the closest match.


### 4.2 Eroded, sloping and ravine land

Hedgerow cropping on sloping land in north-east India reduced soil loss by 94% and runoff by 78% (Saha et al. 2012). Grass filter strips and Indigofera hedgerows conserved SOC (43%) and available N, P and K. In the Himalayan foothills, bamboo with semicircular trenches stopped runoff and soil loss after the fifth year. In ravines, Acacia nilotica and A. tortilis with Cenchrus produced 28.7 and 27 Mg/ha of fuelwood. A silvipasture at Jhansi (Uttar Pradesh) lost only 0.9 Mg/ha of soil, against 12–43 Mg/ha on deforested black soil.


### 4.3 Salt-affected and other problem soils

Chemical degradation covers about 17.4 Mha. For sodic soils, Acacia nilotica, Albizia procera, Leucaena, neem and Eucalyptus hybrid were the best-suited trees; Prosopis juliflora with Kallar grass can be grown for 4–5 years before the land returns to crops. Strip plantations of Eucalyptus tereticornis lowered a high water table by 0.75 m in five years and raised crop yields 3–4 times on waterlogged saline soil (Table 9).


## 5. Conclusions

1. Agroforestry (agri-silviculture, silvipasture, agri-horticulture) has strong potential for sustainable rehabilitation of degraded land, with ecological and economic benefits. 2. India's many suitable species should be brought into agroforestry-based business models; supply chains, buy-back with MSP, insurance, credit and quality planting material are needed. 3. Agroforestry can help meet the Bonn Challenge goal of restoring 26 Mha of degraded land by 2030 and the land degradation neutrality target.


## 6. Limitations

- A review: all numbers come from cited studies of mixed quality and methods.
- Table 4 gives one system and one study per zone; values are not zone averages and depend on species, density and tree age.
- Few values are specific to eastern Uttar Pradesh or the Varuna basin.

### 01. Individual trees from space

# Severe decline in large farmland trees in India over the past decade


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Severe decline in large farmland trees in India over the past decade Martin Brandt, Dimitri Gominski, Florian Reiner, Ankit Kariryaa, Venkanna Babu Guthula, Philippe Ciais, Xiaoye Tong, Wenmin Zhang, Dhanapal Govindarajulu, Daniel Ortiz-Gonzalo, Rasmus Fensholt

**Authors:**
Martin Brandt, Dimitri Gominski, Florian Reiner, Ankit Kariryaa, Venkanna Babu Guthula, Philippe Ciais, Xiaoye Tong, Wenmin Zhang, Dhanapal Govindarajulu, Daniel Ortiz-Gonzalo, Rasmus Fensholt

**Journal:**
Nature Sustainability, vol. 7, pp. 860–868 (July 2024)

**Dates:**
Received 29 September 2023 · Accepted 19 April 2024 · Published online 15 May 2024

**Paper type:**
Article: satellite remote sensing with deep learning, plus interviews

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-024-01356-0

**Cite as:**
Brandt, M., Gominski, D., Reiner, F., Kariryaa, A., Guthula, V. B., Ciais, P., Tong, X., Zhang, W., Govindarajulu, D., Ortiz-Gonzalo, D., & Fensholt, R. (2024). Severe decline in large farmland trees in India over the past decade. Nature Sustainability, 7, 860–868. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-024-01356-0 Figures in this summary are taken from the article (Nature Sustainability, July 2024).


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using 3–5 m satellite imagery and deep learning, the authors mapped about 0.6 billion trees in India's cropland, urban and bare land and tracked them individually. About 11 ± 2% of large trees (mean crown 96 m²) seen in 2010/2011 had gone by 2018–2022, and 5.3 million large trees seen in 2018/2019 were gone by 2020–2022. Hotspots in Telangana and Maharashtra lost up to half their large trees. Villagers linked the losses to new water supplies, paddy expansion and the belief that field trees reduce yields.


## 1. Background

Farmland covers 56% of India and forest only 20%, so many of India's trees are scattered on farms, along roads and in hedgerows. These multipurpose trees (neem, mahua, Acacia nilotica, shisham, jamun and others) provide shade, fodder, fruit, fuelwood and income, and store carbon. Agroforestry is promoted as a natural climate solution, but existing on-farm trees are poorly monitored because satellites coarser than 10 m cannot see individual trees (pp. 860–861).


## 2. Aim of the study

To map individual farmland trees across India and track their disappearance between 2010/2011 and 2018–2022.


## 3. What the authors did

They built country-wide mosaics of RapidEye images (5 m) for 2010 and 2011 and PlanetScope images (3 m) for each year 2018–2022, and trained two deep-learning tree-detection models. Farmland was masked with the 10 m ESA WorldCover map; closed plantations were excluded. Tree crown centres were

matched between years within a 15 m buffer. A 2010/2011 tree not found in any 2018–2022 image, or a 2018/2019 tree not detected in all three years 2020–2022, was classed as disappeared. Only high- confidence losses were reported, so the estimates are conservative. In August 2023 they held 12 qualitative interviews with villagers in Telangana, Haryana, Kerala, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Main numbers (pp. 860–866) Measure Value Trees mapped in cropland, urban and bare land (2018–2022) about 0.6 billion Mean density 0.6 trees/ha (s.d. 1.6); up to 22/ha in Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh Large trees lost, 2010/2011 → 2018–2022 11 ± 2% (mean crown 96 m²) Hotspot losses (Telangana, Maharashtra) up to 50%; up to 22 trees/km² Large trees lost, 2018/2019 → 2020–2022 5.3 million (2.7/km²; mean crown 67 m²) Uncertainty of 2018–2022 losses 21% false losses Outside central India, losses rarely exceeded 5–10%. Rainfall in the decade was above average in most areas, so climate was not the main cause. All interviewees confirmed large reductions in mature trees within and along fields, mainly because new boreholes allowed paddy expansion, and because farmers saw field trees as having low benefit and feared that the shade of large crowns such as neem would reduce yields. Several reported more block plantations. Fungi and climate were not perceived as causes. GROSS LOSS, NOT NET CHANGE The study counts only losses of large trees and masks out plantations, so it does not contradict official reports of a net increase in trees outside forests. The concern is that mature, ecologically valuable trees are being replaced by plantations of lower ecological value.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Large farmland trees have thinned considerably across India in about a decade, with severe hotspots in central India. 2. This is unsettling given the emphasis on agroforestry as a natural climate solution; protecting existing trees deserves attention, not only planting. 3. The method can monitor every large tree yearly at national scale, supporting policy, illegal-felling checks and restoration monitoring.


## 6. Limitations

- Small (< ~10 m² crown) and newly planted trees are not detected; net change is not reported.
- No carbon or biomass estimates.
- Only 12 interviews; drivers are indicative.
- Main losses are in central India, not the Varuna basin.

# Carbon sequestration and credit potential of gamhar (Gmelina arborea Roxb.) based agroforestry system for zero carbon emission of India


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Carbon sequestration and credit potential of gamhar (Gmelina arborea Roxb.) based agroforestry system for zero carbon emission of India Abhay Kumar, M. S. Malik, Swati Shabnam, Rakesh Kumar, S. Karmakar, Soumitra Sankar Das and 11 co-authors (full list in the citation)

**Authors:**
Abhay Kumar, M. S. Malik, Swati Shabnam, Rakesh Kumar, S. Karmakar, Soumitra Sankar Das, Kerobim Lakra, Indra Singh, Rikesh Kumar, Asha Kumari Sinha, Sheela Barla, Nargis Kumari, P. R. Oraon, Muneshwar Prasad, Wajid Hasan, Dinesh Mahto, Jeetendra Kumar

**Journal:**
Scientific Reports, vol. 14, article 4828 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 25 July 2023 · Accepted 29 January 2024

**Paper type:**
Research article: two-year field experiment

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-53162-5

**Cite as:**
Kumar, A., Malik, M. S., Shabnam, S., Kumar, R., Karmakar, S., Das, S. S., Lakra, K., Singh, I., Kumar, R., Sinha, A. K., Barla, S., Kumari, N., Oraon, P. R., Prasad, M., Hasan, W., Mahto, D., & Kumar, J. (2024). Carbon sequestration and credit potential of gamhar (Gmelina arborea Roxb.) based agroforestry system for zero carbon emission of India. Scientific Reports, 14, 4828. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-53162-5 Open access article (Scientific Reports, CC BY 4.0). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

A two-year trial at Ranchi compared gamhar (Gmelina arborea) agroforestry with arhar, cowpea-mustard or greengram-mustard intercrops against sole trees and sole crops. Because the trees were only 1–2 years old, sole greengram-mustard gave the highest total carbon stock (7.33 t C/ha, pooled) and credits (26.9 t CO₂/ha), while sole gamhar gave the lowest (0.84 t C/ha). Gamhar + arhar built the most soil carbon. The authors expect gamhar systems to sequester much more as the trees grow.


## 1. Background

The paper cites India's GHG emissions rising from 746.5 Mt CO₂e in 1970 to 3375 Mt CO₂e in 2018, and India's net-zero 2070 target (Panchamrit). Agroforestry is promoted under the National Agroforestry Policy (2014), the Sub-Mission on Agroforestry and the Trees Outside Forests in India (TOFI) programme, which aims to add 2.8 Mha of tree cover and 420 Mt CO₂-eq of sequestration (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To assess the carbon sequestration and carbon credit potential of gamhar-based agroforestry compared with sole gamhar and sole crops.


## 3. What the authors did

The trial was at Birsa Agricultural University, Kanke, Ranchi (625 m altitude; Eastern Plateau and Hill Region) in 2016–17 and 2017–18. Seven treatments (gamhar + arhar; gamhar + cowpea-mustard; gamhar + greengram-mustard; sole gamhar; sole arhar; sole cowpea-mustard; sole greengram-mustard) were laid out in a randomised block design with five replications. Five-month-old gamhar seedlings were planted in June 2016 at 8 × 2.5 m (500 trees/ha). Tree stem volume came from the quarter-girth formula and wood density (530 kg/m³); root biomass was assumed to be 25% of above-ground biomass. Crop biomass was measured by uprooting plants per m². Soil carbon (0–30 cm) = SOC% × depth × bulk density. Carbon was converted to CO₂ to give credits (1 credit = 1 t CO₂), valued at about ₹1,500 (US$20). Emissions from inputs were estimated with the ICAR- IIFSR GHG tool, and net emission = emission − sequestration.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Total (tree + intercrop + soil) carbon, pooled over two years (Table 7) Treatment C stock (t/ha) Credits (t CO₂/ha) Value (US$/ha) Gamhar + arhar 6.68 24.50 490.0 Gamhar + cowpea-mustard 6.79 24.89 497.8 Gamhar + greengram-mustard 6.87 25.21 504.2 Sole gamhar 0.84 3.10 62.0 Sole arhar 5.33 19.56 391.2 Sole cowpea-mustard 7.17 26.30 526.0 Sole greengram-mustard 7.33 26.89 537.8

- Trees: gamhar biomass was slightly higher with intercrops (e.g. +16.5% with arhar in 2016–17), but treatment differences were not significant. Stem made up 50–60% of tree biomass, leaves 19.2– 20%, branches 10.7–12.7%, roots about 20% (by assumption).
- Crops: biomass was lower under trees; sole greengram-mustard had 88.7% more crop carbon than gamhar + arhar (pooled).
- Soil: gamhar + arhar had the highest soil carbon stock, 348.5% above sole gamhar (pooled).
- Net emission: lowest in sole greengram-mustard (760.7% lower than sole gamhar, pooled); negative values mean sequestration exceeded emission. READ WITH CARE The 348.5% gain for gamhar + arhar is for soil carbon, not total carbon. The total stocks (0.84–7.33 t C/ha) are far below a typical 0–30 cm soil carbon stock, so the soil values appear to be increments rather than full stocks (our assessment).

## 5. Conclusions

1. In the first two years, sole greengram-mustard gave the highest total biomass, carbon stock, sequestration, credits and carbon value. 2. Carbon emission from tree components was low and declined each year. 3. Gamhar is fast-growing, so gamhar agroforestry should have high long-term sequestration and support India's tree-cover and net-zero goals.


## 6. Limitations

- Trees were only one to two years old, so agroforestry benefits are understated.
- One site in Jharkhand; root biomass assumed rather than measured.
- Credit price (US$20) is an assumption and varies by market.

# Speaking from experience: Preferences for cooking with biogas in rural India


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Speaking from experience: Preferences for cooking with biogas in rural India Marta Talevi, Subhrendu K. Pattanayak, Ipsita Das, Jessica J. Lewis, Ashok K. Singha

**Authors:**
Marta Talevi, Subhrendu K. Pattanayak, Ipsita Das, Jessica J. Lewis, Ashok K. Singha

**Journal:**
Energy Economics, vol. 107, article 105796 (2022)

**Dates:**
Received 5 February 2021 · Revised 7 December 2021 · Accepted 19 December 2021 · Online 6 January 2022

**Paper type:**
Research article: discrete choice experiment (household survey)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2021.105796

**Cite as:**
Talevi, M., Pattanayak, S. K., Das, I., Lewis, J. J., & Singha, A. K. (2022). Speaking from experience: Preferences for cooking with biogas in rural India. Energy Economics, 107, 105796. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2021.105796 Published version made available under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (LSE Research Online). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

A discrete choice experiment with 503 rural households in Odisha (surveyed 2011–12) found that households will pay a premium for biogas but not for an improved biomass (rocket) stove (mean premium −INR 2,768). The biogas premium depends on experience: INR 7,348 after a good experience, 5,744 after malfunctions and 2,837 with no experience. Households valued smoke reduction (INR 4,785) and fuel efficiency (INR 3,074). The authors recommend adding trials, quality products, maintenance and customer service to subsidies.


## 1. Background

About 2.8 billion people lacked clean cooking access in 2018, and almost one-third of Indians still cook mainly with polluting fuels. Biogas can meet rural cooking needs while reducing fuel and fertiliser costs, pressure on forests, and emissions of PM₂.₅ and methane. Many past biogas programmes produced plants that broke down, so households differ in what they know about the technology.


## 2. Aim of the study

To measure household preferences for biogas and an improved biomass cookstove and their attributes, and to test how past biogas experience and risk and time preferences shape willingness to pay (WTP).


## 3. What the authors did

They surveyed  503 households in 42 villages in 8 districts of Odisha between November 2011 and February  2012,  stratified  by  biogas  experience  (good:  plant  never  broke;  bad:  broken  or  past malfunctions; none). In a discrete choice experiment, respondents chose between a biogas system, a rocket stove and the traditional chulha, described by price (4,000, 7,000 or 10,000 INR), maintenance assistance, smoke and fuel need. A random-parameters logit in WTP space was estimated. Risk aversion

and impatience were measured with hypothetical payment questions; 64% of respondents were classed as risk-averse.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Mean willingness to pay (INR, 2011–12 prices; Table 2) Item Mean WTP Significance Biogas premium, good experience 7,348 p < 0.001 Biogas premium, bad experience 5,744 p < 0.001 Biogas premium, no experience 2,837 p < 0.001 Rocket stove premium −2,768 p < 0.01 Maintenance assistance 609 not significant Smoke reduction 4,785 p < 0.001 Fuel efficiency 3,074 p < 0.001 Values are in 2011–12 rupees; the paper converts 1,000 INR then to about 1,850 INR in 2021. Risk-averse and impatient respondents had lower WTP for the rocket stove; for biogas the gap appeared only among households without experience. The authors note that the WTP distributions overlap in most cases, so 'it is unclear to what extent time and risk preferences matter'. Biogas users tended to be lower- and middle- income households with more livestock.


## 5. Conclusions

1. Households value smoke reduction and fuel efficiency and will pay a premium for biogas, but not for the improved biomass stove. 2. Negative experiences (malfunctions) reduce the value placed on biogas. 3. Biogas uptake could be improved by complementing subsidies with technology trials, good-quality products, maintenance and customer service to reduce uncertainty.


## 6. Limitations

- Data are from 2011–12; prices, LPG access and schemes have changed since.
- Stated preferences, not observed purchases; most respondents were men.
- One state (Odisha); no emission measurements.

# Are households shifting toward cleaner cooking fuel? Empirical evidence from India during 2005–2021


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Are households shifting toward cleaner cooking fuel? Empirical evidence from India during 2005–2021 Raja Rajendra Timilsina, Dil B. Rahut, Madhu Sudan Gautam, Raman Mishra, Tetsushi Sonobe

**Authors:**
Raja Rajendra Timilsina, Dil B. Rahut, Madhu Sudan Gautam, Raman Mishra, Tetsushi Sonobe

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Environmental Economics, vol. 2, article 1137248 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 4 January 2023 · Accepted 3 July 2023 · Published 16 August 2023

**Paper type:**
Original research (econometric analysis of survey data)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/frevc.2023.1137248

**Cite as:**
Timilsina, R. R., Rahut, D. B., Gautam, M. S., Mishra, R., & Sonobe, T. (2023). Are households shifting toward cleaner cooking fuel? Empirical evidence from India during 2005–2021. Frontiers in Environmental Economics, 2, 1137248. https://doi.org/10.3389/frevc.2023.1137248 Open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using three rounds of India's National Family Health Survey (2005–06, 2015–16, 2019–21; 1,276,508 household records), the authors show a clear shift to LPG: rural gas use rose from 11% to 39% and urban from 63% to 86%. Still, 48% of rural households used wood as their main fuel in 2019–21. A multinomial logit model finds that education, wealth, urban location and female headship raise the odds of using LPG, while larger households use more straw and dung.


## 1. Background

Household cooking with firewood, dung, kerosene and straw harms health and adds to emissions. The 'energy ladder' idea says households move to LPG and electricity as they get richer. Little was known about how India's household fuel choices changed over the last two decades.


## 2. Aim of the study

To describe trends in household cooking fuel in India from 2005 to 2021 and identify the factors that drive the choice of fuel.


## 3. What the authors did

They pooled NFHS-3, NFHS-4 and NFHS-5 (1,276,508 households; 71% rural). Households average about five members; 84% of heads are male, with an average age of 48. The main cooking fuel (nine categories) was modelled with a multinomial logit, with wood as the base category, controlling for age, gender, education, household size, wealth, caste, rural location, survey round and state.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Main cooking fuel shares (Section 4.1) Indicator 2005–06 2019–21 Gas, all India ≈35.5% 51.6% Wood, all India 44% ≈38% Gas, rural 11% 39% Wood, rural 68% 48% Gas, urban 63% 86% Wood, urban 17% 8%

- LPG use by households with no education rose from 11% to 17% to 36%; with higher education it was 84%, 78% and 83%.
- In 2019–21, higher-educated rural households used about 60% LPG and 20% wood; urban ones above 90% and below 2%.
- More than 70% of the poorest households use firewood, almost unchanged over time.
- Compared with 2005–06, the 2019–21 odds ratios for LPG, electricity and biogas were 19.0, 17.2 and 5.1. CORRECTION: GENDER The abstract says female-headed households have been unable to switch to LPG, but the regression (Section 4.2) and conclusion find that female-headed households are more likely to use LPG and less likely to use dung. This summary follows the regression result.

## 5. Conclusions

1. A large number of Indian households switched toward LPG and electricity between 2005 and 2021. 2. Rural, the poorest and uneducated households lag behind. 3. Policies for income growth and education can reduce household-energy emissions; LPG and electricity subsidies should target poor households.


## 6. Limitations

- Only the main cooking fuel is recorded, so fuel stacking is not captured.
- Repeated cross-sections, not a panel; associations, not causal effects.
- National analysis with no emission estimates.

**Authors:**

**Dates:**
Received 18 June 2020 · Accepted 9 December 2020

**Paper type:**
Research article: on-farm paired trials

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-79883-x

**Cite as:**
Sapkota, T. B., Jat, M. L., Rana, D. S., Khatri-Chhetri, A., Jat, H. S., Bijarniya, D., Sutaliya, J. M., Kumar, M., Singh, L. K., Jat, R. K., Kalvaniya, K., Prasad, G., Sidhu, H. S., Rai, M., Satyanarayana, T., & Majumdar, K. (2021). Crop nutrient management using Nutrient Expert improves yield, increases farmers’ income and reduces greenhouse gas emissions. Scientific Reports, 11, 1564. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-79883-x Open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Across 1,594 paired on-farm trials in Punjab, Haryana and Bihar (2013–14 to 2016–17), Nutrient Expert (NE) fertiliser advice cut N use by about 18% and modelled global warming potential by about 2.5% in rice and 12–20% in wheat compared with farmers' practice, while raising yields by about 4–12%. More than 80% of farmers gained yield and income, although NE's extra potash raised fertiliser cost for about half of them. Scaled to all of India, the authors estimate 13.9 Mt more grain, 1.44 Mt less N and about


### 5.24 Mt CO₂e less GHG per year (the abstract says 5.34 Mt).


## 1. Background

Fertiliser N is a major source of N₂O. India uses 14% of the world's fertiliser but has one of the lowest nutrient use efficiencies, and rice and wheat use half of India's fertiliser. Nutrient Expert (NE) is a decision-support tool that gives field-specific nutrient advice with or without a soil test, but it had not been tested on many farms.


## 2. Aim of the study

To test whether NE-based site-specific nutrient management raises yield and income and lowers GHG emissions in rice and wheat compared with farmers' own fertiliser practice (FFP) across the Indo- Gangetic Plains (IGP).


## 3. What the authors did

Over four seasons (2013–14 to 2016–17) they ran 1,594 paired trials: 1,094 in Haryana, 245 in Punjab and 251 in Bihar (730 rice, 864 wheat). Each farm had an NE plot and an FFP plot. Yield was measured from three 3 m² quadrats per plot. GHG emissions were estimated per plot with the CCAFS Mitigation Options Tool, not measured in the field.


## 4. Main findings

- NE cut N use (about 10% in East IGP and 25% in West IGP) and P₂O₅ use (except West IGP rice), but increased K₂O.
- NE out-yielded FFP in all 135 East IGP rice pairs, 78% of 116 East IGP wheat pairs, 83% of 595 West IGP rice pairs and 91% of 748 West IGP wheat pairs.
- GWP fell by about 2.5% in rice and 12–20% in wheat; cuts were larger in West IGP and where farmers used more N and P₂O₅.
- Fertiliser cost rose for 55% of rice and 51% of wheat farmers, but yield gains generally outweighed it; revenue gains were larger where farmers used under 125 kg N/ha. Table A. Range of emissions across trials (Results, pp. 3–4) Crop GWP (kg CO₂e/ha) Intensity (kg CO₂e/t) Rice 2,463 – 5,482 509 – 1,606 Wheat 287 – 2,463 71 – 769 CHECK ON THE NATIONAL FIGURE The national GHG saving assumes the upper wheat value (20%) and is 0.61 Mt (rice) + 4.63 Mt (wheat) = 5.24 Mt CO₂e per year, as given in the Discussion and Conclusion. The abstract's 5.34 Mt does not match these parts.

## 5. Conclusions

1. NE-based nutrient management raises yields and income for most farmers while cutting N use and GHG emissions. 2. Benefits depend on crop, agro-ecology, soil and the farmer's current fertiliser rate. 3. NE is practical for smallholders where soil testing is hard, and could be scaled through extension and the Soil Health Card Scheme.


## 6. Limitations

- Emissions are modelled with CCAFS-MOT, not measured.
- No trials in Uttar Pradesh; Bihar is the closest site to the Varuna basin.
- National totals assume trial results apply to all rice and wheat land and the upper wheat value.
- Extra K₂O use has cost and import implications that were not studied.

#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Long-term zero tillage with residue retention boosts yield, enhances energy efficiency, and mitigates greenhouse gas emissions in the western Indo-Gangetic rice–wheat systems Ved Prakash Chaudhary, Chetankumar Prakash Sawant, Ajita Gupta, Rahul Gautam, Abhijit Khadatkar, Ajit Pralhad Magar, Goraksha C. Wakchaure, Vijay Kumar, Rahul Chaudhary

**Authors:**
Ved Prakash Chaudhary, Chetankumar Prakash Sawant, Ajita Gupta, Rahul Gautam, Abhijit Khadatkar, Ajit Pralhad Magar, Goraksha C. Wakchaure, Vijay Kumar, Rahul Chaudhary

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, vol. 9, article 1672467 (2025)

**Dates:**
Received 24 July 2025 · Accepted 29 August 2025 · Published 23 September 2025

**Paper type:**
Original research: 15-year field experiment

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2025.1672467

**Cite as:**
Chaudhary, V. P., Sawant, C. P., Gupta, A., Gautam, R., Khadatkar, A., Magar, A. P., Wakchaure, G. C., Kumar, V., & Chaudhary, R. (2025). Long-term zero tillage with residue retention boosts yield, enhances energy efficiency, and mitigates greenhouse gas emissions in the western Indo-Gangetic rice–wheat systems. Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 9, 1672467. https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2025.1672467 Open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

A 15-year experiment (2006–07 to 2020–21) at Modipuram, UP compared four rice and five wheat establishment methods. Zero-till direct-seeded rice followed by Happy Seeder wheat with residue (ZTDSR-THSW + R) used the least energy (47,110 vs 65,830 MJ/ha for puddled rice + tilled wheat), had the highest energy use efficiency (13.6) and 53–54% lower GWP, with comparable system yield. The GWP cut comes mostly from dropping puddled rice, because methane was assumed negligible in direct- seeded rice; emissions were estimated from emission factors, not measured.


## 1. Background

Puddled transplanted rice (PTR) and conventionally tilled wheat (CTW) dominate the Indo-Gangetic rice– wheat system. They use much energy, emit GHGs and degrade soil. Conservation agriculture (CA), with zero tillage and residue retention, may save energy and cut emissions.


## 2. Aim of the study

To evaluate the long-term effects of rice and wheat establishment methods on yield, energy use, carbon indices and GHG emissions in the rice–wheat system.


## 3. What the authors did

At ICAR-IIFSR, Modipuram (upper IGP; farm under CA since 1998), a split–split plot experiment with three replicates ran from 2006–07 to 2020–21. Main plots were four rice methods (ZTDSR, drum-seeded DSDSR, machine-transplanted puddled PMTR, puddled PTR); sub-plots were five wheat methods (zero-till ZTW, Turbo Happy Seeder with residue THSW + R, bed planter BPW, rotary till RTW, conventional CTW). Energy budgets covered all inputs. GWP = N₂O × 298 + CH₄ × 34 + CO₂ was estimated with emission factors (Lal 2004 and others); CH₄ was counted only for puddled rice.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Selected systems (Tables 3 and 4, 15-year means) System Energy (MJ/ha) Yield (kg/ha) GWP (kg CO₂e/ha) ZTDSR-THSW + R 47,110 10,744 5,377 ZTDSR-ZTW 47,838 10,715 5,354 DSDSR-CTW 57,949 10,555 6,041 PTR-THSW + R 58,373 11,298 11,310 PTR-CTW 65,830 11,083 11,688

- Fertiliser (27–37%), electricity (22–28.5%) and irrigation water (21–25%) were the largest energy inputs; irrigation was 45–53% of energy by operation.
- Direct-seeded rice with conventional wheat used 14–21% less energy than puddled rice with conventional wheat; ZTDSR-THSW + R used 28% less than PTR-CTW (computed).
- Zero-till combinations had 53–54% lower GWP than PTR-CTW and PMTR-CTW; wheat tillage alone changed GWP by under 5%.
- Interaction effects on yield and energy were not statistically significant. CORRECTION: CARBON INDICES The abstract's 'carbon efficiency ratio (11.43)' is the carbon sustainability index in Table 4; the CER is 13.43. Neither matches the paper's own formulas (8,907 ÷ 2,293 ≈ 3.9), so these indices should not be reused.

## 5. Conclusions

1. ZTDSR with zero-till or Happy Seeder wheat was the most energy-efficient and lowest-GWP system. 2. System productivity stayed comparable despite slightly lower ZTDSR rice yields. 3. DSR plus zero-till wheat with residue management is a viable climate-smart pathway for the IGP.


## 6. Limitations

- Research farm in western UP, not farmers' fields in eastern UP.
- GHG emissions estimated with general emission factors, not measured; CH₄ from DSR assumed negligible.
- Carbon index values are internally inconsistent.
- Access to Happy Seeders and zero-till drills may be limited in villages.

# GHG emissions and carbon footprint in wheat cultivation practices in Bihar state of India


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

GHG emissions and carbon footprint in wheat cultivation practices in Bihar state of India Ram Pal, Sanjay Kumar Patel, Prem Kumar Sundaram, Ratnesh Kumar Jha, Pawan Jeet, Abdus Sattar, Sanjay Kumar

**Authors:**
Ram Pal, Sanjay Kumar Patel, Prem Kumar Sundaram, Ratnesh Kumar Jha, Pawan Jeet, Abdus Sattar, Sanjay Kumar

**Journal:**
Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, vol. 9, article 1661999 (2025)

**Dates:**
Received 21 July 2025 · Accepted 15 October 2025 · Published 19 November 2025

**Paper type:**
Original research: farmer survey with input-based life-cycle assessment

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2025.1661999

**Cite as:**
Pal, R., Patel, S. K., Sundaram, P. K., Jha, R. K., Jeet, P., Sattar, A., & Kumar, S. (2025). GHG emissions and carbon footprint in wheat cultivation practices in Bihar state of India. Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 9, 1661999. https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2025.1661999 Open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

A 2022–23 survey of 1,168 wheat farmers in three Bihar districts compared 12 conventional-tillage and 6 no-till practices using input-based emission factors. No-till wheat had lower input emissions (as low as 1,746 kg CO₂e/ha, NT-2), higher yields (up to 5,268 kg/ha) and positive carbon sustainability index values. Chemical fertilisers made up 74–83% of emissions. However, the paper's headline totals, carbon offsets and CSI values disagree between the abstract, text and tables, so its direction of results is more reliable than its single figures.


## 1. Background

India is the world's second-largest wheat producer. Machinery, diesel, irrigation, fertiliser and plant protection all add to wheat's GHG emissions, so practices need to be judged on both yield and environmental cost. In the survey districts, no-till wheat was promoted under Bihar's Climate Resilient Agriculture programme.


## 2. Aim of the study

To compare conventional-tillage and no-till wheat in Bihar for CO₂-equivalent emissions, energy sources, carbon offset potential and the carbon sustainability index (CSI).


## 3. What the authors did

They interviewed 1,168 farmers in Begusarai (Zone I, 423), Madhepura (Zone II, 395) and Buxar (Zone III, 350) in 2022–23. Practices were grouped into CP-1 to CP-12 (rotavator or disc tillage, broadcast sowing) and NT-1 to NT-6 (zero-till seed-cum-fertiliser drill), differing in weed pressure and harvest method.

Inputs were multiplied by emission factors (Table 3) within a farm-gate boundary. Carbon offset was based on collected straw; CSI = (offset − emission) ÷ emission.


## 4. Main findings

- Fertilisers were the main source (74–83% of emissions), followed by diesel; indirect energy made up 81–88% and non-renewable energy 91–93%.
- No-till practices had the lowest input emissions (NT-2: 1,745.66 kg CO₂e/ha).
- Yield ranged from 3,575 kg/ha (CP-1) to 5,268 kg/ha (NT-3 and NT-6); carbon footprint from about 0.50 to 0.82 kg CO₂e/kg grain, highest in CP-1.
- All no-till practices had positive CSI in Table 7; CP-1 had the lowest (−0.29). Table A. Conflicting values within the paper Item Abstract Text / tables Emission range (kg CO₂e/ha) 1,746–2,239 Max CP-3 2,331 (text); 2,490–3,075 (Discussion) Highest CSI NT-4: 0.079 NT-3: 0.13 (text); NT-3: 0.17 (Table 7) Lowest CSI CP-1: −0.363 CP-1: −0.29 (text and Table 7) Highest carbon offset NT-6: 2,597 NT-3 and NT-6: 3,054 (Table 7) DATA CHECK In Table 4, 7 of 18 printed totals (CP-5, CP-6, CP-8, CP-9, CP-12, NT-3, NT-6) do not equal the sum of their direct and indirect parts. Only the direction of the results (no-till lower) is consistent throughout.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Conventional tillage wheat is more emission-intensive, mainly because of fertiliser and diesel use. 2. No-till wheat lowers emissions, raises yield and improves carbon sustainability. 3. Policymakers should support no-till and better nutrient management in Bihar.


## 6. Limitations

- One season of survey (recall) data; no field measurements.
- Input-based only: soil carbon change and field N₂O are not fully measured.
- Many internal inconsistencies in totals and indices.
- Bihar, not Uttar Pradesh; practice variants mix several factors.

# Mapping and Monitoring of Land Use/Land Cover Transformation Using Geospatial Techniques in Varanasi City Development Region, India


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Mapping and Monitoring of Land Use/Land Cover Transformation Using Geospatial Techniques in Varanasi City Development Region, India Atul K. Tiwari, Anindita Pal, Rolee Kanchan

**Authors:**
Atul K. Tiwari, Anindita Pal, Rolee Kanchan

**Journal:**
Nature Environment and Pollution Technology, vol. 23, no. 1, pp. 365–379 (2024)

**Dates:**
Received 14 July 2023 · Revised 22 August 2023 · Accepted 21 September 2023

**Paper type:**
Original research: remote sensing land use/land cover change

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.46488/NEPT.2024.v23i01.031

**Cite as:**
Tiwari, A. K., Pal, A., & Kanchan, R. (2024). Mapping and monitoring of land use/land cover transformation using geospatial techniques in Varanasi City Development Region, India. Nature Environment and Pollution Technology, 23(1), 365–379. https://doi.org/10.46488/NEPT.2024.v23i01.031 Open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using Landsat images from 1991, 2001, 2011 and 2022 classified with random forest in Google Earth Engine, the authors mapped seven land classes in the Varanasi City Development Region (673 km²). Built-up land rose 507.8% (29.97 to 182.16 km², about six times), with growth speeding up each decade. Agricultural land fell by a net 91.8 km² (72.9% to 59.3% of the area), and 114.8 km² of farmland was converted to built-up land. Overall map accuracy was 86.8–92.8%.


## 1. Background

Economic development and population growth drive land use and land cover (LULC) change. Varanasi, between the Varuna and Assi rivers, is one of the world's oldest cities and a growing religious and service centre, so its surrounding farmland and green cover are under pressure.


## 2. Aim of the study

To analyse the pattern, dynamics and transformation of LULC in the Varanasi City Development Region (VCDR) for 1991, 2001, 2011 and 2022 using Google Earth Engine and machine learning.


## 3. What the authors did

May images from Landsat-5 TM (1991, 2001, 2011) and Landsat-9 OLI-2 (2022) at 30 m were classified into seven classes with a random forest classifier in Google Earth Engine, using stratified training polygons checked against ESRI and NRSC land cover. Change matrices were produced in SAGA GIS. Accuracy was assessed with 735 reference points per year (105 per class), using user, producer and overall accuracy and the Kappa coefficient.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Land cover in 1991 and 2022 (Tables 9 and 10) Class 1991 (km²) 2022 (km²) Change Built-up 29.97 182.16 +152.19 (+507.8%) Agricultural land 491.16 399.37 −91.79 (−18.7%) Barren land 49.92 9.78 −40.14 (−82.4%) Fallow land 34.95 25.80 −9.15 (−26.2%) Vegetation cover 43.94 34.20 −9.74 (−22.2%) Water bodies 10.52 10.01 −0.51 (−4.8%)

- Built-up land grew by 37.4 km² (1991–2001), 43.38 km² (2001–2011) and 71.41 km² (2011–2022).
- Of the 2022 built-up area, 114.8 km² was farmland, 14.81 km² barren land and 12.93 km² vegetation cover in 1991 (Table 14).
- Vegetation cover declined to 2011 but recovered slightly by 2022 (30.4 to 34.2 km²).
- Growth was concentrated in and around the municipal area and along roads and railways.
- Overall accuracy: 91.83% (1991), 87.89% (2001), 86.80% (2011), 92.79% (2022); Kappa 0.846–0.916. NOTE ON '507.8%' A 507.8% increase means the 2022 built-up area is about 6.1 times the 1991 area, not five times. The 114.8 km² figure is a gross transfer of farmland to built-up; the net loss of farmland was 91.8 km² because some other land became farmland.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Built-up land in VCDR expanded rapidly, mostly at the expense of fertile farmland. 2. This trend is unsustainable and risks food scarcity, environmental degradation and lower quality of urban life. 3. The results give planners a scientific basis for sustainable land use planning in VCDR and other cities.


## 6. Limitations

- Covers the city development region, not the full Varuna basin.
- 30 m resolution misses scattered trees and small plots.
- Only four dates, all in May.
- No carbon stock or emission estimates.

**Authors:**
Sarah Duddigan, Liz J. Shaw, Tom Sizmur, Dharmendar Gogu, Zakir Hussain, Kiranmai Jirra, Hamika Kaliki, Rahul Sanka, Mohammad Sohail, Reshma Soma, Vijay Thallam, Haripriya Vattikuti, Chris D. Collins

**Journal:**
Agronomy for Sustainable Development, vol. 43, no. 2, article 31 (2023)

**Dates:**
Accepted 6 March 2023

**Paper type:**
Research article: replicated on-farm field experiments

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s13593-023-00884-x

**Cite as:**
Duddigan, S., Shaw, L. J., Sizmur, T., Gogu, D., Hussain, Z., Jirra, K., Kaliki, H., Sanka, R., Sohail, M., Soma, R., Thallam, V., Vattikuti, H., & Collins, C. D. (2023). Natural farming improves crop yield in SE India when compared to conventional or organic systems by enhancing soil quality. Agronomy for Sustainable Development, 43(2), 31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13593-023-00884-x Open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

On 28 farms in six districts of Andhra Pradesh (2019–2020), side-by-side no-till plots compared Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF), organic and conventional farming. Across 44 farm experiments, ZBNF yield z-scores were higher (0.58 vs −0.34 organic and −0.24 conventional), but the gain was significant only for groundnut and tomato and varied by district. ZBNF plots were wetter and cooler and had more earthworms, likely because only they were mulched. Most soil nutrients did not differ from conventional, and soil organic carbon did not change.


## 1. Background

India's roughly 159 Mha of arable land supports the world's second-largest farm output, but heavy synthetic fertiliser and pesticide use harms water, health and farm finances. Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF) is a grassroots movement backed by Andhra Pradesh's extension programme, but its yield claims lacked controlled, statistically tested evidence.


## 2. Aim of the study

To test whether ZBNF changes yield and soil properties compared with organic and conventional farming, and to test three ZBNF claims: better soil moisture, enough nutrients without fertiliser, and more soil biological activity.


## 3. What the authors did

Three 6 × 6 m plots were set up on each of 28 farms across six districts and run in Kharif 2019, Rabi 2019–20 and Kharif 2020. Because of Covid-19, only 3 farms took part in all three seasons, 15 in two and 10 in one. ZBNF used Bijamrita, Jiwamrita (desi cow dung and urine) and mulch; organic used purchased manure and vermicompost without mulch; conventional used synthetic inputs. No plot was tilled. Yields were z-transformed to compare across crops and analysed with mixed-effects models.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Yield z-scores across 44 farm experiments (Abstract, Fig. 2) Treatment Mean z-score Note ZBNF 0.58 ± 0.08 Significantly higher overall (p < 0.05) Conventional −0.24 ± 0.07 — Organic −0.34 ± 0.06 —

- The ZBNF effect was significant only for groundnut and tomato; groundnut kernel yield was about 30–40% higher.
- ZBNF beat both alternatives in Prakasam, Nellore and Kadapa; only conventional in Krishna; only organic in Anantapur. In Visakhapatnam conventional yields were higher but not significantly.
- ZBNF plots had higher soil moisture, lower soil temperature (not in every season) and more earthworms in all seasons.
- P, K and micronutrients mostly did not differ; in season 3 conventional plots had more extractable N.
- Soil organic carbon and bulk density did not change with treatment. CAUTION Only ZBNF plots were mulched, so the yield benefit cannot be split between mulch and the cow-based inputs. Results come from short, uneven participation (3 farms in all seasons) and mostly vegetables, pulses and groundnut, not rice or wheat.

## 5. Conclusions

1. ZBNF had no yield penalty in any district studied, and some districts saw a yield gain. 2. The benefit likely comes from mulch: wetter, cooler soil and more earthworms. 3. Long-term and landscape-scale trials, and tests of each ZBNF input, are needed.


## 6. Limitations

- Three seasons with uneven farm participation.
- Crop and district are confounded; benefit significant in two crops only.
- No GHG measurements; no rice–wheat data.
- All treatments untilled, unlike most farmer practice.

**Authors:**
Neha Kalonia, Dipti Grover, Ajay Kumar Mishra, Manas Ranjan Sahoo

**Journal:**
Plant Science Today, vol. 13, special issue 5, pp. 1–11 (2026)

**Dates:**
Received 19 March 2026 · Accepted 29 May 2026 · Online 22 July 2026

**Paper type:**
Research article: farm survey with Cool Farm Tool modelling

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.14719/pst.14598

**Cite as:**
Kalonia, N., Grover, D., Mishra, A. K., & Sahoo, M. R. (2026). Productivity-emission trade-offs across conventional, organic and natural farming in rice-wheat systems of northwest India. Plant Science Today, 13(sp5), 1–11. https://doi.org/10.14719/pst.14598 Open access under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

On 27 rice–wheat farms in Kaithal, Kurukshetra and Karnal (Haryana), 9 each under conventional, organic and natural farming, emissions for 2023 and 2024 were estimated with the Cool Farm Tool. Compared with conventional farming, rice emissions were about 32% lower under both organic and natural farming, with yield losses of 18% and 9%. In wheat, emission cuts were small (9.4% and 7.2%) while yields fell 16% and 40%. Natural farming gave the best balance in rice; organic did better in wheat.


## 1. Background

Rice-based and nitrogen-intensive cropping are the main sources of agricultural GHG in India, through CH₄ from flooded fields and N₂O from fertilised soils. Organic and natural farming may cut emissions, but lower yields can raise emissions per kg of grain, so productivity and emissions must be judged together.


## 2. Aim of the study

To compare GHG emissions and yields under conventional, organic and natural farming in the rice–wheat system of north-west India.


## 3. What the authors did

Twenty-seven farms (9 per system, at least 5 years under the system) were selected across three districts in one agro-climatic zone. Farmer interviews, yield records and 0–15 cm soil samples were collected for 2023 and 2024. Emissions were estimated with the Cool Farm Tool from activity data on fertiliser, residues, tillage, irrigation and energy. Natural farming inputs were represented through management proxies because the tool cannot model microbial inputs.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Change relative to conventional farming (Discussion, p. 8) Crop and system GHG Yield Ratio Rice, organic −31.9% −18.0% 1.77 Rice, natural −31.6% −8.99% 3.52 Wheat, organic −9.35% −16.38% 0.57 Wheat, natural −7.18% −40.0% 0.18

- Rice was the dominant source of emissions in all systems, because of flooding, CH₄ and residue handling.
- Kurukshetra had the highest emissions (36.16% of the total), linked to intensive rice and groundwater pumping.
- Emission intensity was higher for rice (about 0.75–1.60 kg CO₂e/kg) than wheat (below 0.65 kg CO₂e/kg).
- Yield variability increased from conventional to organic to natural farming. CORRECTION Earlier notes read the abstract as natural farming cutting emissions by about 62% (rice) and 80% (wheat). The Discussion states the reductions are 31.6% (rice) and 7.18% (wheat) for natural farming and 31.9% and 9.35% for organic. The abstract's 83.47% and 36.5% 'conventional emissions' are not explained.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Conventional farming maximises yield but has the highest emissions. 2. Natural farming gives the best productivity–emission balance in rice; organic farming does better in wheat. 3. Mitigation should be crop- and region-specific, combining residue management, less tillage, optimised N and water-saving irrigation.


## 6. Limitations

- Emissions are modelled with the Cool Farm Tool, not measured.
- Only two years and 27 farms; observational design.
- Several reported numbers conflict (district ranking, figure values, abstract percentages).
- Haryana, not eastern UP.

# Driving sustainable agroforestry through carbon credit-based policies: Realities and perspectives


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Driving sustainable agroforestry through carbon credit-based policies: Realities and perspectives Nyong Princely Awazi

**Authors:**
Nyong Princely Awazi

**Journal:**
Natural Resources Conservation and Research, vol. 8, no. 1, article 10184 (2025)

**Dates:**
Received 8 November 2024 · Accepted 2 January 2025 · Online 25 January 2025

**Paper type:**
Systematic review of 150 empirical studies

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.24294/nrcr10184

**Cite as:**
Awazi, N. P. (2025). Driving sustainable agroforestry through carbon credit-based policies: Realities and perspectives. Natural Resources Conservation and Research, 8(1), 10184. https://doi.org/10.24294/nrcr10184 Open access under the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY 4.0) license. Content in this summary is taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

This review of 150 empirical studies argues that carbon credit policies, which have focused on forests, wetlands and heavy industry, should include agroforestry. It sets out three credit types: removed emissions (tree planting), avoided emissions (not cutting trees) and reduced emissions (energy-efficient technology). Credit income could offset the cost of establishing trees, the main barrier for smallholders. India's 2014 National Agroforestry Policy, the world's first, already lists carbon credit schemes as a pathway. The review is qualitative and gives no prices or incomes.


## 1. Background

Carbon taxes and cap-and-trade can burden developing countries, and carbon accounting suffers from double counting  and weak verification. Carbon  credit policies have mostly  supported  forests and wetlands, even though agroforestry is a climate-smart practice used by many smallholders.


## 2. Aim of the study

To examine how carbon credit-based policies can drive sustainable agroforestry, especially in developing countries.


## 3. What the author did

A systematic review of 150 English-language empirical papers from Google Scholar, Web of Science and Scopus. The review describes the national agroforestry policies of India and Nepal, classifies emissions trading and credit schemes, summarises the main credit types, and lists credit schemes that promote agroforestry by country.


## 4. Main findings

- The most common schemes are government-led: China's CCER, the EU ETS and California's Global Warming Solutions Act, aimed at transport, steel and cement.
- Three credit types guide policy: avoided emissions (not cutting trees), reduced emissions (energy- efficient technology) and removed emissions (tree planting, carbon capture).
- Agroforestry fits removal and avoided-emission credits; examples come from India, Nepal, Ghana, Kenya, Costa Rica, the USA and the EU (Table 4).
- Establishment and management costs are a key barrier that credit income could offset.
- Challenges include weak monitoring and verification, double counting, permanence and smallholder access to markets. INDIA'S POLICY India's National Agroforestry Policy (2014) was the world's first. Its pathways include secure land tenure, certified planting material, simpler rules for farm trees, insurance and credit, and establishing carbon credit schemes for agroforestry.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Agroforestry should be brought into carbon credit schemes. 2. Using all three credit types would encourage smallholders to adopt agroforestry by offsetting its costs. 3. Co-benefits include jobs, technology transfer, energy access, livelihoods and better environmental quality; robust verification and market access are needed.


## 6. Limitations

- Qualitative: no credit prices, incomes or carbon amounts.
- English-only search in three databases; single author.
- Verification costs are named as a challenge but not quantified.

#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using the GEOS-Chem adjoint model for 2003–2019, the authors estimate that crop residue burning in India caused 44,000–98,000 premature deaths a year from PM₂.₅, costing about 23 billion USD a year. Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh account for 67–90% of the deaths, and six Punjab districts alone for 40%. Fire-related exposure came 64% from Punjab, 11% from Haryana and 5.7% from Uttar Pradesh. Burning two hours earlier in November in Punjab could avert about 9,600 deaths a year on average.


## 1. Background

PM₂.₅ exposure causes more than four million premature deaths a year worldwide, 10–25% of them in India. India produces about 500 Mt of crop residue a year and burns about 100 Mt, mainly after the wheat harvest (April–May) and the rice harvest (October–November) in north-west India. Bans and fines have had limited effect.


## 2. Aim of the study

To estimate how agricultural burning affects air quality and health across India, and to quantify the benefit of targeted district-level and timing-based actions.


## 3. What the authors did

GFED v4.1s burning emissions were combined with district crop data. The GEOS-Chem adjoint model computed how the PM₂.₅ exposure of India's population responds to burning at each location and hour from 2003 to 2019. An Integrated Exposure Response function gave premature deaths, and an India- adjusted value of statistical life gave monetised cost. Scenarios tested 1% emission cuts by district and shifts in burning time.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Key results (2003–2019 averages) Indicator Value Premature deaths per year 44,000–98,000 Monetised cost per year 23 bn USD (95% CI 3.5–53) Added population-weighted PM₂.₅ 6.7 µg/m³ Exposure share: Punjab / Haryana / UP 64% / 11% / 5.7% Six Punjab districts 40% of impacts; 27,000 deaths; 9.0 bn USD Burning 2 h earlier in November (Punjab) About 9,600 deaths averted; 3.2 bn USD

- Post-monsoon (rice) burning gave 64% and pre-monsoon (wheat) burning 28% of the added exposure.
- Punjab's impact was six times Haryana's, partly because Haryana grows more basmati rice, whose straw is used.
- Sangrur, Patiala and Ludhiana provide two-thirds of the benefit achievable in Punjab.
- The cost rose from 29% to 40% of India's total health expenditure between 2003 and 2019.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Residue burning imposes a large and growing health cost on India. 2. A small number of districts and burning times could be prioritised for the greatest benefit. 3. Targeted, potentially low-cost actions can complement mechanisation, pending cost-effectiveness and feasibility studies.


## 6. Limitations

- Covers primary PM₂.₅ only; no ozone and no greenhouse gases.
- The IER function was not developed for India and treats all PM₂.₅ as equally toxic.
- A single assumed daily burning profile; the timing benefit needs field checks.
- No village- or Varanasi-level results.

Review article

**Cite as:**
Kaur, M., Malik, D. P., Malhi, G. S., Sardana, V., Bolan, N. S., Lal, R., & Siddique, K. H. M. (2022). Rice residue management in the Indo-Gangetic Plains for climate and food security. A review. Agronomy for Sustainable Development, 42, 92. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13593-022-00817-0 Open access (© The Author(s) 2022). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

India grows paddy on 43.8 Mha, producing 118.43 Mt of grain and about 165.8 Mt of straw. About 50 Mt of straw is burned each year, releasing about 1.5 Mt of particulates and 150 Mt of CO₂. The review shows that in-situ options (Happy Seeder, SMS, chopper-spreader, plough) and ex-situ uses (biofuel, biochar, power, bales) are profitable and better for soil, but adoption is slow. Uttar Pradesh produces the largest share of India's kharif (19.1%) and rabi (17%) crop biomass.


## 1. Background

Burning is the most common way to clear rice residue because it is simple and cheap, mechanical harvesting has spread, the gap between rice harvest and wheat sowing is short, and straw has few viable uses. About 50 Mt of rice straw is burned each year, nearly half in north-west India in October– November (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To review how residue burning affects the environment and health, and how in-situ and ex-situ management can cut pollution and improve soil health, crop yield and farm income.


## 3. What the authors did

A narrative review of farmers' practices and perceptions, the claimed benefits of burning (disease and weed control), its harms (pollution, health, soil), in-situ technologies, ex-situ uses and government interventions.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Key figures reported in the review Item Value Rice area and grain (2019–20)


### 43.8 Mha; 118.43 Mt

Straw (about 1.4 Mg per Mg grain)


### 165.8 Mt

Rice straw burned per year About 50 Mt Emissions from burning About 1.5 Mt particulates; 150 Mt CO₂ UP share of kharif / rabi biomass 19.1% / 17% SMS + Happy Seeder investment US$3,610 (US$1,805 subsidised)

- Farmers mostly remove residue (about 37%), then mulch with the Happy Seeder (31%), rotavator (14%) or super seeder (7.7%) (one survey, p. 5).
- In one Punjab survey, over 90% of farmers agreed the Happy Seeder saves water, labour and fuel and 88% that it cuts air pollution, but only 67.1% agreed it raises short-term yield (p. 13).
- Incorporation or mulching improves soil physical, chemical and biological properties more than removal.
- Retaining rice residue could cut CO₂ by 150 Mt and add 240 Mt C of SOC a year, a cited estimate (Chen et al. 2019) that is not India-specific.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Rice residue burning harms climate, air, health and soil. 2. In-situ management is profitable and improves soil health. 3. Ex-situ uses add value and cut pollution; both should be promoted.


## 6. Limitations

- A review: numbers come from many sources and years.
- Most field data are from Punjab and Haryana, not eastern UP.
- Machine costs and subsidies vary by region and time.

**Authors:**

Venkatramanan, V., Shah, S., Rai, A. K., & Prasad, R. (2021). Nexus between crop residue burning, bioeconomy and sustainable development goals over north-western India. Frontiers in Energy Research, 8, 614212. https://doi.org/10.3389/fenrg.2020.614212 Open access, Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using the IPCC (1996) formula R = P × N × D × B × F, the authors estimate that India generated 516.8 Mt of dry crop residue in 2017–18 and burned 116.3 Mt, releasing about 176.1 Tg CO₂, 313.9 Gg CH₄, 8.14 Gg N₂O, 453.4 Gg PM₂.₅ and 935.9 Gg PM₁₀. Wheat, rice and sugarcane give about 80% of the burning. The burned amount rests on the IPCC default that 25% of all residue is burned. The paper proposes a four-pronged bioeconomy model to end burning.


## 1. Background

Residue burning in north-west India causes air pollution, health problems, greenhouse gas emissions and loss of soil organic matter. It continues despite the 2014 National Policy for Management of Crop Residues, partly because the rice–wheat turnaround is short.


## 2. Aim of the study

To  estimate  residue  burning  and  its  emissions  for  India,  recommend  crop  residue  management interventions, and propose a residue management–bioeconomy model.


## 3. What the authors did

Crop production for eight crop groups from 1950–51 to 2017–18 was combined with crop-specific residue ratios and dry-matter fractions, an IPCC default burned fraction of 0.25 and burn efficiency of 0.9 (Equation 1.1, Table 1). Emissions were dry matter burned × emission factor.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Estimates for 2017–18 (Tables 2–3) Item Value Residue generated (fresh / dry)


### 640.6 Mt / 516.8 Mt

Dry matter burned


### 116.3 Mt

CO₂ / CO


### 176.1 Tg / 10.7 Tg

CH₄ / N₂O


### 313.9 Gg / 8.14 Gg

PM₂.₅ / PM₁₀


### 453.4 Gg / 935.9 Gg

CH₄ + N₂O as CO₂e 9,114.8 Gg

- Residue burned rose from 18 Mt (1950–51) to 116 Mt (2017–18); decadal growth averaged 32%, and 45% in the 1980s.
- Wheat (33.6 Mt), rice (32.7 Mt) and sugarcane (30.1 Mt) give about 80% of burned dry matter.
- Particulate emissions rose 137% between 1980–81 and 2017–18. DATA CHECK The Discussion cites about 0.027 Gt CO₂e for burning, whereas Table 3's CH₄ and N₂O total about 9.1 Tg CO₂e. Use the table values.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Residue generation is rising with intensification and mechanisation. 2. The estimates can be a proxy for a national inventory of burning pollutants. 3. A four-pronged bioeconomy model (smart farming, waste bioeconomy, capacity building, policy) can cut burning and support several SDGs.


## 6. Limitations

- One burned fraction (25%) for all crops and states, from IPCC 1996.
- No state or district breakdown despite the north-west focus.
- The bioeconomy model is conceptual, without costs.

Review article

Dhanda, S., Yadav, A., Yadav, D. B., & Chauhan, B. S. (2022). Emerging issues and potential opportunities in the rice–wheat cropping system of north-western India. Frontiers in Plant Science, 13, 832683. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2022.832683 Open access, Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY). Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The rice–wheat system (9.2 Mha in India) is stagnating in north-west India because of soil decline, groundwater fall (8.91 m in Punjab, 2000–2019), labour shortage, residue burning (11.3 Mt of paddy straw in Punjab and Haryana) and greenhouse gases. The review shows that dry direct-seeded rice saves 11–18% water and 11–66% labour, and cited Punjab data show its methane at 0.1–0.3 vs 0.8–1.9 t CO₂e/ha for puddled rice. Adoption needs awareness, capacity building and supporting policy.


## 1. Background

Rice–wheat covers 9.2 Mha in India, mainly in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. Rice is puddled and transplanted, wheat follows after intensive tillage, and the short gap between them delays wheat: sowing after 15 November loses about 32 kg/ha a day (p. 4). Agriculture causes about 16% of India's GHG emissions; methane from livestock (38.9%) and rice (36.9%) dominates (p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To summarise the status and challenges of the rice–wheat system in north-west India and review precision and sustainable intensification options for productivity, profitability and sustainability.


## 3. What the authors did

A narrative review of studies and official statistics on soil health, groundwater, residue burning, costs, labour, emissions and weeds, and on direct-seeded rice, zero tillage, residue retention, diversification and nutrient management.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Key figures reported in the review Item Value Groundwater fall, Punjab (2000–2019) 8.91 m Over-exploited blocks: Punjab / Haryana 80% / 61% Paddy straw burned, Punjab + Haryana (2018)


### 11.3 Mt of 28.1 Mt (40%)

DDSR water / labour saving 11–18% / 11–66% Methane: puddled vs DDSR (Punjab) 0.8–1.9 vs 0.1–0.3 t CO₂e/ha Total GWP: transplanted vs DDSR 2.91 vs 1.94 t/ha

- Weeds can cut DDSR yields by 50–90% if not controlled.
- A 7-year Haryana study found DDSR–zero-till wheat cost USD 448/ha vs USD 555/ha for the conventional system.
- Satellite data show fire events in UP fell 24% in 2018 vs 2017 and 32% vs 2016. CORRECTION TO EARLIER NOTES The '>90% less methane and 20% lower GWP' applies to dry seeding of rice in moist soil, not to conservation practices in general. The review's own cited data give about one-third lower GWP (1.94 vs 2.91 t/ha) and 82–87% lower methane (Gupta et al. 2016).

## 5. Conclusions

1. The rice–wheat system faces soil, water, air and climate problems. 2. Many intensification technologies cut irrigation, labour, tillage and straw burning. 3. Awareness, capacity building and matching policy must come first for adoption.


## 6. Limitations

- A narrative review: values come from different studies, years and places.
- Focus on mechanised Punjab and Haryana, not eastern UP.
- Methane and GWP reductions are cited, not measured by the authors.

More than 80% of rice straw in the region is burned because it has little value and the window before wheat is short. Residues influence soil phosphorus availability, but P advice under long-term residue management was lacking (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To study how long-term crop residue management interacts with phosphorus levels to affect wheat productivity, P requirement and soil health.


## 3. What the authors did

Six residue and tillage practices (T1–T6) established in 2008 formed the main plots. After 11 years, three P levels (0, 30, 60 kg P₂O₅/ha) were added as sub-plots for 2019–20 and 2020–21. Soil physical, chemical and biological properties and wheat yield were measured (Table 2).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Wheat grain yield, pooled 2 years (t/ha), Table 6 Practice 0 kg P 30 kg P 60 kg P T1 residue removed, zero till 4.62 5.25 5.77 T2 residue removed, conventional 4.76 5.34 5.84 T3 rice straw, conventional 5.56 5.95 6.03 T4 rice straw, zero till 5.60 6.01 6.08 T5 both straws, zero till 6.10 6.22 6.26 T6 partial burning 5.04 5.65 5.87

- T5 had the lowest bulk density (1.34 g/cm³), highest infiltration (2.2 cm/h) and most large aggregates (Table 3).
- Fungi, actinobacteria, bacteria and enzyme activity were highest in T5 and lowest with burning or removal (Table 4).
- P level did not significantly change SOC, available N or K. DATA CHECK The abstract reports SOC of 0.80% (+73.9%) for retained residues, but the text gives +38.7% and +42.5% versus T1 and T2. The abstract also says the highest yields came from 60 kg P without residue, which Table 6 does not show. Use Table 6 values.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Residue retention or incorporation improves soil physical, chemical and biological properties. 2. With rice residue alone, half the recommended P (30 kg) gave yield equal to the full dose. 3. With both residues retained, no P fertiliser was needed; P doses should be adjusted to residue practice.


## 6. Limitations

- One sandy loam site in Punjab; only two seasons of the P study.
- No greenhouse gas or SOC stock measurements.
- Several abstract and text figures conflict with the tables.

#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Rice residue management alternatives in rice– wheat cropping system: impact on wheat productivity, soil organic carbon, water and microbial dynamics S. Korav, D. B. Yadav, A. Yadav … E. A. Mahmoud (8 authors; full list in the citation)

**Authors:**
Santosh Korav, Dharam Bir Yadav, Ashok Yadav, G. A. Rajanna, Jagdish Parshad, Sridevi Tallapragada, Hosam O. Elansary, Eman A. Mahmoud

**Journal:**
Scientific Reports, vol. 14, article 1822 (2024) Site CCS Haryana Agricultural University Regional Research Station, Karnal (sandy loam)

**Paper type:**
Research article: two-year field experiment

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-52319-6

**Cite as:**
Korav, S., Yadav, D. B., Yadav, A., Rajanna, G. A., Parshad, J., Tallapragada, S., Elansary, H. O., & Mahmoud, E. A. (2024). Rice residue management alternatives in rice–wheat cropping system: impact on wheat productivity, soil organic carbon, water and microbial dynamics. Scientific Reports, 14, 1822. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024- 52319-6 Open access, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Over two wheat seasons at Karnal, zero-till wheat sown with a Happy Seeder into full rice residue raised soil microbes (47.9–60.4% at harvest), soil moisture (13.4–23.6%) and grain yield (9.8–11.3%) compared with burning or removing the straw. Final SOC reached 0.42% (from 0.35%) under Happy Seeder, against 0.32–0.33% with burning or removal. Zero-till options had the lowest costs, with net returns of ₹43,160– 57,080/ha and B:C of 1.52–1.70.


## 1. Background

The north-west IGP rice–wheat system covers 4.1 Mha and produces about 34 Mt of rice residue. Combine harvesting leaves loose straw, and the window before wheat sowing is short, so farmers burn it, harming soil microbes and organic matter (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To assess how Happy Seeder-based and other rice residue options affect soil microbes, enzymes, organic carbon, moisture and wheat productivity in sandy loam soils of Haryana.


## 3. What the authors did

Ten treatments were tested in 2018–19 and 2019–20: conventional wheat after burning, removal or incorporation, and zero-till wheat with anchored stubble, partial or full burning, or full residue sown by

Happy Seeder (Table 1). Soil (0–15 cm) was analysed for microbes, enzymes, pH, SOC and moisture; yield and economics were recorded.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Soil organic carbon (%), Table 3 Treatment Initial Final T1 conventional, after full burning 0.34 0.33 T2 conventional, after removal 0.34 0.32 T3 zero till, anchored stubble 0.35 0.38 T6 Happy Seeder, full residue 0.35 0.42 T7 Happy Seeder after chopper and spreader 0.34 0.41 T9 chopper, spreader and rotavator 0.34 0.40

- Happy Seeder after chopper and spreader raised microbial counts 23.7–38.3% at 75 days and 47.9– 60.4% at harvest over burning and removal.
- Grain yield rose 9.8–11.3% and biomass 7.4–9.6% over burning and removal.
- Soil pH fell slightly, from 7.49 to 7.27, under residue retention.
- Zero-till options (partial residue and Happy Seeder full residue) had the lowest costs and the highest net return and B:C. CORRECTION TO EARLIER NOTES The '0.36–0.42% increase in organic carbon' is the final SOC level in zero-till plots, not an increase. The gain over conventional wheat without residue is about 0.03–0.10 percentage points.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Planting method and residue management strongly affect soil microbes, SOC and enzyme activity. 2. Zero-till wheat with Happy Seeder in full residue gives higher yield and soil health than burning. 3. Rice residue should be managed by sowing wheat with suitable zero-till machinery.


## 6. Limitations

- One site and two seasons.
- No greenhouse gas measurements; SOC is a concentration only.
- Yields are given in a figure, not a table.

#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT
