**Authors:**
C. P. Nath, Asik Dutta, K. K. Hazra, C. S. Praharaj, Narendra Kumar, S. S. Singh, Ummed Singh, Krishnashis Das

**Journal:**
Scientific Reports, vol. 13, article 6508 (2023) Site ICAR-Indian Institute of Pulses Research, Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh

**Paper type:**
Research article: long-term field experiment (since 2003)

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-33255-3

**Cite as:**
Nath, C. P., Dutta, A., Hazra, K. K., Praharaj, C. S., Kumar, N., Singh, S. S., Singh, U., & Das, K. (2023). Long-term impact of pulses and organic amendments inclusion in cropping system on soil physical and chemical properties. Scientific Reports, 13, 6508. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-33255-3 Open access, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

In a long-term trial at Kanpur, UP (started 2003, soil sampled in 2017), adding pulses to maize–wheat improved porosity, water holding, available nutrients and aggregates. SOC at 0–20 cm was 4.33 g/kg under pigeonpea–wheat vs 3.82 under maize–wheat (from 2.8 at the start), a 10–18% rotation effect. Integrated nutrient management with FYM raised SOC a further 11–18%. Adding mungbean raised maize and wheat yields by 26% and 21% in 2015–16.


## 1. Background

Maize–wheat mono-cropping, tillage and continuous chemical fertiliser have degraded IGP soils. Rice– wheat (9.64 Mha) and maize–wheat (1.83 Mha) dominate the region. Pulses and organic amendments may restore soil properties (p. 1).


## 2. Aim of the study

To evaluate the long-term impact of pulse-based rotations with integrated nutrient management on soil physical and chemical properties, and their links with yield and its sustainability.


## 3. What the authors did

Four rotations (M–W, M–W–Mb, M–W–M–C, P–W) were combined with three fertility levels (control, RDF 120:60:40 for cereals, INM with FYM and residue) in a split-plot design with three replications at IIPR Kanpur. Soil at 0–20 and 20–40 cm was sampled after 14 years (April 2017).


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Soil organic carbon at 0–20 cm (g/kg), Table 3 Rotation or fertility SOC Change Maize–wheat (M–W) 3.82 baseline Maize–wheat–mungbean 4.19 +10% Maize–wheat–maize–chickpea 4.22 +10% Pigeonpea–wheat 4.33 +13% RDF (fertiliser only) 3.91 baseline INM (fertiliser + FYM + residue) 4.64 +19%

- P–W and M–W–Mb raised porosity 7–9% and volume expansion 9–25%; P–W raised water holding capacity 10%.
- Available P rose 42–73% and K 8–16% in pulse systems at 0–20 cm.
- Carbon input over 13 years was 96.0 (P–W), 95.3 (M–W–Mb), 91.3 (M–W–M–C) and 72.4 (M–W) Mg C/ha.
- M–W–Mb raised maize yield 26% and wheat 21% in 2015–16, and 23% and 8% in the 14th cycle. CORRECTION TO EARLIER NOTES The '25–50% SOC increase' from the abstract compares particular rotation–fertility plots with M–W under RDF. The rotation effect alone is 10–18%; INM adds 11–18% over RDF.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Including pulses improves soil physical and chemical properties over cereal–cereal systems. 2. INM with FYM and residue works best with pulse rotations. 3. Pigeonpea–wheat gave the highest sustainable yield index for wheat.


## 6. Limitations

- One research station; not farmers' fields.
- SOC as concentration; no stocks or sequestration rates.
- No greenhouse gas measurements.

**Authors:**

**Journal:**
Current Science, vol. 120, no. 6, pp. 1083–1088 (25 March 2021) Site Farmers' agroforestry, Dhanauri range, Haridwar, Uttarakhand

**Paper type:**
Research communication: destructive biomass sampling

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.18520/cs/v120/i6/1083-1088

**Cite as:**
Kumar, A., Tewari, S., Singh, H., Kumar, P., Kumar, N., Bisht, S., Devi, S., Nidhi, & Kaushal, R. (2021). Biomass accumulation and carbon stock in different agroforestry systems prevalent in the Himalayan foothills, India. Current Science, 120(6), 1083– 1088. https://doi.org/10.18520/cs/v120/i6/1083-1088 Published by Current Science Association. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper for study notes.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Eight tree species planted at 4 × 4 m in 2007 with wheat were sampled destructively in the Himalayan foothills. Eucalyptus stored the most carbon in trees (43.85 Mg C/ha, 160.5 Mg CO₂/ha) and soil (37.5 Mg C/ha to 30 cm), followed by poplar (41.33 and 30.75). Tree carbon ranged from 30.0 to 43.85 Mg C/ha. Stems held 77–81% of tree biomass. Several abstract figures (leaf and root leaders, 45.33 Mg C/ha) conflict with the tables, so table values are used here.


## 1. Background

Agroforestry stores much more carbon than sole cropping; India's average potential is cited as 25 t C/ha over 96 Mha. Little was known about carbon in each tree component and in intercrops (p. 1083).


## 2. Aim of the study

To quantify the biomass of each component of agroforestry systems and the carbon stock in biomass and soil.


## 3. What the authors did

Three trees of each of eight species (Populus deltoides, Toona ciliata, Eucalyptus tereticornis, Albizia procera, Melia azedarach, Terminalia bellirica, Anthocephalus cadamba, Sapindus mukorosi) were felled, separated and weighed, with roots dug out. Wheat biomass and soil carbon (0–30 cm) were measured, and data were analysed by ANOVA.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Carbon density (Mg C/ha), Table 4 System Trees Wheat Soil Eucalyptus tereticornis 43.85 3.34 37.50 Populus deltoides 41.33 3.59 30.75 Toona ciliata 37.53 3.11 25.93 Anthocephalus cadamba 35.70 3.14 24.41 Albizia procera 33.08 3.07 26.56 Terminalia bellirica 30.00 3.65 26.53

- Eucalyptus had the highest stem (69.43 Mg/ha) and leaf (2.85 Mg/ha) biomass; poplar the highest branch biomass (5.04 Mg/ha).
- CO₂ mitigation by trees ranged from 109.8 (Terminalia) to 160.5 Mg CO₂/ha (eucalyptus).
- Wheat biomass was highest under poplar (11.85 Mg/ha) and lowest under Melia (9.59 Mg/ha). CORRECTIONS TO EARLIER NOTES Leaf biomass was highest in eucalyptus, not poplar. Albizia's 'highest root biomass' (14.01 Mg/ha) is inconsistent with its total and root carbon. Stems were 77–81% of tree biomass; the '~50%' is a value cited from other studies.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Biomass and carbon are concentrated in the stem, then root, branch and leaf. 2. Eucalyptus and poplar systems store the most carbon in trees and soil. 3. Trees on farmland with crops suit biomass production and carbon storage.


## 6. Limitations

- Himalayan foothills, not the Gangetic plain; one tree age.
- Only three trees per species; no treeless control for soil carbon.
- Abstract and text figures conflict with the tables in several places.

To assess biomass, carbon stock and carbon sequestration potential of prominent agroforestry systems in south Kashmir for climate change mitigation.


## 3. What the authors did

Multistage random sampling chose six tehsils, one block each, four villages per block and ten farmers per village (240 farmers, 25% intensity). Tree biomass came from diameter and height equations; fruit trees, crops and grasses were estimated separately. Carbon = 0.45 × biomass and CO₂e = C × 3.67.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Biomass and carbon by system (t/ha), Tables 2–4 System Total biomass Carbon stock CO₂e Horti-silvipasture 66.55 29.94 ≈110* Agri-horti-silviculture 50.18 22.56 82.8 Horti-agriculture 36.22 16.28 59.83 Boundary plantation 34.87 15.67 57.58 *Tree 92.04 + crop 17.93 t CO₂e/ha from Table 4; the total cell was not legible in the PDF.

- Fruit trees gave 45.86%, forest trees 37.83% and crops 16.29% of horti-silvipasture biomass.
- Boundary plantations had the highest crop biomass (15.54 t/ha) and lowest tree biomass (19.3 t/ha).
- Carbon stock and CO₂e follow biomass, since both are fixed multiples of it. DATA CHECK The text gives 38.82 t C/ha tree carbon for agri-horti-silviculture, but Table 3's parts sum to about 17.5. The study altitude is printed as 2,900–5,900 m. Use the Table 3 totals.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Agroforestry systems differ significantly in biomass and carbon. 2. Horti-silvipasture stores the most carbon; boundary plantation the least. 3. Agroforestry supports climate mitigation and farm income.


## 6. Limitations

- Temperate, apple-based Kashmir systems; one survey year.
- Default 0.45 carbon fraction; no soil carbon measured.
- 'Sequestration potential' is a stock, not an annual rate.

**Authors:**
Sachin Kumar, Sandeep Kumar, Vinod Prasad Khanduri, Bhupendra Singh, Reena Joshi, Manoj Kumar Riyal, Deepa Rawat, Kewat Sanjay Kumar

**Journal:**
Carbon Research, vol. 4, article 6 (2025) Site Nine villages, Uttarkashi district, Garhwal Himalaya, Uttarakhand

**Paper type:**
Original article: field survey and measurements

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1007/s44246-024-00158-5

**Cite as:**
Kumar, S., Kumar, S., Khanduri, V. P., Singh, B., Joshi, R., Riyal, M. K., Rawat, D., & Kumar, K. S. (2025). Tree diversity, carbon sequestration and production potential of Oryza sativa L. in traditional agroforestry systems of Garhwal Himalaya, India. Carbon Research, 4, 6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44246-024-00158-5 Open access, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Traditional rice-based agroforestry was surveyed in nine Uttarkashi villages across three elevation bands. Tree carbon rose from 30.49 to 34.43 Mg C/ha with elevation, and net tree sequestration reached about


### 9.13 Mg CO₂e/ha/yr. Soils under trees had higher SOC and lower bulk density than sole rice. But rice

grain yield was 14–17% lower under trees at every elevation, so carbon gains come with a food trade-off.


## 1. Background

Agroforestry offers social and ecological benefits, and traditional systems are common in the Garhwal Himalaya. Their carbon, soil and crop effects across elevations were not well known.


## 2. Aim of the study

To evaluate tree diversity, carbon sequestration, soil carbon, oxygen production and rice productivity under traditional agroforestry at different elevations.


## 3. What the authors did

Three villages in each of three elevation bands (800–1200, 1200–1600, 1600–2000 m) were sampled with 0.04 ha quadrats. Tree carbon = biomass × 0.50; yearly sequestration = CO₂e divided by tree age reported by farmers. Soil was sampled at three depths, and rice yield was measured in 1 × 1 m plots in agroforestry and sole rice fields.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Tree carbon and rice grain yield by elevation Elevation Tree carbon (Mg C/ha) Rice, agroforestry (q/ha) Rice, sole (q/ha) 800–1200 m 30.49 17.49 21.05 1200–1600 m 33.80 16.63 19.31 1600–2000 m 34.43 11.48 13.71

- Tree diversity was highest at 1200–1600 m (Shannon 1.29, Simpson 0.69).
- Total oxygen production was highest at 1600–2000 m (91.79 Mg/ha).
- SOC reached 3.67% under agroforestry vs 2.73% in sole rice (upper band, 0–15 cm).
- Agroforestry soils had lower bulk density and higher pH. NOTE ON THE NUMBERS The 34.43 Mg/ha is carbon in trees only, not soil. Table 2 prints the above-ground total as 24.71, but the text gives 26.71, which is the value that sums to 34.43.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Tree density, diversity, carbon and oxygen vary with elevation. 2. Traditional agroforestry improves soil carbon and structure. 3. Rice yield is lower under trees, so management must balance ecological and economic needs.


## 6. Limitations

- Hill terraces with different species from the plains.
- Tree ages, used for yearly rates, came from farmers' recall.
- One season of rice yield.

# Agricultural emissions reduction potential by improving technical efficiency in crop production


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

Agricultural emissions reduction potential by improving technical efficiency in crop production A. Khatri-Chhetri, T. B. Sapkota, S. Maharjan, N. C. Konath, P. Shirsath

**Authors:**
Arun Khatri-Chhetri, Tek B. Sapkota, Sofina Maharjan, Noufa Cheerakkollil Konath, Paresh Shirsath

**Journal:**
Agricultural Systems, vol. 207, article 103620 (2023)

**Dates:**
Received 20 July 2022 · Accepted 20 February 2023 · Online 16 March 2023

**Paper type:**
Research article: survey data, efficiency and emission modelling

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agsy.2023.103620

**Cite as:**
Khatri-Chhetri, A., Sapkota, T. B., Maharjan, S., Konath, N. C., & Shirsath, P. (2023). Agricultural emissions reduction potential by improving technical efficiency in crop production. Agricultural Systems, 207, 103620. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agsy.2023.103620 Open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Using 2017–18 plot data for about 10,700 rice and 5,200 wheat plots across India, the authors estimated emissions with CCAFS-MOT and efficiency with a stochastic frontier. Mean technical efficiency was 0.83 in rice and 0.77 in wheat. Higher efficiency lowered emissions per kg of grain but not total emissions per hectare. Many smallholders were both efficient and low-emitting. In Uttar Pradesh, efficiency was 0.807 for rice and 0.780 for wheat.


## 1. Background

Agricultural policy tends to push new technology rather than better use of existing technology. India ranks third globally in agricultural emissions, and small and marginal farmers are 86% of all farmers (p. 2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To assess how technical efficiency relates to GHG emissions, testing whether better efficiency reduces crop emissions.


## 3. What the authors did

Plot-level data from the 2017–18 Cost of Cultivation Survey (18 rice and 13 wheat states) were combined with soil, climate and water-regime data. CCAFS-MOT estimated GWP and emission intensity; a translog stochastic frontier estimated efficiency and its drivers.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Efficiency and emission groups Measure Rice Wheat Mean technical efficiency 0.83 0.77 Plots below average efficiency >40% ≈25% High efficiency, low emission intensity 39% 43% High efficiency, low GWP 46% 40% Low efficiency, high emission intensity 11% 16% Uttar Pradesh mean efficiency 0.807 0.780

- Machinery, irrigation and improved seed reduced inefficiency in rice; irrigation and seed mattered most in wheat.
- Large farms with high efficiency had high emissions per hectare from mechanisation, frequent irrigation and more fertiliser.
- Smallholders (<1 ha) often combined high efficiency with low emissions. CORRECTION TO EARLIER NOTES The 17% and 23% are efficiency gaps (0.17 and 0.23), not output gains. Reaching the frontier would raise output by about 1/TE − 1, roughly 20% for rice and 30% for wheat.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Better use of existing technology can cut emissions per unit of food. 2. Total emissions per hectare may not fall as efficiency rises. 3. Farming practices, not farm size, mainly drive efficiency and emissions.


## 6. Limitations

- Emissions are modelled with CCAFS-MOT, not measured.
- Cross-sectional, one survey year (2017–18).
- Farm-size results (Table 4) are given only as an image.

# The 2019 methane budget and uncertainties at 1° resolution and each country through Bayesian integration Of GOSAT total column methane data and a priori inventory estimates


#### SIMPLIFIED REPORT

The 2019 methane budget and uncertainties at 1° resolution and each country through Bayesian integration Of GOSAT total column methane data and a priori inventory estimates J. R. Worden, D. H. Cusworth, Z. Qu … D. J. Jacob (13 authors; full list in the citation)

**Authors:**
John R. Worden, Daniel H. Cusworth, Zhen Qu, Yi Yin, Yuzhong Zhang, A. Anthony Bloom, Shuang Ma, Brendan K. Byrne, Tia Scarpelli, Joannes D. Maasakkers, David Crisp, Riley Duren, Daniel J. Jacob

**Journal:**
Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, vol. 22, pp. 6811–6841 (2022)

**Dates:**
Received 16 November 2021 · Accepted 1 May 2022 · Published 25 May 2022

**Paper type:**
Research article: satellite-based inversion

**DOI:**
https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-22-6811-2022

**Cite as:**
Worden, J. R., Cusworth, D. H., Qu, Z., Yin, Y., Zhang, Y., Bloom, A. A., Ma, S., Byrne, B. K., Scarpelli, T., Maasakkers, J. D., Crisp, D., Duren, R., & Jacob, D. J. (2022). The 2019 methane budget and uncertainties at 1° resolution and each country through Bayesian integration Of GOSAT total column methane data and a priori inventory estimates. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 22, 6811–6841. https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-22- 6811-2022 Open access under CC BY 4.0. Figures in this summary are taken from the paper.


#### IN ONE PARAGRAPH

The authors used GOSAT satellite methane data with the GEOS-Chem model to estimate 2019 emissions by sector at 1° and for each country. Agriculture and waste gave 263 ± 24 Tg CH₄/yr, fossil fuels 82 ± 12 and wetlands/aquatic 180 ± 10. For India, the satellite estimate of human emissions was 39.5 Tg CH₄/yr against 24.5 in the inventory, mostly from livestock. The authors treat such gaps as a starting point for research, since satellite estimates may have systematic errors.


## 1. Background

Methane is the second most important human greenhouse gas and has a lifetime of about 9 years. The Paris Agreement global stocktake (from 2023) relies on bottom-up inventories, which can carry large uncertainties (pp. 1–2).


## 2. Aim of the study

To show how satellite data can test and update sector and country methane emissions for the global stocktake.


## 3. What the authors did

Optimal estimation turned GOSAT total-column CH₄ into fluxes using GEOS-Chem. A new Bayesian method projected fluxes to sectors at 1° and to countries, with uncertainty and degrees of freedom for signal (DOFS). Prior swapping tested inventories with larger aquatic and fossil emissions.


## 4. Main findings

Table A. Global emissions by sector, 2019 (Tg CH₄/yr, Table 1) Sector Prior Satellite (posterior) Wetlands/aquatic 199.8 ± 52.8 179.8 ± 10.0 Livestock 87.6 ± 17.2 146.1 ± 10.3 Rice 36.9 ± 12.9 67.6 ± 6.8 Waste 57.7 ± 11.9 49.6 ± 7.1 Oil + gas + coal 97.5 82.1 Total 526 ± 128 561 ± 52 Table B. India, top-down vs inventory (Tg CH₄/yr, Table A1) Sector Satellite Inventory Livestock 23.9 ± 2.0 13.0 ± 4.1 Rice 6.3 ± 1.6 5.9 ± 1.7 Waste 6.8 ± 1.2 3.7 ± 1.3 Total anthropogenic 39.5 24.5

- About 57 countries are resolved (DOFS > 1); India's DOFS is 20.8.
- Brazil, China, India, Russia and the USA emit about half of human methane.
- Swapping priors had little effect, so results come from the observations. CORRECTION TO EARLIER NOTES Earlier notes gave no India values. The paper's Table A1 gives India 39.5 Tg CH₄/yr from the satellite vs 24.5 in the inventory, mostly livestock (23.9 vs 13.0). The authors present gaps like this as a starting point for research, not proof that inventories are wrong.

## 5. Conclusions

1. Satellite estimates can differ substantially (within uncertainty) from inventories. 2. The Bayesian method lets other priors be tested easily. 3. Higher-resolution satellites can cut uncertainty further.


## 6. Limitations

- Possible systematic errors in satellite data and model transport.
- Rice, waste and livestock signals overlap in India.
- 1° resolution and a single year (2019).
